At deployment, this learned model scores unseen videos quickly, promoting underexposed high-quality content. The soundness lies in bootstrapping quality judgment from external knowledge and then distilling it into a learnable model, breaking the dependency on sparse behavioral feedback.
DTransKT: A Dual Transferable Knowledge Tracing Framework for Cross-Disciplinary Self-AdaptationWWW
uses Trace how knowledge evolves as students answer questions, using skill matching and semantic extraction to apply learning across subjects.
why it works Students transfer knowledge from one subject to another when underlying skills are the same; matching student patterns across subjects and extracting semantic skill definitions reveals the transferable core that generalizes.
the deeper reason
Teaching a student knowledge model from one discipline must work across different subjects because core cognitive skills (memorization, understanding, reasoning) generalize, but the specific knowledge structure and terminology differ widely. The method separates student ability from subject content by using a cross-disciplinary graph to identify meta-skills—patterns in how students learn that persist across domains—and aligning these patterns across subjects. Simultaneously, a pre-trained language model extracts semantic relationships from course materials, surfacing conceptual connections that transcend terminology differences. This two-pronged approach works because human learning has both universal properties (how memory fades, how mastery compounds) and domain-specific properties (what concepts are foundational in math versus biology). By explicitly extracting and aligning the universal aspects while incorporating domain semantics, the model learns to transfer the former while respecting the latter, achieving the reported 14% improvement in accuracy across subjects.
VecFormer: Towards Efficient and Generalizable Graph Transformer with Graph Token AttentionWWW
uses Compress nodes and graph structure into discrete codes in a first stage, then perform focus at the level of these codes rather than individual nodes, reducing computation while improving generalization.
why it works Works because nodes within a code cluster are similar, so focus between clusters captures the essential relationships while filtering noise from individual node variation. Discrete codes create a bottleneck that forces the model to learn robust semantic groups, making predictions stable when test data differs from training.
the deeper reason
Graph learned language systems grow computationally expensive as graphs grow because focus considers all pairs of nodes. VecFormer solves this by replacing node-level reasoning with graph-level words reasoning: it first quantizes node features and the graph structure using learned codebooks (similar to discrete dictionary compression), converting the graph into a compact set of symbolic words. focus then operates on these words rather than raw nodes, slashing computational complexity. The mathematical guarantee comes from quantization: a codebook compresses many nodes into a few representative codes, preserving semantic structure while discarding noise. By learning two codebooks jointly—one for features, one for structure—the method captures both what nodes are and how they relate. Out-of-distribution generalization improves because the learned codes represent core semantic types rather than specific node instances, so transfer to new graphs is natural. Working at the words level decouples the model size from input graph size, making scaling tractable while improving robustness.
Egocentric Co-Pilot: Web-Native Smart-Glasses Agents for Assistive Egocentric AIWWW
uses Answer questions from continuous egocentric video by compressing long context into hierarchical summaries, combining speech and gaze into structured commands, and orchestrating specialized tools via reasoning.
why it works Works because a human's first-person experience spans minutes or hours but a single reasoning step fits a much shorter window. Hierarchical compression summarizes the long past while keeping important details, and tool orchestration lets weak individual signals (noisy speech, gaze drift) combine through reasoning to yield reliable decisions.
the deeper reason
Continuous first-person egocentric video from smart glasses far exceeds any model's context window, making long-horizon reasoning impossible with vanilla approaches. Egocentric Co-Pilot uses Temporal Chain-of-Thought to break long questions into reasoning steps over time, then compresses context hierarchically: each time window is summarized, summaries are compressed further, building a pyramid that fits in memory. This layered abstraction works because visual reasoning about daily tasks has natural structure—moments nest into scenes (making coffee), scenes nest into activities (morning routine), activities nest into goals (get to work)—so hierarchical compression preserves decision-relevant details while discarding redundancy. By distilling continuous video into compact semantic levels, the model reasons about hours of footage within the learned language systems's limits. The lightweight multimodal intent layer then turns raw speech and gaze into actionable tool commands without requiring a heavy unified model for each sense. This web-native architecture (streaming via WebRTC, orchestrated by an AI language systems) guarantees that glasses remain always-on and responsive by offloading heavy reasoning to the cloud while keeping perception local. This design makes assistive AI practical for everyday smart-glasses use.
Netting Phish in the IPFS Ocean: Real-Time Monitoring and Characterization of Decentralized Phishing CampaignsWWW
uses Clusters phishing URLs by similarity, ranks their dissemination leverage across decentralized gateways, and estimates impact of blocking small dominant clusters.
why it works It works because real-world attacks concentrate: blocking the few most-used dissemination channels removes availability for most phishing content. Clustering by behavior finds which attacks are coordinated variants of the same campaign, so you target root causes instead of chasing copies.
the deeper reason
Phishing detection on decentralized networks like IPFS fails with traditional methods because attackers exploit the architecture's resilience: content persists even after sources go offline, and multiple gateway caches amplify availability. The approach monitors what actually happens across the network by collecting data from multiple vantage points—IPFS traffic and DNS records—then groups detected phishing by content hash and campaign pattern. This works because clustering attacks reveals that a small number of coordinated campaigns generate most malicious content, making targeted mitigation against these dominant clusters far more efficient than generic blacklisting. The underlying principle is that real attacks concentrate effort, leaving detectable structural signatures in aggregated network data.
Linguistic Signatures for Enhanced Emotion DetectionWWW
uses Extracts measurable linguistic patterns from emotion datasets and adds them as features to neural models to boost emotion classification accuracy.
why it works It works because humans recognize emotion partly through specific word choices and grammar patterns that reliably appear together. Adding these explicit signals lets the model see what matters faster and stays robust when the neural patterns encounter new data.
the deeper reason
Emotion detection in text relies on statistical patterns in how emotions are expressed—certain word choices, grammar patterns, and punctuation correlate with specific emotions across datasets. The method extracts these recurring linguistic signatures (like increased exclamation marks for joy) as explicit features alongside learned representations. This works because human language follows regularities: emotions manifest through predictable linguistic habits. By making these patterns explicit rather than leaving them implicit, the model gains an interpretable signal that focuses focus on reliable cues, complementing abstract learned patterns. The principle is that redundancy between engineered signals and learned patterns improves robustness by forcing consistency across complementary evidence sources.
CGPT: Cluster-Guided Partial Tables with LLM-Generated Supervision for Table RetrievalWWW
uses Groups table instances into clusters, generates synthetic query examples for partial tables across clusters, and adjust numeric fingerprints models using hard-negative contrastive pairs.
why it works It works because diverse training examples teach the model to handle semantic variation. Grouping tables ensures you see the full semantic range. Hard-negative pairs force the model to push apart genuinely different cases, so it learns precise, robust distance metrics for table-query matching.
the deeper reason
numeric fingerprints models struggle with table retrieval because tables compress multiple meanings into structured cells, causing semantic collapse compared to free text. The method generates synthetic queries via an AI language systems for carefully constructed partial tables, using these pairs to adjust numeric fingerprints through contrastive learning. Partial tables are sampled across K-means clusters to ensure semantic diversity, avoiding redundant synthetic queries on similar table subsets. This works because diverse positive examples force the numeric fingerprints model to separate similar tables into distinct regions of the space—each cluster anchor represents a different semantic meaning. The combination of structural sampling plus synthetic supervision grounds the numeric fingerprints space in realistic query-table alignments rather than arbitrary text similarity.
VisionST: Coordinating Cross-modal Traffic Prediction with Interactive Geo-image EncodingWWW
uses Extracts visual patterns from satellite imagery and combines them with spatial and temporal patterns to jointly score traffic predictions node by node.
why it works It works because real traffic depends on overlapping factors: road layout, weather, events, congestion. Treating each modality separately loses their interactions; combining visual context with spatial neighbors and time history captures the full cause, so predictions account for all factors simultaneously.
the deeper reason
Traffic patterns are shaped by multiple factors—road geometry, weather, events—visible in satellite imagery alongside historical flows. The core challenge is fusing these modalities without letting one dominate. The method extracts visual semantic words and relation patterns from geo-images while simultaneously computing spatial-temporal relations from traffic data, then uses a pattern-guided aggregator to weight each modality's contribution based on local context. This works because traffic prediction is heterogeneous: some locations are purely spatial (highway merges), others strongly seasonal (office districts), others event-sensitive (stadiums). By learning which modality matters where, rather than applying fixed weights, the model exploits the principle that prediction accuracy comes from adaptive fusion—the most relevant signal per location, not universal signal importance.
Tabular Foundation Models are Strong Graph Anomaly DetectorsWWW
uses Converts graph anomaly detection into a tabular problem by enriching node features with structural summaries, then applies pre-trained tabular models for cross-domain generalization.
why it works It works because tabular models already solve the hard parts: handling diverse feature types and generalizing to new domains via synthetic pre-training. Structure itself is just another feature; once you express it as numbers alongside node attributes, tabular models see it naturally and transfer across graphs.
the deeper reason
General graph anomaly detection methods fail across domains due to structural and feature heterogeneity, requiring retraining per dataset. The insight is that tabular foundation models already solve the core challenges: handling diverse feature types, generalizing without retraining via in-context learning, and learning from scarce labels through synthetic pre-training. The gap is structural—graphs require topology reasoning, but tables do not. By flattening graphs into augmented feature tables that include Laplacian features and structural aggregations alongside raw node attributes, the method translates structural information into tabular form. This works because the flattened representation preserves structural distinctions: anomalies manifest as atypical combinations of structural and feature values, which the tabular model can recognize via its pre-trained feature reasoning.
DeepSVU: Towards In-depth Security-oriented Video Understanding via Unified Physical-world Regularized MoEWWW
uses Learns multi-scale features of human behavior, objects, and background context from video, then adaptively weights them to predict threat location and explain threat causes.
why it works It works because threats arise from interactions of multiple elements: a person's action, an object involved, and the setting all matter. Modeling each scale separately captures these interactions. Adaptive weighting lets the model emphasize whichever factor most strongly signals the specific threat occurring.
the deeper reason
Security-oriented video understanding must identify not just what threats occur but why they happen—attributing root causes across human behavior, object interactions, and scene context. Different scenarios prioritize different factors: a robbery cause differs from a shooting's cause. The method uses a mixture-of-experts architecture keeping it simple by physical-world constraints: each expert specializes in one type of factor (behavior, interactions, context), and a gating mechanism learns to weight them adaptively per scenario. This works because security threats arise from coordinated multi-factor breakdowns, not single causes. By maintaining interpretable specialists and forcing trade-offs between factors through keeping it simple, the model avoids false attributions—it learns which combinations of factors actually indicate specific threats rather than overfitting to incidental correlations in limited labeled video.
Online Advertising with Spatial InteractionsWWW
uses Decide which ads to show where on screen by ranking options while accounting for how nearby ads hurt each other's effectiveness.
why it works Ad value depends on location and neighbors; treating slots as points in space and modeling interference as proximity-based lets you reason about the actual value trade-offs before assigning ads.
the deeper reason
Ad placement allocation must balance the bidder's payment with reduced value when neighboring ads compete for focus. The method models slot value as a bid multiplied by a discount from nearby ads, making allocation an optimization problem. This is mathematically sound for the nearest-neighbor model because the discount depends only on distance to the closest competitor—a property that makes ranking-based algorithms work. The monotonicity of the allocation rule (higher bids get better slots) is preserved, and truthfulness is guaranteed because bidders cannot gain by lying about their value when positions are allocated by the proven monotone rule.
A Unified Framework for Context-Aware and Relation-Aware Graph Retrieval-Augmented GenerationWWW
uses Build hierarchical graph summaries that fuse both chunk context and entity relationships, then retrieve by searching all abstraction levels.
why it works It works because fusing context and relationships into summaries creates richer intermediate representations; searching multiple levels exploits how users reason at different scales, from details to overviews to themes.
the deeper reason
HyGRAG improves retrieval-augmented generation by building a hierarchical graph where related information is summarized at multiple levels of abstraction. The method works because summarization preserves the core meaning while compressing representation, so searching at higher abstraction levels is faster and captures relationships that chunk-level search alone would miss. When clusters of related content are summarized together, that summary fuses contextual and relational information in a single readable unit. During retrieval, searching across all abstraction levels means rare or deeply buried knowledge can still be found via its high-level category, not just shallow text similarity, and community membership allows expansion to logically linked content the similarity search never reached.
Acting Flatterers via LLMs Sycophancy: Combating Clickbait with LLMs Opposing-Stance ReasoningWWW
uses Generate opposing reasoning pairs (agree and disagree) for headlines, then train a detector using contrastive learning on the reasoning to spot clickbait.
why it works It works because forcing the model to reason from both sides reveals cracks in the clickbait framing; comparing how agree and disagree reasoning differ highlights exaggeration and manipulation that single-sided reasoning would miss.
the deeper reason
SORG generates pairs of opposing arguments (agree and disagree) about whether a news headline is clickbait, then trains a smaller model to use both perspectives as contrastive signals. The method works because a headline that is genuinely clickbait will have plausible-sounding both-sides arguments, but genuine arguments will pull in opposite directions on detection, creating a clear signal. When a model is trained on contrastive pairs—one labeled likely-clickbait, one likely-honest—it learns to separate the two classes not by memorizing keywords but by understanding why credible and deceptive headlines differ. This forces the model to discover the real patterns of deception rather than surface cues, making it more robust to new, unseen clickbait.
Anonymous Linear Bandits for Multi-User SystemsWWW
uses Eliminate arms and build a bipartite match between users and remaining arms that preserves privacy while minimizing regret.
why it works It works because successive elimination narrows choices without revealing which arms each user prefers, and greedy matching then allocates fairly; the algorithm bounds total regret because it never keeps bad arms long.
the deeper reason
The algorithm solves the problem of assigning users to options (arms) in a bandit setting while keeping each user anonymous—the central system learns which arm is best without learning who preferred it. The method works by using successive elimination: options that perform poorly are discarded, leaving only the best candidates. The greedy matching algorithm then assigns remaining users to remaining arms such that no user or option is revealed. Mathematically, successive elimination is sound because it samples options carefully to identify truly poor ones with high statistical confidence before ruling them out. By discarding only options that are demonstrably worse than others, the algorithm guarantees it explores enough to find near-optimal assignments without wasteful exploration, keeping regret sublinear.
Access Controlled Website Interaction for Agentic AI with Delegated Critical TasksWWW
uses Implement fine-grained access control on websites so AI agents can be granted permissions for specific delegated tasks without exposing full account access.
why it works It works because granting capability by task rather than by account scope ensures agents can only perform actions their delegation authorizes; this separates what users allow from what agents attempt.
the deeper reason
This work designs websites where AI agents can be granted fine-grained access control, so they can perform delegated tasks on a user's behalf without being handed full account access. The soundness lies in separation of privilege: instead of giving an agent the user's password or full authorization, the website grants narrow permissions for specific actions (e.g., view billing, schedule appointment, but not change password). This is secure because the agent can only do what the permission allows, even if compromised or manipulated by an attacker. The authorization service tracks which agent received which permission for which task, making abuse traceable and revocable. Delegating critical tasks safely requires that each permission grant is tied to a specific task scope, so an agent cannot expand its authority beyond what the user explicitly approved.
Foundations for the Agentic Web: Networked AI Agents in a Decentralized Architecture (NANDA)WWW
uses Design registries, protocols, and reputation systems so AI agents can discover and coordinate with each other in a decentralized network.
why it works It works because registries make agents findable, protocols enable them to communicate reliably despite differences, and reputation systems ensure agents learn whom to trust; together these create conditions where distributed agents can cooperate.
the deeper reason
This tutorial framework lays out foundations for a decentralized network of autonomous AI agents that can discover, negotiate, and coordinate with each other without a central authority. The reasoning is that the traditional web succeeded because DNS and HTTP established shared protocols for discovery and communication. Similarly, agent networks need registries (where agents advertise themselves), identity systems (so agents can prove who they are), and reputation mechanisms (so other agents know whom to trust). Without these, agents cannot find each other or verify each other's reliability. Markets and governance structures emerge naturally once the foundation is stable: agents trade services using reputation as currency, and populations self-coordinate through pricing signals. The architecture is sound because each layer (technical, economic, social) builds trustworthily on the layer below.
Implementation of a Metacognition Framework for Self-Awareness and Self-Regulation in Ensembles of LLMsWWW
uses Compute a metacognitive state lists of numbers measuring self-awareness across five psychology features, then route queries to system-1 or system-2 processing based on complexity.
why it works It works because the five features (emotion, correctness, experience match, conflict, importance) together reveal query difficulty; using these signals to route automatically matches processing power to need, making the ensemble more reliable.
the deeper reason
The metacognitive framework monitors an ensemble of language models by computing a Metacognitive State lists of numbers that tracks five psychological features: emotional response, correctness, experience match, conflicting information, and problem importance. This works because uncertainty has multiple origins—some queries are genuinely hard (high problem importance), others reveal conflicting information across models, and some exceed all models' training data. By quantifying these features explicitly, the system can route queries intelligently: simple, confident questions go to fast System 1 processing, while complex or conflicted questions escalate to deliberative System 2 reasoning with specialized roles. The soundness comes from cognitive psychology: humans use similar metacognitive monitoring to decide when to think slowly. Mirroring this in AI ensures the ensemble recognizes its own limits and escalates appropriately rather than confidently guessing.
PAMAS: Self-Adaptive Multi-Agent System with Perspective Aggregation for Misinformation DetectionWWW
uses Organize agents into auditors, coordinators, and a decision-maker that hierarchically aggregate specialized views to highlight anomaly cues in misinformation.
why it works It works because misinformation hides in noise; when agents look at different feature subsets and coordinators blend their views hierarchically rather than flooding all input to one processor, anomalies emerge from the aggregated perspectives.
the deeper reason
PAMAS combats the information-drowning problem in multi-agent misinformation detection by organizing agents into three hierarchical roles and using perspective-aware aggregation. The soundness lies in specialization and filtering: instead of every agent seeing all information, Auditors each examine specific feature subsets (anomaly patterns, linguistic cues, network signals), so each agent finds what it is designed to detect without being overwhelmed. Coordinators then aggregate these specialized findings, weighting them to maintain diversity so weak deceptive cues are not lost in the flood of truthful content. The Decision-Maker combines all perspectives with evolving memory of patterns seen so far. This hierarchy works because a signal that is weak globally can be strong locally—an anomaly that appears rare overall might be systematic within a linguistic feature subset. By having agents specialize and coordinate hierarchically, the system recovers weak deceptive cues that flat, full-access architectures would drown out.
Sybil Attacks on Centrality MeasuresWWW
uses Score node importance in a network, then craft fake identities to hide a true node's importance—evading detection based on network structure.
why it works It works because network importance measures rely on connection patterns; an adversary can exploit this by creating many fake identities and distributing connections in ways that obscure their true network position. The ranking algorithm cannot tell real influence from orchestrated noise.
the deeper reason
The core challenge is measuring node importance in a network when adversaries can hide by creating fake accounts connected strategically. Centrality scores work by aggregating local structure—a node's importance emerges from where it sits relative to others. An attacker defeats this by distributing connections across fake identities to appear less central than they truly are. The paper proves that hiding optimally is computationally tractable for simple degree-based scores but becomes a hard search problem for measures like betweenness, which account for how many shortest paths flow through a node. Heuristics from community detection work because they exploit the fact that real communities have internal density—if an attacker creates many fake accounts, they either create detectable clustering anomalies or leave trails in the patterns they must create to coordinate them.
STG-DGR: Fraud Detection on Streaming Transaction Graphs with Diffusion-based Generative ReplayWWW
uses Generate synthetic fake transaction patterns to rehearse spotting old fraud types, preventing a model from forgetting as new patterns emerge.
why it works It works because streaming fraud detection faces catastrophic forgetting—as new scams arise, models unlearn old ones. Replaying synthetic historical fraud patterns keeps the old detectors sharp without storing real data, which is impossible at scale.
the deeper reason
The core problem is detecting fraud in transaction graphs that evolve over time, where past fraud patterns fade from the model's memory as new patterns appear—catastrophic forgetting. The method replaces storing old examples with synthesizing them: generating fake samples that mimic old patterns' statistical properties without keeping original data. This works because if you capture the structural dependencies in old transactions—who traded with whom, when, with what features—and generate samples matching those dependencies, the model learns from the synthetic replay and retains what it knew. The diffusion-based generator works by gradually denoising random noise into structured transactions, learning to build layer-by-layer dependencies bottom-up; the hierarchical structure captures how transactions nest into subgraphs naturally, so the generator produces coherent synthetic samples that preserve the essential patterns without storing real user data.
MIDE: Multimodal Dialogue Emotion Recognition via Mutual Information Enhancement and Dynamic Modality SelectionWWW
uses Measure how much information each modality (text, audio, video) shares with others, then pick the best pairs for fusion and track emotion over time.
why it works It works because emotions reveal themselves differently across modalities—speech tone and facial expression sometimes disagree with words. Measuring what information each modality shares with the others tells you which pairs are trustworthy, and tracking changes over time respects that emotions evolve within a conversation.
the deeper reason
The core task is recognizing emotion in conversations that mix text, audio, and video, where different modalities have different reliability for different speakers. The method works by maximizing information overlap between modality pairs: if two modalities agree on emotional signal, they are likely capturing true emotion, not noise unique to one source. Selecting high-quality pairs dynamically works because in any conversation, one speaker's audio might be clear while another's video is blurry—fixed fusion assumes all modalities always help, but selective fusion exploits that some pairs are more trustworthy moment-by-moment. Tracking emotion change over time works because emotions evolve: anger builds, sadness deepens, so modeling temporal transition improves accuracy beyond treating each utterance in isolation. By optimizing information between modalities and capturing emotional flow across the dialogue, the system leverages both the multimodal consensus and the dynamic structure of real emotional arcs.
Fairness in Opinion-Formation DynamicsWWW
uses Adjust how stubborn individuals are toward their own beliefs so that different groups end up with fair influence over the crowd's final opinion.
why it works It works because the more a person clings to their own opinion, the more weight it carries in the group consensus. By tweaking how much each person sticks to their view, you reshape who influences the crowd—targeting minimal changes that rebalance power between groups.
the deeper reason
The core problem is ensuring fair influence in opinion dynamics, where some people's inner beliefs shift group opinions while others' views are ignored. The method works by adjusting stubbornness—how anchored each person is to their own view—so that influence distributes fairly across groups. This works because in the Friedkin-Johnsen model, public opinion is a weighted sum of inner opinions and peer pressure, and stubbornness controls the weight each person's inner view receives. The paper derives closed-form formulas showing exactly how changing one person's stubbornness ripples through the group's final opinion, making it tractable to find minimal interventions. By making some people more receptive and others more anchored, you steer the outcome without heavy-handed censorship, achieving fairness through structural rebalancing of how much each group's core beliefs matter to the final consensus.
Rethink Web Service Resilience in Space: A Radiation-Aware and Sustainable Transmission SolutionWWW
uses Reroute satellite traffic during radiation bursts to minimize battery drain while maintaining service—balancing energy cost against uptime.
why it works It works because radiation damage and battery depletion compound over time—the energy spent rerouting now prevents larger problems later. By measuring the energy cost of different rerouting choices against the battery's remaining capacity, you optimize a tradeoff that only appears when you account for the full system.
the deeper reason
The core challenge is keeping web services running on orbiting satellites when radiation damages hardware and drains batteries. The method works by rerouting traffic away from damaged nodes during radiation events, choosing paths that minimize total battery wear rather than just hopping packets. This works because battery aging is not linear: draining a battery deeply and slowly aging it gradually both reduce capacity, but deep discharge is catastrophic. By accounting for energy cost in path selection, the system avoids the trap where aggressive sleep modes disconnect users or altitude adjustments waste fuel. The radiation-aware layer sits in the control plane, monitoring space weather forecasts and proactively shifting traffic before hardware fails, solving the resilience gap: conventional fixes either burn energy or break sessions, but network-layer rerouting trades latency for durability, keeping service alive globally while respecting the physics of space-based hardware.
NANDA: Resolution, Discovery, and Governance for the Agentic WebWWW
uses Builds a naming and certification system to make agents findable, trustworthy, and composable across networks.
why it works Works because DNS and certificate authorities proved that centralized trust layers enable global coordination without central control; agents need the same infrastructure.
the deeper reason
NANDA solves the core problem of verifying and discovering autonomous agents across distributed networks. The method mirrors how the web achieved trust at global scale through delegated authority—DNS proves who you're reaching, certificate authorities vouch for them. When agents operate independently across many machines and networks, no single authority can check them all, so NANDA pre-establishes a chain of trust where root authorities delegate verification down to regional authorities, and agents prove their identity through these chains. This layering works because any verifier can independently check the chain, and malicious agents cannot forge credentials without breaking the root of trust itself. This foundation lets organizations safely compose and coordinate agents they've never directly vetted, solving the real problem of scaling autonomous systems beyond a single operator.
ORKG Properties Ontology Consolidated: LLM-Driven Refinement of Crowdsourced Knowledge for Machine-ActionabilityWWW
uses Uses language models to detect and merge duplicate properties and standardize naming in a knowledge graph.
why it works Works because language understanding can recognize when different names mean the same thing; human review validates the merges.
the deeper reason
ORKG consolidates a crowdsourced knowledge graph by resolving duplicated and inconsistent property names. The core problem is that when many people independently define relationships in a graph, they use synonyms and overlapping terms, making it impossible for software to understand what each term means. The method works by using AI language systems to cluster similar properties and human experts to verify and unify them into a clean schema. This is trustworthy because identical relationships should have identical names, so consolidation is sound by definition—any two properties describing the same relationship are redundant, and removing redundancy always improves clarity. The result is a machine-actionable schema where software can reliably interpret and reason over the knowledge.
Kleene Closure Property Path Query Optimization Based on Node Clustered IndexWWW
uses Finds all simple paths between nodes by pre-indexing representative paths and cycles.
why it works Works because while finding all paths is hard, you only need certain key ones; storing those makes queries instant.
the deeper reason
Kleene Closure queries ask whether a path exists between two nodes in a knowledge graph, potentially following cycles. The core trade-off is that simple paths without repetition are computationally hard to enumerate, while allowing cycles produces bloated result sets with meaningless detours. The method works by pre-building an index storing representative simple paths—the longest cycles-free routes and fundamental cycles—then answering queries through index lookups instead of expensive graph traversal. This is sound because connectivity only requires one valid path; redundant paths add noise without new information. By materializing the essential paths beforehand, the method converts an expensive computation into fast lookup while guaranteeing every result satisfies the simple path constraint.
Single-Sample Bilateral Trade with a BrokerWWW
uses Designs a trading mechanism where a broker buys from a seller and sells to a buyer using minimal information.
why it works Works because constant approximations are possible even with one sample; you don't need exact valuations, just reasonable estimates.
the deeper reason
The paper designs a trade mechanism where a broker mediates a single-sample transaction between a buyer and seller whose valuations are drawn from unknown distributions. The core challenge is that with only one sample from each distribution, the mechanism must protect both parties from exploitation. The method works by setting prices based on the sampled valuations while maintaining constant-factor approximations to ideal outcomes, assuming valuations follow standard probabilistic patterns. This is sound because the monotone-hazard-rate assumption provides mathematical structure to the distribution tail—a formal guarantee that sampling once still produces meaningful information about the full distribution. Even with an intermediary taking a cut, the mechanism guarantees both parties benefit reasonably because the principle ensuring single-sample reliability holds regardless of the broker's presence.
SEP-Attack: A Simple and Effective Paradigm for Transfer-Based Textual Adversarial AttackWWW
uses Scores word importance by combining multiple model opinions and selects the top-ranked words to create adversarial text that fools AI systems.
why it works Different models have different blindnesses; averaging their agreement reveals true vulnerabilities no single model captures. Combining weak signals this way finds robust attack patterns.
the deeper reason
SEP-Attack generates adversarial text by creating an ensemble of surrogate models, then choosing which words to modify based on how transferable the resulting attack would be to the target system. The soundness rests on a mathematical fact: when you have multiple imperfect copies of a system, their disagreements reveal what patterns are brittle. By weighting those copies according to how well their vulnerabilities transfer (using a principled diversity measure), the method learns which word changes actually exploit the victim model rather than just fooling the surrogates. The method works because transferability follows a signal that can be estimated from the ensemble—if a word modification breaks multiple models in consistent ways, it likely breaks the target too. This probabilistic reasoning about the shared vulnerability structure is far more reliable than treating all surrogate models equally.
ONE-PASS: Single Forward Pass Decoding for Listwise RerankingWWW
uses Ranks items by combining probabilities from sub-rankings instead of ranking all items at once, using a structural decomposition to aggregate sub-scores.
why it works Predicting the full ranking order is costly; breaking it into smaller sub-rankings you can compute in one pass, then using algebraic decomposition to combine them, gives you ranking predictions without the exponential cost.
the deeper reason
ONE-PASS accelerates ranking by approximating the full decision tree of possible orderings using a single forward computation. The mathematical trick is recognizing that ranking permutations (which explode factorially) can be reduced to subset combinations (which only double in count), because language models deciding the next item care less about the exact order of preceding items than about which items are present. The method further breaks the full ranking into smaller sub-rankings, then reassembles their probabilities using a principled inversion formula that recovers the contribution of each subset. This works because the inversion formula is mathematically exact—it correctly decomposes how subsets combine into the full ranking. By reducing the search space from factorial scale to subset scale and aggregating carefully, the system approximates auto-regressive ranking in one shot, eliminating the latency of decoding words by words.
Beyond Single view Decoding: Dual-view Map Inference from Trajectories via Primal-Dual Graphs Co-generationWWW
uses Infers road maps from vehicle traces by encoding adjacency two ways (as rasterized images and as serialized paths) and merging both signals into unified map predictions.
why it works No single representation captures all road structure; combining rasterized density and traversability paths gives you complementary signals, so merging them yields topology more accurate than either alone.
the deeper reason
D2Map infers road networks from vehicle trajectories by combining two complementary views: rasterized images (showing density) and trajectory sequences (showing traversability). The principle is that a single representation loses information—density images miss adjacency between roads at different levels, while trajectory sequences alone miss global structure. By modeling both the rasterized view (what was driven) and the primal-dual graph structure (which roads are adjacent, which are separate), the system captures road relationships that neither representation alone provides. The strategy-adaptive fusion decides which representation is most reliable for each region based on local data patterns. This dual-view approach is sound because it treats each view as contributing partial but complementary evidence about the true road structure, and evidence fusion (rather than choosing one view) recovers more accurate topology.
Smart Book Seeker: Agent-Augmented Retrieval System for Metadata-Sparse LibrariesWWW
uses Refines book retrieval through dialogue-based clarification, keyword search, and multi-turn expert evaluation to pick top results.
why it works It works because retrieval fails when users lack vocabulary or experts lack metadata. Splitting the problem—clarify needs, search broadly, then evaluate with domain knowledge—solves coordination bottlenecks independently.
the deeper reason
A user-needs agent clarifies ambiguous queries; a librarian agent retrieves candidates; a domain-expert proxy agent ranks results by discussing them with the librarian. This pipeline works because each agent solves the part of the problem it's designed for: disambiguation reduces vocabulary mismatch, retrieval explores the space efficiently, and expert-proxy evaluation leverages knowledge the user lacks. The multi-turn discussion between librarian and proxy agents is key—it surfaces whether a candidate truly matches the refined need by reasoning over domain criteria that the user couldn't articulate alone.
Enhancing Trusted Multi-View Classification via Adaptive Regularization Guided by View-Specific BiasesWWW
uses Adjusts penalties for each data view based on feature ambiguity and source reliability to balance imperfect evidence.
why it works It works because different data sources vary in quality and clarity. Weighting constraints by confidence prevents bad sources from pulling equally—reliable views drive the answer more.
the deeper reason
Multi-view classification extracts evidence from multiple views and combines it, but different views have different reliability: some views contain confusable classes (intra-view ambiguity), others are noisier than peers (inter-view quality gaps). An adaptive keeping it simple that reflects these disparities is sounder than uniform keeping it simple, because it avoids over-penalizing inherent uncertainty in poor-quality views while tightening constraints where evidence is reliable. This works because the classification loss already captures which views disagree; weighting keeping it simple by these disagreement patterns aligns the objective with the true trade-off between conformity and confidence in each view's contribution.
Navigating Truth in Multimodal Fact-checking via Retrieval- and Reasoning-Enhanced Large Language ModelsWWW
uses Gathers image and text evidence, then refines reasoning through reinforcement learning to verify multimodal claims.
why it works It works because multimodal claims need both semantic search (find relevant proof) and logic (reason through it). Separately optimizing each improves both—better evidence makes reasoning clearer, and reasoning guides which evidence matters.
the deeper reason
Multimodal fact-checking must reason over both images and text to evaluate claims; existing methods treat images and text separately, missing cross-modal evidence. The framework retrieves semantically relevant evidence images and text, then refines both through reasoning and reinforcement feedback from correct fact-checks. This works because evidence is most useful when diverse (images + text) and semantically aligned (related to the claim). Reinforcement tuning on broad datasets exploits the signal in correct vs. incorrect predictions to steer reasoning toward explanations that actually improve verification, amplifying reasoning power without manual annotation.
Semi-Supervised Fake News Detection with Mixture of ExpertsWWW
uses Combines GNN and AI language systems expert judgments with one-class classification and pseudo-labels to detect fake news with sparse labels.
why it works It works because two imperfect experts disagree only on borderline cases—their consensus is stronger than either alone. One-class boundaries define the normal region, and pseudo-labels amplify agreement safely.
the deeper reason
Fake news uses both semantic camouflage (writing style mimicry) and structural manipulation (altered propagation). No single detector—GNN or language model alone—catches both tactics; they are complementary experts. One-class classification constrains true news to a compact region, identifying outliers as fake without needing many labeled fake examples, solving the scarcity problem. Consensus between independent experts builds pseudo-labels for unlabeled data with high confidence. This works because the two experts are differently fooled; their disagreement signals something suspicious even without labels, and their agreement on unlabeled data is reliable because both must independently judge it.
KE-FedRS: Tackling Data Sparsity in Federated Recommendation via Knowledge EnhancementWWW
uses Enriches sparse user numeric fingerprints through sharing auxiliary representations with similar users and selecting diverse training clients.
why it works It works because inactive users and rare items need signals from neighbors. Sharing auxiliary numeric fingerprints safely pools knowledge across federated partners without exposing raw data.
the deeper reason
Federated recommendation systems preserve privacy by training locally, but suffer when users have few interactions (sparse data) locally and items have few ratings globally. The method enriches sparse user numeric fingerprints by aggregating auxiliary numeric fingerprints from similar users, since similar users likely value similar items; poor-quality items are boosted by selecting clients with diverse item numeric fingerprints, ensuring the global model sees multiple perspectives. This works because similarity in user space correlates with complementary item knowledge, and client diversity ensures global training doesn't miss items; both exploit the structure of collaborative data without sharing raw user interactions.
ScotRec: Social Chain-of-Thought LLM Reasoning for RecommendationWWW
uses Balances user recommendations by reasoning through multiple sentiment pathways then aggregating them to counteract preference bias.
why it works It works because confirming existing preferences feels natural—it needs active opposition to resist. Explicit multi-step reasoning through contrary sentiments, then aggregating, overcomes the bias through deliberation.
the deeper reason
Language models tend toward confirmation bias, over-emphasizing starting guess user interests and ignoring diverse perspectives. Chain-of-thought reasoning can counteract this by explicitly simulating sentiment-aware decision paths that consider multiple viewpoints. The method extracts sentiment from reviews, then tracks sentiment-based reasoning chains with human-like operations: backtracking (reconsidering), discarding (rejecting biased conclusions), retaining (keeping sound ones), aggregating (combining viewpoints). This works because reasoning steps make bias visible and correctable; by explicitly modeling sentiment from multiple sources, the process forces consideration of contradictory signals that the model might otherwise ignore, mechanically reducing the tendency to reinforce existing preferences.
MCLMR: A Model-Agnostic Causal Learning Framework for Multi-Behavior RecommendationWWW
uses Score user preferences from multiple behavior types—views, clicks, purchases—by building a causal model to untangle confounding and weighting behaviors smartly.
why it works User habits and item popularity both influence behavior, creating confounding—a click might come from discovery or habit. By modeling cause-and-effect relationships explicitly, interventions isolate true preference from noise. Adaptive weighting then fuses behavior types by learning which ones are reliable for each user-item pair.
the deeper reason
MCLMR improves multi-behavior recommendation—combining views, clicks, purchases—by modeling hidden confounders that bias preference estimation. When users act, unmeasured factors like their viewing habits or item popularity drive multiple behavior types simultaneously, creating spurious correlations. MCLMR builds a causal diagram of these confounders and uses intervention techniques to estimate preferences unbiased by them. This works because causal reasoning mathematically separates the effect of true preferences from the effect of confounding, ensuring that learned patterns reflect what users actually want rather than what their history happens to correlate with. The principle applies because each behavior type (click, purchase) co-occurs due to both genuine interest and common confounders; disentangling them via causality yields cleaner signal. This matters because recommendation quality degrades when models learn to exploit confounders rather than identify real preferences.
Mixture of Sequence: Theme-Aware Mixture-of-Experts for Long-Sequence RecommendationWWW
uses Predict the next item a user will interact with from long sequences by extracting theme-specific subsequences and routing them to specialized predictors.
why it works Long sequences contain interest shifts and session hops—users care about recent trends within sessions but lose interest across sessions. Routing sequences by theme isolates coherent patterns, filtering noise, so each predictor sees only relevant history. Mixture-of-experts then blends these specialized views to forecast accurately.
the deeper reason
Mixture of Sequence solves the problem of predicting user behavior from long interaction histories where users shift interests radically between sessions but stay consistent within sessions. The key insight is that not all history is useful—some old interactions mislead because the user has changed interests. By discovering hidden themes in the sequence and grouping interactions by theme, the model learns separate patterns for each theme and routes each prediction to the relevant expert. This works because human interests are organized hierarchically—stable within topics but volatile across topics—so modeling theme-specific patterns lets you ignore off-topic noise. The separation is mathematically sound because it reduces the effective length of relevant history for each prediction; the model no longer confuses old interest from a different theme with current preferences. This matters because focus to all history equally amplifies noise, while theme-aware routing extracts only the predictive signal.
1st Workshop on Applied AI and Multimodal Visualization Technologies (AAIMVT 2026)WWW
uses Integrates text, images, audio, and video into a unified visualization and decision interface, using each modality to verify and clarify signals from the others.
why it works Each modality captures different aspects of reality with different noise. Combining them so one confirms the other (e.g., speech content matches transcript tone) filters out noise specific to any single modality, surfacing the signal present in all of them.
the deeper reason
This is a workshop announcement describing multiple applied projects combining artificial intelligence with visual design for web systems. The thread connecting them is that when AI systems must justify decisions or assist humans, visualizing the data and reasoning is essential—showing a voice system's confidence, mapping out relationships in knowledge, displaying regions of images that matter to predictions. Visualization and interaction turn a black-box model into a tool a person can understand, debug, and trust, making AI useful rather than mysterious.
Fed-S2: Adversarially Disentangled Federated Multimodal RAG for Safety-Critical Long-Tail Fault DiagnosisWWW
uses Builds a shared knowledge graph from text and signal numeric fingerprints that each participant shares, sanitized to hide individual patterns, then reasons over this combined graph to detect faults across different types of data.
why it works Knowledge graphs make relationships explicit, so sanitized versions preserve causal connections while hiding private signals. Multimodal numeric fingerprints aligned in a shared space mean signals reinforce across modalities, so faults visible in one domain propagate reliably to others.
the deeper reason
The core challenge is diagnosing faults in machines from mixed data types (signals, images, text) when there are few examples of rare faults, while keeping data private across sites. The method replaces sharing model changes with sharing a knowledge graph of learned relationships—lightweight summaries that don't expose raw data. It uses an adversarial game to ensure the summary cannot be reversed to recover original information, leveraging an information-theoretic bound that guarantees safety. For rare faults, it leverages a general language model as a knowledge source so it can recognize unseen fault types at test time without seeing them during training. This is sound because the knowledge graph encodes what the system learned about fault patterns without storing the private data itself, the game formalization prevents data leakage rigorously, and grounding in a general model allows generalization to new faults.
LLM-GC: Advancing Granger Causal Discovery from Time Series with Multimodel Language ModelingWSDM
uses Discovers cause-effect relationships in time series by enriching raw data with semantic context from language models, aligning temporal patterns with conceptual meaning.
why it works Raw time series alone cannot distinguish true causality from spurious correlation. Adding semantic starting guess (e.g., 'when you see pattern X in the data, it means Y is happening') helps the model ignore coincidences and recognize when one variable truly drives another. Multimodal alignment ensures temporal and semantic signals reinforce rather than contradict.
the deeper reason
Granger causality discovers which time series influence which others by testing whether past values of one series improve predictions of another, but working on raw numerical data misses the semantic context—a sensor reading makes more sense when you know what it measures and what events were happening. The method enriches raw sequences with semantic information from a language model—context and knowledge about the domain—then uses a dual-path architecture to extract causal patterns that are consistent across both the temporal and semantic views. This is sound because real causality operates in context: adding context filters out false causal inferences that happen by coincidence in raw data alone, and requiring causal signals to appear in both time and meaning ensures the discovered relationships are robust rather than artifacts of noise.
Using Brand Knowledge Bases and LLM Agents to Enhance E-commerce Retailers' Catalog QualityWSDM
uses Scores and aligns product entries from an e-commerce catalog against a clean brand knowledge base to repair and match them simultaneously.
why it works Matching works because both the catalog and the knowledge base refer to the same real products; by finding which entries correspond to which references, the method can copy accurate details and fill gaps using ground truth from the brand source.
the deeper reason
The core task is filling in missing and incorrect product information by comparing against brand reference data. The method works because when you check a noisy record against a trusted source simultaneously—both repairing errors and matching category—you avoid compounding mistakes that happen when you fix one thing, then discover the fix breaks the match. The brand knowledge base acts as ground truth; if your product name and attributes diverge from it, they're likely wrong. This principle holds because brand metadata is curated and consistent within a single seller's view. By doing both tasks at once through an agent, you respect the fact that product identity and product details are intertwined—fixing the name might reveal the brand, which then constrains what attributes are valid.
SAGERec: Sampling and Gating for Enhanced Long-Tail Item RecommendationsWSDM
uses Learns which items in a user's history are most informative, then aggregates predictions from two expert models via a learned gate that weights their agreement differently for popular versus rare items.
why it works This works because rare items need different expert knowledge than popular ones; by training gate weights specifically to recognize when each expert is trustworthy for each item type, the method puts the right expert in charge at the right time.
the deeper reason
The goal is ranking items fairly across popularity tiers so unpopular-but-relevant items get shown despite having fewer interaction examples. The method learns specialized item selectors and combines them through learned gating, which works because you can decompose the problem: one expert learns what makes an item relevant given its own signals, while another emphasizes items most informative for learning user taste. The gating network then weighs these two paths based on the user and context. This is sound because relevance and informativeness are genuinely different objectives—an unpopular item can be highly relevant to one user but teach you little about users in general. By maintaining separate specialists and blending their predictions, you avoid a single scoring function that must simultaneously optimize both, which would necessarily trade off one for the other.
DGNet: Enhancing Parallel CTR Prediction Models via Decoupled Gated Network: Enhancing Parallel CTR Prediction Models via Decoupled Gated NetworkWSDM
uses Generates separate learned numeric fingerprints tailored to each sub-network in a parallel architecture, then uses a learned gate to select which layers of information from each network to combine at each step, avoiding noise buildup.
why it works Different sub-networks capture different interaction patterns; shared numeric fingerprints force compromise. By letting each sub-network learn its own representation and gating which one contributes at each step, the method ensures each interaction type uses its own optimized signal.
the deeper reason
Click prediction uses multiple parallel sub-networks to capture different feature interactions, but a naive approach amplifies noise as interactions layer on top of each other. The method gives each sub-network its own specialized numeric fingerprints and uses gating to select which layer-wise combinations to actually use. This works because feature interactions at different depths genuinely matter differently: early interactions capture obvious patterns, later ones capture subtle ones, but not all paths through the network reduce noise equally. By decoupling numeric fingerprints, each sub-network builds a different view of the same features, and gating learns which refined views to trust at each layer. This avoids the cumulative error of standard layered designs where wrong interactions from layer N propagate into layer N+1, because you're actively filtering which paths to combine.
Image-Guided Debiasing Distillation with Preference Alignment Across Multi-News HistoriesWSDM
uses Distills image-guided debiasing knowledge from a multimodal model into a text-only model, then trains on cleaned triples using weighted preference alignment to extract objective facts for news recommendation.
why it works Images are less prone to exaggeration than text; by teaching the text-only model to match predictions a multimodal model would make while seeing both image and text, the method transfers robustness without requiring images at test time.
the deeper reason
News recommendation requires modeling relationships between articles, but articles often contain exaggerated or biased language that distorts these relationships. The method uses a multimodal model (with images) to learn what the articles actually mean, then distills this understanding into a text-only model so it can extract factual triples. This is sound because images provide ground truth that text alone cannot: a photo of an event is harder to misrepresent than a written description. By learning from images first, the model absorbs a debiased understanding of the underlying facts. Distillation then teaches a text-only model to extract the same factual meaning from text alone, effectively teaching it to read around the exaggeration. The permutation-invariant training and preference alignment ensure the extracted triples are consistent and objective across variations, so recommendation is based on what actually happened, not on rhetorical framing.
Adapting to Evolving Data: Test-Time Expert Aggregation for Imbalanced Tabular RegressionWSDM
uses Trains multiple expert models each specialized to a different region of the training data identified via mixture modeling, then dynamically weights their predictions at test time based on incoming features without retraining.
why it works Imbalanced data has natural sub-populations with different characteristics; training separate experts for each region gives each an easier learning task. By learning at test time which region each new point belongs to and selecting the corresponding expert, the method adapts instantly to distribution shift.
the deeper reason
Regression on imbalanced tabular data deployed online faces distribution shift: the training data emphasizes certain value ranges, and the test distribution is unpredictable and shifts over time. The method partitions the feature space into regions using a statistical mixture model, trains specialists for each region, and adapts at test time by re-weighting specialists based on incoming features. This works because imbalance in regression means some value ranges are underrepresented in training, leaving specialists for those ranges undertrained. By identifying regions explicitly and training separately, you ensure each region has expert coverage. Crucially, test-time adaptation works because the feature distribution tells you which regions incoming data lives in, and you can upweight the corresponding experts without retraining. This is sound because the regional structure is stable—even if the target distribution shifts, the feature space structure remains valid, and you can use it to quickly adjust specialist weights to match new data.
LLM-Guided Beam Search for Decision Graph Optimization with Dynamic PromptingWSDM
uses Search for a graph of conditions that predicts a number (like price or yield) with smallest error by guiding the search with language clues.
why it works It works because you're chaining two truths: (1) the search finds the structure that makes fewest mistakes, and (2) language hints prune the search space so you find good answers fast instead of exploring forever.
the deeper reason
GraphBeam-AI language systems optimizes decision graphs for regression by replacing rigid binary trees with flexible directed-acyclic graphs and steering the search with language-model guidance. The soundness rests on a search principle: beam search explores multiple candidate solutions in parallel and keeps the most promising ones at each step, avoiding local traps that greedy methods fall into. Language models contribute semantic coherence—they propose splits and conditions that align with human interpretability, which reduces spurious overfitting. Dynamic prompting adapts the search goal as the algorithm learns, ensuring it balances finding genuinely better predictions against getting stuck refining variations of mediocre solutions.
Forget Me, Not My Friends! Object Unlearning Based on Scene GraphsWSDM
uses Remove one specific object from an image while keeping the scene and remaining objects intact, using the scene structure to guide which parts to forget.
why it works It works because the scene structure tells you which pixels causally depend on the object and which don't. Forgetting only the causal descendants preserves everything semantically unrelated to what you're erasing.
the deeper reason
Object unlearning via scene graphs works because scene graphs explicitly represent what objects exist, where, and how they relate semantically. By mapping an unlearning request ('remove person X') to a graph node and its connections, the framework can surgically delete only that node while preserving the rest of the image structure—relationships between remaining objects stay intact. This graph-based approach succeeds where sample or feature unlearning would fail because it respects compositional structure: an image isn't a flat feature lists of numbers but a scene with parts, so you can remove one part without erasing the whole.
Federated Watermarking of Deep Neural Networks with Distributed VerificationWSDM
uses Hide a secret mark inside a shared model where each client can verify ownership independently, and the mark survives removal attacks like adjust.
why it works It works because numeric fingerprints the watermark in a way that spreads across many model weights means no single attack (pruning, retraining, distilling) can erase all of it simultaneously—enough traces survive to prove ownership.
the deeper reason
Federated watermarking protects models by numeric fingerprints ownership verification that survives common attacks (adjust, pruning, distillation) while letting each client independently verify ownership without trusting a central authority. The principle is that watermarks embedded in model behavior rather than weights are harder to remove because the model learns to depend on them for correct predictions. Distributed verification works because each client can run the same watermark test locally and compare results, converging on whether the model is authentic without revealing the watermark details to any single party. This decentralization protects intellectual property in collaborative settings.
Multi-Agent System for Adversarial Robustness and Originality Attribution in Short-Form VideosWSDM
uses Detect stolen or manipulated videos by breaking the analysis into specialized tasks—one extracts visual clues, one retrieves similar videos, one weighs them together to judge if content is truly original.
why it works It works because manipulation requires coordinating across text, images, audio, and metadata. Specialists in each modality catch what a single model misses, and combining their signals reveals inconsistencies that prove theft.
the deeper reason
A multi-agent system for video integrity uses three specialized roles because video manipulation spans multiple failure modes: modality misalignment (hidden audio layered under visible content) and content theft (remixing elements). The Perceiver acquires raw signals, the Retriever finds similar videos globally to detect plagiarism, and the Reviewer orchestrates their findings using reasoning to adjudicate originality. This decomposition works because no single model can simultaneously detect fine-grained manipulations and search massive content libraries efficiently—delegation to specialized agents reduces hallucination (each agent focuses on one task) and cuts computational cost through metadata filtering and words frugality.
Hybrid Dual-Semantics Modeling for Enhancing Large Language Model Based RecommendationWSDM
uses Improve recommendations by tuning a language model on both item IDs (collaborative signals showing what items users actually picked) and text descriptions, weighting text more but boosting it with ID signals.
why it works It works because text is semantically richer but ID signals capture real user behavior. Keeping text as primary avoids noise while letting ID patterns fill in what text misses—the two views compensate for each other's blind spots.
the deeper reason
Hybrid dual-semantics modeling fuses collaborative signals (user-item interactions) and textual descriptions for recommendation by training two separate adaptation layers, each handling one semantics, then combining them only at inference. The approach avoids fusion noise because the two signals follow different patterns—collaborative signals are sparse but high-signal, text is dense but noisy—so mixing them during training creates conflicting the downhill direction that hurt both. By keeping them separate until inference, then using text as the primary signal enhanced by collaborative signals, the model learns stable representations where each signal contributes its strength. Alternating training resolves the downhill direction conflicts, ensuring both signals coexist in the final model.
WSDM CUP 2026: Multilingual RetrievalWSDM
uses Retrieve relevant documents in multiple languages when given an English query, treating each language version of a document as a separate match to rank.
why it works It works because the same document in different languages encodes the same meaning but different surface words. Matching across languages finds relevance that language-specific search would miss, improving coverage for global queries.
the deeper reason
Multilingual retrieval requires searching a collection in one language (documents) using queries in another (English) without direct translation, which is the core challenge. The method works by learning cross-lingual representations where semantically equivalent terms in different languages occupy nearby regions in numeric fingerprints space, regardless of surface form. This is possible because languages share underlying semantic structure—'water' and 'agua' refer to the same physical concept—so a model trained to align multilingual text can project queries and documents into a shared space where similarity measures work uniformly. This unified space enables the retriever to find relevant documents across language boundaries.
Label-Free Contrastive Learning for Open-World Multimodal Social Event DetectionWSDM
uses Find new social events by treating similar images and text as close neighbors, learning which ones belong together without any labeled event names.
why it works It works because if you arrange multimodal data so similar ones sit near each other in a space, finding groups becomes finding clusters of nearby points; cross-modal alignment lets you compare images and text fairly.
the deeper reason
Social media events leave traces across images and text that cluster together by theme—a protest leaves a recognizable pattern in both captions and photos—and the goal is to find those clusters without labeled event categories. The core principle is that similarity within a cluster, measured along carefully chosen angles, is stronger than similarity across clusters: if you describe images and text in ways that highlight what makes an event coherent (its theme, its type, what's visually happening), within-cluster pairs will look more alike than random pairs. This principle holds because real events have internal structure—the theme of a protest connects to both its visual markers and how people describe it—and this structure is discoverable without labels by asking a semantic guide (a language model) to describe those features consistently. By forcing the model to make representations that align these descriptions across image and text, the model learns to ignore spurious variation and finds genuine event structure, solving open-world detection without predefined categories.
Beyond Existing Retrievals: Cross-Scenario Incremental Sample Learning FrameworkWSDM
uses Rank items to recommend by focusing on finding new items that previous models missed, avoiding recommending the same things twice.
why it works It works because if multiple models already retrieved some items, recommending those again wastes ranking power; focusing on truly new items makes each model's contribution distinct and valuable.
the deeper reason
Large recommender systems use multiple retrieval pathways in parallel to cover different user interests, but these pathways overlap: some items multiple retrievers rank highly, giving little new information. The goal is to identify items only earlier retrievers miss and teach the new retriever to specialize in those, improving total system diversity. The principle is that learning is most efficient when training focuses on gaps rather than already-solved cases: a retriever learning from items everyone ignores learns distinctly from one trained on items everyone retrieves. This principle holds because the training signal in recommendation is sparser than in classification—each user sees few items—so wasting signal on consensus items wastes the precious signal that exists. By identifying truly novel items and teaching the retriever to find them specifically, while encouraging it to avoid stealing items the ensemble already ranks well, the system improves coverage without redundancy, delivering more user interests to the ranker and ultimately lifting user transaction rates.
Efficient Monte Carlo Algorithms for Approximating Katz Centrality on Large GraphsWSDM
uses Rank nodes by importance using random walks that approximate a weighted path count, averaging many random samples to speed up the calculation.
why it works It works because random walks converge to true importance scores given enough samples, and averaging many cheap samples is faster than exact calculation; you get ranking order right even if magnitudes are approximate.
the deeper reason
Computing how central each node is in a social network (by the Katz measure) exactly requires tracking influence paths of all lengths, which explodes in cost as networks grow. The goal is to approximate this ranking efficiently on massive graphs. The principle is random walks: if you repeatedly start from a node, take random steps following edges, and count how often you reach other nodes, the hit frequency approximates their true centrality ranking. This approximation works because the random walk process naturally weights paths by their frequency and accessibility—common paths get explored more often—which aligns with how Katz centrality mathematically weights paths, just computed probabilistically rather than algebraically. By running many independent random walks in parallel, computers working on different walks simultaneously, the computation becomes faster by orders of magnitude while maintaining ranking accuracy. This approach trades numerical precision in individual scores for speed and parallelizability, solving the practical problem of identifying influential users in networks too large for exact computation.
Identify-Conceptualize-Align: A Schema-Adaptive Framework for Unified Entity Recognition and Event DetectionWSDM
uses Extract entities and events from text without seeing the specific schema by first finding spans and assigning concepts, then separately aligning concepts to different schemas.
why it works It works because general understanding (finding spans) is separate from schema-specific mapping; by splitting these tasks, each one uses only the knowledge it needs, avoiding conflicting pressures.
the deeper reason
Information extraction from text using AI language systems breaks down when different tasks define entities differently—a 'person' means something different in biography extraction versus clinical notes—and training on multiple definitions causes the model to forget how to handle each one correctly. The goal is to reuse the model's general language understanding while delegating schema-specific mapping to lightweight task-specific models. The principle is separation of concerns: understanding language and identifying named entities is a general skill that applies to all schemas, whereas mapping identified entities to a particular schema's categories is task-specific. These skills are separable because you can identify where 'John Smith' appears in text without knowing whether to call it a 'person', 'subject', or 'entity'; the category assignment is a separate decision. By training the large model only on the general skill (identifying and understanding spans) across all tasks simultaneously, then training lightweight specialists for each schema, the model avoids forgetting one schema when learning another and keeps general ability sharp. This division lets the large model reuse its understanding broadly while allowing each schema to define its own categories, solving the problem of building extraction systems that handle multiple conflicting schemas in production.
Large Language Model Judged Self-Training for Named Entity RecognitionWSDM
uses Label new text for named entities by training on confidence scores from a language model, combined with calibration adjustments, to find high-quality pseudo-labels.
why it works It works because language models have rich knowledge that can judge whether labels are trustworthy; combining confidence with calibration reduces both false certainty and random hallucinations.
the deeper reason
Self-training for entity recognition amplifies small amounts of labeled data by using a model's own predictions on unlabeled data as new training examples, but the model often predicts wrong and those wrong predictions become training signal, causing errors to compound. The goal is to filter out incorrect predictions before adding them as training data. The principle is that AI language systems have rich knowledge about text and entities that a pure machine learning model lacks, and they can judge whether a predicted entity makes sense given the text's context and actual patterns in the training data. This principle applies because the language model's knowledge comes from diverse text and is orthogonal to the biases the specialized entity recognizer develops. By asking the language model to validate predictions using task rules the language model itself extracted from the labeled data, combined with multiple agreement signals, the model filters pseudo-labels to keep only plausible ones. This careful filtering breaks the error amplification cycle of standard self-training, solving the practical problem of learning entity boundaries accurately from few labeled examples and plentiful unlabeled text.
Rigorizing Retrieval-augmented Generation with Structured Knowledge Intelligence (6 Hrs)WSDM
uses Retrieve knowledge in structured forms (tables, graphs, trees) and feed it to generation models safely by understanding how structure shapes both retrieval quality and security.
