The soundness rests on a mathematical guarantee: limiting how much task-irrelevant information flows through the channel provably forces the remaining information to be what truly predicts the outcome, because random noise and modality-specific artifacts add how much surprise that the bottleneck must shed. By requiring that essential information compress into a small discrete codebook shared across all modalities, you ensure that only robust, cross-modal patterns survive the transmission; noise and redundancy fall away naturally because they offer no compression benefit. This lets the receiver reconstruct meaning even when channels fail or data goes missing, because what was sent was already the distilled essence.
Unveiling the Underground Phishing Ecosystem: A 12-Year Longitudinal Study of Deep and Dark Web ForumsWWW
uses Extract attack components from forum posts and track their availability over time to reveal emerging threats and attack methodologies.
why it works Components that suddenly become available signal new attack capability; components that disappear show declining risk. Observing longitudinal trends exposes cause-and-effect between ecosystem changes and real attacks.
the deeper reason
The study mines phishing forums to understand attack supply chains rather than just post-breach aftermath. It works because the Deep and Dark Web forums are where attackers pool tools, credentials, and techniques before attacks deploy—analyzing 394,000 posts reveals the pre-attack state of the ecosystem where patterns and trends actually emerge. The principle is that infrastructure and knowledge sharing leave traces, and those traces aggregate into statistical signals about what attacks are becoming common, which targets are lucrative, and how difficulty or cost is evolving. By mapping forum activity to a canonical seven-stage attack model, researchers extract causal structure from the chaos: which components cluster together, which services get targeted, and what timescales drive adaptation. This predictive visibility—knowing what attacks are being built now—lets defenders prepare before waves of attacks appear.
Evaluating Trustworthiness in Reactive Web Architectures: A Structured Framework and Comparative AnalysisWWW
uses Measure recommender trustworthiness directly through human-centered metrics like agency and transparency, not through engagement proxies.
why it works Engagement (clicks, dwell time) is a side effect of trustworthiness, not a cause. Measuring engagement confuses correlation with causation; measuring trust and agency directly reveals what genuinely satisfies users in the long run.
the deeper reason
This work argues that recommender systems should be evaluated on whether users trust them and feel understood, not just whether users click, because sustainable engagement requires human alignment. The framework reorients assessment toward features like transparency (users understand why they got a recommendation), agency (users feel they can control recommendations), and satisfaction (recommendations genuinely match their values, not just their clicks). The principle is that engagement metrics like clicks optimize for short-term capture, which can mean showing sensational or addictive content that users regret later, whereas trust and transparency build long-term relationships where users return because they value the system. By developing qualitative methods to assess these human-centered features, the work reveals trade-offs: some engagement-maximizing design choices (aggressive ranking, minimal explanation) actively harm trust, creating a false choice. Measuring what users actually value lets systems and researchers escape the trap of optimizing the wrong thing.
Towards Rare Social Event Prediction via Mediator LearningWWW
uses Extract precursor events as mediators via information-theoretic routing, then model observed events, mediators, and rare events in hierarchical graph layers.
why it works Past events that carry the most information about rare events are the true precursors; routing by mutual information finds them automatically. Hierarchical layering lets the model learn what precursors matter and how they combine to trigger rare events.
the deeper reason
The framework predicts rare events (like protests or crises) in social media streams by explicitly modeling hidden intermediate events that precede them. It works because rare events don't appear randomly—they're caused by chains of earlier events and conditions that, individually, might also be rare but collectively predictable. By extracting precursor events as mediators using information theory, the method identifies which earlier events actually predict the rare outcome. Then hierarchical graph networks model observed events at the bottom level and rare events at the top, with intermediate propagation conditioned on how likely lower-level events are. The principle is that dependencies between events create causal structure: earlier events constrain which later events can happen, and modeling this hierarchy lets you estimate rare-event probability through the chain of starting guess events rather than directly from their scarcity. This decomposition of dependencies makes the imbalanced classification problem tractable because you're not learning to predict the rare event alone; you're learning to propagate plausible event sequences up through a graph.
Assessing the Reliability of Persona-Conditioned LLMs as Synthetic Survey RespondentsWWW
uses Tests whether conditioning a language model with demographic information improves its ability to mimic real survey respondents or instead distorts answers.
why it works It works because agreement with real data is the ground truth: by comparing model answers to actual respondents across thousands of cases, you can measure whether a technique like persona prompting creates accuracy or noise. Worse performance on underrepresented groups reveals redistribution of error, not overall improvement.
the deeper reason
This work tests whether adding demographic context to AI language systems prompts improves survey response accuracy or instead biases them. The authors measure alignment by comparing thousands of synthetic responses (from persona-prompted models) against real survey data, and find that personas often degrade performance for minority subgroups. This is important because demographic conditioning redistributes error in ways that are hard to predict; what looks good on average masks hidden distortions for underrepresented populations.
SGExplainer: Balanced Path-based Signed Graph Neural Network Explanation for Link Sign PredictionWWW
uses Identifies balanced paths through a network with both positive and negative connections to explain when the model predicts an edge will be good or bad.
why it works It works because in networks with positive and negative edges, a balanced path—one where positive and negative multiply to form a stable pattern—reveals why edges should exist. By generating balanced paths as explanations, you expose the causal structure the model learned: certain sequences of interactions naturally lead to positive or negative relationships.
the deeper reason
Signed graph networks predict whether an edge will be positive or negative by learning complex representations, but black-box predictions are untrustworthy. SGExplainer uses balanced paths—sequences of edges where positive and negative signs alternate to reach a consistent conclusion—to explain each prediction. This is sound because balanced path theory from graph mathematics guarantees that such alternating-sign paths represent coherent logical arguments; enforcing this structure ensures explanations are both faithful to the model's reasoning and interpretable to humans.
The Algorithmic Self-Portrait:Deconstructing Memory in ChatGPTWWW
uses Analyze which memory entries an AI system infers about users, then alert when inferences reveal sensitive patterns.
why it works User inputs contain both direct statements and hidden clues to deeper traits; distinguishing stated facts from inferred psychology lets us see what the system learns and flag when inference chains accidentally expose sensitive information.
the deeper reason
The core observation is that conversational AI systems now autonomously create and store summaries of user conversations as 'memory,' building profiles of users without explicit permission. Understanding this requires examining what these memories contain and how they were formed. The analysis reveals that 96% are system-generated unilaterally, half contain psychological inferences, and most faithfully represent the conversation. The contribution is not mathematical but empirical and ethical: measuring where agency lies and what personal data is encoded in algorithmic memory. The Attribution Shield framework responds by training the model to anticipate sensitive inferences and alert users, a control-feedback loop that respects the mathematical principle that most harms from data processing stem from asymmetric information—users don't know what the system learned about them, so making predictions visible restores some symmetry.
TGNN: Enhancing Pixel Tracking Detection via LLM-driven Annotation and GAT-powered Structural RepresentationWWW
uses Detect stealthy pixel trackers by modeling third-party associations on websites as a graph, then scoring which edges truly track users.
why it works Trackers survive because they hide in cross-site connections; modeling websites and third parties as a graph makes hidden patterns visible, and scoring edges separates tracking infrastructure from normal traffic.
the deeper reason
Pixel tracking—invisible embedded images that leak user browsing to third-party servers—is hard to detect using rules or surface features because trackers use common infrastructure (CDNs, ad networks) that legitimate services also use. The method formulates detection as identifying which cross-site associations are tracking-related by constructing a directed graph where nodes are websites and edges represent HTTP traffic patterns. By encoding traffic into structured tuples and learning both semantic content and interaction patterns, the system can spot the correlations that distinguish genuine tracking from benign multi-site hosting. To overcome label scarcity, it uses an AI language systems with minimal expert guidance to auto-generate labels, bootstrapping a training set. The soundness here is that tracking leaves structural fingerprints in who talks to whom across sites; by explicitly modeling that structure and letting the system learn what patterns matter, detection becomes feasible without manual feature engineering.
Rethinking Implicit Hate Speech Detection: Focusing on Latent Hate Components via Dual-Process ArgumentationWWW
uses Find the actual hateful semantic units hidden in obfuscated text by mining candidates then debating their meaning, separating false surface cues from real harmful intent.
why it works Works because implicit hate uses misdirection — surface words seem innocent but underlying components carry the true message. Mining broadly then deliberating with reasoning separates noise from genuine signal, mimicking how humans detect what wasn't meant to be obvious.
the deeper reason
Implicit hate speech hides meaning behind layers—coded phrases, metaphors, tone—so surface-level keywords miss it. DuPL's core idea is that every hateful message contains hidden semantic pieces (units of hostile meaning) that must be identified before judgment. The framework works in two phases: first, a high-recall miner aggressively extracts candidate hate components while a quick judge exits early on obvious cases, then a deliberation phase breaks down the components and reasons about each one separately before reaching a final integrated decision. This two-stage structure guarantees sound reasoning because it separates the act of finding potential meaning from the act of judging it—by forcing explicit detection and argumentation rather than end-to-end pattern matching, the model avoids the pseudo-reasoning trap where large models chase spurious cues. Because implicit hate lives in semantic depth rather than surface words, centering detection on explicitly mined components and structured argument transforms opaque decision-making into interpretable steps. This makes hate detection both more accurate and auditable for web moderation.
Task-Aligned Unlearning for Multimodal Large Language ModelsWWW
uses Unlearn sensitive information by simultaneously pushing three separate goals: lower decision confidence on protected content, force refusals when asked about it, and suppress recall under both image and text prompts.
why it works Works because sensitive information is learned at multiple layers and gets triggered by different input types. Hitting it from three angles — decision making, generation, and recall — ensures no hidden path lets it leak out, and balances forgetting across all the behaviors the model learned.
the deeper reason
Multimodal models trained on huge corpora inevitably memorize private information, but unlearning it fairly is hard because different evaluation tasks (classification, free-form generation, entity recall) require different kinds of forgetting. TAU's core insight is that trying to forget with a single objective creates trade-offs: you might suppress classification confidence but keep generating the sensitive info verbally, or you over-suppress and break unrelated knowledge. By decomposing unlearning into three task-aligned objectives that directly target the specific behaviors tested—confidence reduction for classification, refusal generation for free-form, recall suppression for cloze—each objective pulls the model in the right direction for its task. The mathematical guarantee comes from joint optimization: these objectives aren't competing when they're matched to their tasks; instead, they converge toward balanced forgetting where private info is lost across all behaviors while general knowledge survives. This alignment principle lets practitioners achieve privacy-preserving multimodal models without collateral damage.
Knowledge Graph Editing Model for Enhancing Recommendation SystemsWWW
uses Improve recommendations by denoising the knowledge graph to remove false associations, then reweight edges to highlight the ones that actually matter for the recommendation task.
why it works Works because real-world knowledge graphs contain spurious connections that add noise and mislead the recommendation model. Denoising removes false correlations, and task-specific reweighting emphasizes edges that distinguish good recommendations from bad ones, focusing signal on what matters for predicting user preferences.
the deeper reason
Knowledge graphs used for recommendation contain noise (incorrect relationships) and task-irrelevant clutter that mislead the recommender. The framework cleans the graph by learning which edges matter for the specific recommendation task, using two complementary operations. Diffusion-based filtering denoise the graph structure—treating the graph as a noisy signal and iteratively averaging to smooth away spurious edges while preserving strong patterns. Task-specific triplet reconstruction then re-learns which relationships actually predict good recommendations by scoring edges and selectively reconstructing important ones. This two-pass approach is sound because denoising and task refinement address different problems: denoising removes corruption from any source, while reconstruction aligns what remains to the actual prediction goal. Because real-world graphs conflate multiple types of relationships (some critical, some misleading), separating cleanup from task alignment ensures both noise reduction and goal-directed pruning. With a refined graph, the recommender system sees clearer signals about which items belong together, yielding more accurate predictions.
How Social Media Peer Comments Influence Privacy Decisions in Photo Sharing: Context and Individual Differences Cause Comments to BackfireWWW
uses Measures how peer comments change the likelihood that a user shares a sensitive photo, separately for different user types and comment mixes.
why it works It works because randomized comment variants isolate what caused the sharing decision. Comparing outcomes when only the comment changes reveals which factors actually drive behavior versus what merely appears correlated.
the deeper reason
This study examines how peer feedback changes privacy decisions about sharing others' photos. The reasoning rests on a core principle: people adjust behavior when social norms are made visible through peer signals. When discouraging comments signal that sharing is unacceptable, most users internalize this norm and comply. However, for users with past misconduct, the opposite occurs—social disapproval paradoxically increases sharing. This backfiring happens because the feedback contradicts their self-image, causing them to reassert autonomy through noncompliance. The framework explains why simple nudges fail: identical social cues operate through competing psychological mechanisms depending on users' starting guess experience.
Towards Fair Large Language Model-based Recommender Systems without Costly RetrainingWWW
uses Identifies which training examples cause bias in recommendations, then removes their influence on the model to improve fairness without full retraining.
why it works It works because removing the true bias-causing examples fixes the model at its core. You don't need to retrain from scratch; small adjustments that undo the influence of those few examples efficiently flip wrong predictions back to fair ones.
the deeper reason
Recommendation systems trained on biased data amplify existing societal prejudices, harming fairness for underrepresented groups. Since retraining massive models is infeasible, the method reformulates debiasing as machine unlearning: identify which training samples induced the bias, then estimate and remove their influence on model parameters without retraining. This works because model predictions arise from accumulated influence across training samples; selectively removing influence of problematic samples reduces bias without corrupting overall performance. The bias-agnostic mask adapts to different fairness definitions (gender, race, etc.) because the underlying principle—unfair influence can be isolated and suppressed—holds regardless of which demographic features you measure.
When to Invoke: Refining LLM Fairness with Toxicity AssessmentWWW
uses Detects when demographic-related variation in toxicity judgments is likely to occur, then applies targeted refinement to reduce group-level disparities in model outputs.
why it works It works because unfairness concentrates: certain inputs consistently produce biased outputs. Identifying these risky cases and applying corrective scrutiny at inference time stops bias before it propagates, without needing expensive retraining or model changes.
the deeper reason
AI language systems used for toxicity moderation produce inconsistent judgments on subtle expressions and implicit hate speech, introducing demographic bias—some groups face harsher judgments for identical content. Direct model retraining is infeasible. Instead, the method works at inference time by identifying which inputs are prone to demographic variation (where the model hesitates or produces contradictory signals) and invoking additional assessment specifically for these cases. This works because bias is not uniform: it concentrates in ambiguous cases where training data contained conflicting signals. By detecting demographic-sensitive inputs and applying extra scrutiny only where needed, the framework reduces bias spread of error without model retraining. The principle is that fairness can be achieved through targeted, adaptive inference strategies rather than global model changes.
HGSA: Heterogeneity-Guided Sarcasm Adaptation for Video Sentiment Analysis via Polarity DisentanglementWWW
uses Separate sarcasm signals from straightforward signals by tracking how sentiment flips across different types of content—text, audio, video.
why it works Sarcasm flips the meaning but only certain parts of the input carry this flip. By keeping sentiment signals separate instead of mixing them, you can see which parts genuinely oppose each other, revealing where sarcasm hides.
the deeper reason
Sarcasm detection requires separating true sentiment from surface-level wording—the opposite of what the words literally say. The method works by keeping video modalities (visual, audio, text) separate during analysis, each feeding its own sentiment signal, rather than averaging them first. This preserves the distinct polarities each modality detects, so sarcasm (where visual content contradicts text) becomes visible as disagreement between modalities. Using these disagreements as guides to untangle sarcasm from the merged signal is sound because the contradictions cannot exist unless genuine opposing sentiment information flows through, making the guides structurally reliable.
From Representation to Clusters: A Contrastive Learning Approach for Attributed Hypergraph ClusteringWWW
uses Learn what nodes belong in the same group by comparing which nodes look alike to each other and which hyperedges hold them together.
why it works When you learn from comparisons—nodes that should cluster together sit near each other—the geometry of similarity directly guides where the clusters form, so clustering becomes reading off natural gaps in that learned space.
the deeper reason
The task is partitioning nodes in a hypergraph into meaningful groups. The method works by learning node representations while simultaneously assigning clusters, using both node relationships and hyperedge structure. This is mathematically sound because node numeric fingerprints trained under clustering supervision cannot encode noise—the learned space must preserve the block structure of the actual clusters, or the clustering loss remains high. By optimizing both numeric fingerprints and cluster assignment end-to-end, the space is shaped directly for the clustering objective rather than indirectly through a separate algorithm, which guarantees the final clusters reflect the true group boundaries encoded in the hypergraph.
Trustworthy Foundation Models for Web Intelligence: Causal Perspectives and ChallengesWWW
uses Foundation models used on the web need causal reasoning to separate real cause-and-effect from coincidental patterns, ensuring they act trustworthy.
why it works Causal reasoning reveals which relationships are real versus accidental; this distinguishes genuine insights from spurious correlations that can mislead the system into unfair or fragile decisions.
the deeper reason
This is a workshop overview paper on building trustworthy foundation models for web applications. The mathematical principle is that causal reasoning lets you prove why a model decision happened—not just that it did—by separating true causes from confounding factors. Causal methods are sound because they encode independence assumptions about how causes actually flow through data, preventing spurious correlations from masking real mechanisms. When you can prove causality, you gain interpretability and control, which directly enables fairness audits, robustness verification, and responsible deployment at web scale.
Proactive Misinformation Forecasting via Incremental Topic Detection and Sentiment PolarizationWWW
uses Forecast misinformation by tracking how sentiment diverges rapidly within emerging topics, using that divergence as an early warning signal.
why it works Polarization creates an echo chamber where misinformation spreads; high divergence means opposing camps, which correlates with how unverified claims propagate, so measuring divergence gives you a predictive edge before false claims take hold.
the deeper reason
Misinformation spreads faster when topics become polarized—people share content matching their existing views. The method continuously tracks topics in real time and measures how split sentiment becomes around each topic using sentiment divergence. This is sound because polarization is a measurable divergence in topic-specific emotion that forms before false claims fully propagate. By detecting topics where sentiment splits dramatically, you identify the conditions under which misinformation flourishes: topics with polarized audiences are fertile ground. The predictive power comes from this temporal lead—polarization rises before viral spread, giving you time to intervene.
Fine-Grained Traceability for Transparent ML PipelinesWWW
uses Compute a score showing how much each sample contributed to the model's decisions, anchored to verifiable checkpoints.
why it works It works because when you track how each data point flows through the system and compute its specific contribution score at known checkpoints, you can later verify whether the data was used and was unchanged, making the flow auditable rather than opaque.
the deeper reason
FG-Trac tracks individual data samples as they move through a machine learning pipeline by recording cryptographic checkpoints at each stage. The soundness comes from cryptography itself: if a record is attached to a tamper-evident commitment (a cryptographic hash tied to a specific time or checkpoint), then any alteration of the data breaks the hash, making tampering instantly detectable. This works because cryptographic commitments are one-way functions where two different inputs almost certainly produce different outputs. The framework can therefore reconstruct a complete, auditable history of which samples were used and when, letting practitioners verify that no data was silently dropped, duplicated, or modified between preprocessing and model training.
From Manipulation to Mistrust: Explaining Diverse Micro-Video Misinformation for Robust Debunking in the WildWWW
uses Classify videos by analyzing both content and external evidence to determine whether manipulation, AI-generation, or out-of-context reuse caused the misinformation.
why it works It works because cross-checking video features against retrieved evidence reveals gaps and contradictions that unmask specific types of deception; different deception types leave distinct fingerprints in content and context.
the deeper reason
FakeAgent detects misinformation in micro-videos by analyzing both the video content itself and external evidence retrieved from the web, then reasoning across both together. The soundness lies in combining two independent signals: a video's visual and audio cues can be deceptive, but external sources (news archives, fact-checking sites) are harder to fake in coordination. When both the content analysis and the evidence analysis point to the same conclusion, that agreement acts as verification—a single deceptive source is unlikely to fool both an AI model seeing the video and independently retrieved evidence. This convergence of multiple reasoning paths from different information sources dramatically reduces the chance of false conclusions.
Does This Button Work? Investigating YouTube's Ineffective User ControlsWWW
uses Quantify how similar unwanted recommendations are to content users explicitly rejected, measuring whether feedback controls actually prevent similar items.
why it works It works because similarity is a meaningful proxy for whether a recommendation actually honors user feedback; if controls fail to prevent similar content reappearing, the gap between user expectation and platform behavior is quantifiable.
the deeper reason
This study experimentally measures whether YouTube's feedback buttons actually reduce unwanted recommendations by having thousands of users trigger different feedback signals and observing what happens next. The soundness is statistical: with 567 million recommendations collected and a control group receiving no feedback, the researchers can measure the true causal effect of each button by comparing recommendation distributions before and after. Large-scale data is essential here because unwanted recommendations are rare, so without millions of samples, random variation would drown out the true effect. By comparing what actually appeared in recommendations (using a trained similarity model), the study reveals the ground truth: most feedback mechanisms fail because recommendations that are similar to disliked content still appear afterward.
From Native Memes to Global Moderation: Cross-Cultural Evaluation of Vision–Language Models for Hateful Meme DetectionWWW
uses Test how well hate-detection models work across different cultures and languages, revealing bias toward Western interpretations.
why it works It works because models trained on Western data absorb Western meanings. By measuring performance separately per culture and prompting in native languages, you expose how much detection relies on cultural cues the model never saw, revealing when translation erases meaning.
the deeper reason
The core issue is that vision-language models trained mostly on Western content fail to recognize hateful memes in other cultures because hate speech relies on local context—symbols, references, and norms that differ across regions. The solution works by prompting models in the native language of the meme and using one-shot learning to inject cultural example into the model's reasoning. Native-language prompting works because models internalize multilingual patterns during training; using the meme's own language guides the model toward culturally-aware interpretation. One-shot learning works better than zero-shot because showing a single example from the same culture primes the model to apply local norms rather than defaulting to Western safety standards. The paper reveals that translating then detecting fails because translation destroys cultural cues and context shifts the model back toward its training-time Western defaults, so the fundamental fix is steering the model toward cultural grounding at inference time rather than assuming universal definitions of harm.
Verifiable Federated Representation Learning for Cross-domain Sequential RecommendationWWW
uses Learn user representations that separate what behavior is shared across platforms from what is unique to each, preserving privacy while enabling transfer.
why it works It works because users behave consistently across platforms in some ways and consistently differently in others. Teasing apart shared patterns from domain-specific ones lets you transfer knowledge—cross-platform insights—without leaking domain-specific data or trusting dishonest servers.
the deeper reason
The core challenge is making federated recommendation work across domains while keeping data private and verifying that participants are trustworthy. The method works by separating domain-shared knowledge from domain-exclusive patterns: shared knowledge transfers between platforms, while exclusive patterns stay private at each site. This separation is sound because user behavior has universal elements—temporal dynamics, preference intensity—alongside domain-specific elements like the types of items available. Verifying contributions works by measuring each client's influence: if a participant's data consistently improves the shared model, their updates are trusted; if their updates harm performance, they are flagged as malicious or low-quality. This two-module design solves the fundamental tension: you gain cross-domain signal without exposing private domains, and you detect adversaries through their measurable impact on model quality, enabling federated learning among untrusted parties.
Concept-Grounded Detection of Vaccine Misinformation in Multimodal Content Using Interpretable Vision-Language ModelsWWW
uses Extract structured concepts (symbols representing visual and rhetorical ideas) from images, then train a transparent model on those concepts to detect vaccine misinfo.
why it works It works because concepts are interpretable—you can see exactly which visual cues (a syringe plus angry face plus text warning) triggered a detection. By grounding detection in human-understandable concepts rather than opaque scores, you get decisions you can audit and explain, making mistakes obvious and correctable.
the deeper reason
The core challenge is detecting vaccine misinformation in images where visual rhetoric and symbolic meaning matter as much as text, and this multimodal meaning is hard to automate reliably. The method works by extracting interpretable concept-level features from images first, then using those features for classification rather than classifying directly. This two-stage approach works because concepts—like a syringe, a graph, a celebrity face—are recognizable visual objects that humans can inspect, making predictions auditable. When a classical model uses those concept features to judge stance, you can explain why it decided the image was misinformation: 'it detected concepts X and Y together, which correlate with false claims.' This beats direct classification, which obscures reasoning inside a black box. By grounding prediction in structured visual concepts rather than opaque multimodal fusion, the system makes detection more transparent and more robust, enabling public health authorities to trust and explain the system's decisions when combating health misinformation at scale.
Emergence of Structural Disparities in the Web of Scientific CitationsWWW
uses Models how biases in who cites whom compound over time, concentrating recognition among some authors.
why it works Works because homophily and preferential attachment are well-established mechanisms; their combination explains present inequality and why representation alone won't fix it.
the deeper reason
The paper quantifies how scientific focus (measured by citations) concentrates unevenly across gender and institutional groups. The core insight is that citations follow two reinforcing mechanisms: homophily, where people preferentially cite similar authors, and preferential attachment, where high-citation authors attract more citations. The model is sound because these mechanisms are measurable properties of citation networks, and their compound effect mathematically guarantees that initial underrepresentation grows into larger disparities over time. This works because each year's citations feed into the next year's attachment scores—a snowball effect. Understanding these mechanisms explains why simply adding more underrepresented authors doesn't solve the problem; the system's structure perpetuates biases independent of who participates.
Re-understanding Graph Unlearning through MemorizationWWW
uses Assesses how hard it is to unlearn each piece of data, then adjusts the removal strategy based on difficulty.
why it works Works because memorization difficulty varies; easy-to-forget items need less effort, hard ones need special techniques.
the deeper reason
Graph unlearning removes sensitive or mislabeled information from trained systems that learn from examples by forgetting specific nodes or edges. The core challenge is assessing what information the network has memorized and prioritizing what to unlearn first. The method works by measuring how much each systems that learn from examples has memorized specific information, then using this measure to adjust unlearning strength—hard-to-forget information gets stronger unlearning pressure, easy information gets gentler treatment. This is sound because network performance is driven by what it memorized; by directly targeting memorization, the method focuses unlearning effort on information that actually matters rather than treating all information equally. The adaptive strategy guarantees better balance between forgetting the target information and preserving the network's general capability.
Enhancing Domain-Adaptive Hashing via Evidential Learning and Progressive AlignmentWWW
uses Handles noisy labels by assigning uncertainty scores, then gradually aligns cross-domain data by trustiness.
why it works Works because uncertainty scores reveal which labels are likely wrong; progressively trusting aligned samples avoids compounding errors.
the deeper reason
ELPA improves cross-domain image retrieval when the source domain labels contain noise from web crawling or crowdsourcing. The core challenge is that noisy labels corrupt the alignment between domains, and existing methods treat all labels as equally valid. The method uses evidential learning to compute uncertainty in each label, identifying which samples are likely mislabeled by comparing belief masses to updated chance probabilities. It then gradually aligns target-domain samples, prioritizing those already well-matched to source concepts. This is sound because uncertainty directly measures label reliability—high uncertainty means the evidence contradicts the label—and selective alignment prevents the model from being misled by noise. By progressively aligning only trustworthy samples, the method builds robust cross-domain knowledge without forcing alignment through faulty labels.
KEGOD: Kernel-enhanced Latent Substructure Learning for Graph Out-Of-Distribution DetectionWWW
uses Detects unusual graphs by finding inconsistency between what neural and similarity function methods say about structure.
why it works Works because in-distribution graphs show consistent structure from multiple angles; out-of-distribution breaks that agreement.
the deeper reason
KEGOD detects out-of-distribution graphs by learning graph structure patterns using both neural and similarity function methods together. The core challenge is identifying genuine structural signatures of in-distribution graphs when training data is limited and unlabeled. The method works by generating augmented graph views that preserve structural information, then learning patterns through both a neural-network branch and a similarity function-based branch, which capture structure in implicit and explicit ways respectively. This dual approach works because structural properties manifest differently in learned representations versus similarity function measures—neural methods find subtle patterns through weights, while similarity function compute explicit structural signatures—so their agreement identifies genuine distributions, and disagreement flags anomalies. The adaptive mechanism adjusts sensitivity per pattern, tuning the model to focus on structural signals that truly distinguish in from out of distribution.
Blockchain-Enabled, W3C Standards-Compliant Decentralized Zero-Knowledge Proof Framework for Mobile Identity AuthenticationWWW
uses Proves user identity by checking a mathematical signature without revealing the user's secret key, using discrete logarithm hard problems.
why it works If only the user knows the secret key, only they can generate signatures that pass the mathematical check; the check's security rests on a problem so hard it can't be inverted, making forgery impossible.
the deeper reason
This framework enables private authentication by proving knowledge of a secret without revealing it, using cryptographic techniques based on the discrete logarithm problem. The soundness comes from a deep mathematical guarantee: the discrete logarithm is computationally hard, meaning if someone can prove they know it (via the Schnorr protocol), they must truly know it—they cannot fake that knowledge. A zero-knowledge proof adds another layer: the proof itself leaks no information about the secret beyond its existence. The system works because it replaces the vulnerable centralized model (where a server stores all secrets and becomes a breach target) with mathematics: authentication happens through proofs that neither party learns anything exploitable, relying only on computational hardness that holds against all known attacks.
How Human Experts Educate Specialized LLMs: Filling Knowledge Gaps in KG-Augmented Generation through Hallucination DetectionWWW
uses Trains a specialized model on expert knowledge while detecting when the model makes up false facts, accepting expert answers for uncertain cases and model answers when confident.
why it works Models sometimes hallucinate; if you can detect when the model is guessing versus confident, you can trust its confident answers and fall back to experts only when needed, minimizing costly expert involvement while keeping quality high.
the deeper reason
EC-spLLM trains specialized language models by selectively combining internal model knowledge with expert-provided answers, using hallucination detection to decide which source to trust. The core principle is that some problems are answered best by the language model's existing knowledge, while others require external expertise—the key is knowing which is which. By detecting when the model's self-generated answers are unreliable (hallucination detection), the system can confidently adopt expert answers in those cases and use model-generated answers when the model is confident. This bootstrapping works because the hallucination detector itself learns from both sources, creating a feedback loop where the growing dataset of high-quality answers improves both the model and the knowledge graph. Over iterations, the system converges toward a synergy where neither source dominates—expert knowledge fills gaps while model knowledge provides reliable background.
SecureSplit: Mitigating Backdoor Attacks in Split LearningWWW
uses Defends against poisoned data by transforming numeric fingerprints to make poisoned samples stick out, then voting to remove them based on majority agreement.
why it works Poisoned samples are rare and different; transforming to make those differences obvious, then using majority voting as a robustness check, filters them out because a single poison can't outweigh the majority of clean data.
the deeper reason
SecureSplit defends split learning (collaborative training) against backdoor attacks by transforming poisoned numeric fingerprints to make them visually distinct, then filtering them out via majority voting. The principle is that malicious participants subtly alter their numeric fingerprints to embed hidden attack triggers, but these alterations leave detectable fingerprints. By applying a dimensionality transformation that amplifies the difference between clean and poisoned numeric fingerprints, the system makes backdoors visible. Once visible, a simple voting scheme removes the poisoned examples while keeping the majority of clean ones. This works because backdoor attacks must be subtle (to avoid detection during normal training), which means they affect only a fraction of numeric fingerprints. When you amplify the subtle differences and use majority voting, the clean data naturally dominates and removes the contamination.
Can LLMs Fool Graph Learning? Exploring Universal Adversarial Attacks on Text-Attributed GraphsWWW
uses Crafts graph and text perturbations that fool both systems that learn from examples and language model detectors simultaneously.
why it works It works because shared reasoning patterns exist between different architectures. Finding perturbations that exploit those shared patterns breaks multiple models at once by targeting their common knowledge.
the deeper reason
Text-attributed graphs combine topology and semantics, creating two surfaces for adversarial attack—structure and text. Existing attacks target one backbone at a time, but universal attacks must fool both GNNs and language models, a much harder constraint. The insight is to use language models themselves to reason about graph knowledge and generate perturbations that are semantically natural yet globally disruptive: the model understands both what makes graphs coherent and what language sounds convincing. This works because a perturbation that a language model finds natural is more likely to transfer across architectures than raw noise, since naturality is a shared objective.
FairGU: Fairness-aware Graph Unlearning in Social NetworksWWW
uses Remove a person's influence from a network graph while ensuring protected characteristics stay fair and accurate.
why it works When you delete someone from a graph, their connections vanish—the method works by carefully rewiring what remains so that sensitive attributes don't accidentally become over-represented or exposed. Fairness protection requires identifying what would have happened naturally versus what shifted only because they left, then adjusting for that difference.
the deeper reason
FairGU addresses the problem of removing a user's influence from a trained model while keeping predictions fair across demographic groups. The core mathematical challenge is that deleting one node ripples through graph edges in unpredictable ways, and naively removing its connections can shift the learned patterns in ways that harm one group disproportionately. The fix works because by explicitly modeling fairness constraints during removal—making sure sensitive attributes stay equally distributed across outcomes—you counteract the mathematical tendency for small perturbations to magnify bias. This principle holds because fairness violations are driven by asymmetric exposure of attributes, so enforcing balanced exposure during each removal step preserves the statistical property you care about. This matters for social networks where users demand both privacy and fair treatment: you cannot separate these concerns without accepting worse predictions or worse fairness.
SemFuzz: A Semantics-Aware Fuzzing Framework for Network Protocol ImplementationsWWW
uses Test network protocols by finding rule-breaking test cases and checking if responses match what the rules say should happen.
why it works Protocol rules are written in language; when you extract rules precisely and then generate test cases that break them on purpose, violations become obvious—you spot bugs because expected output mismatches actual output. The method works because deep semantic flaws show up as discrepancies, not just crashes.
the deeper reason
SemFuzz identifies real security flaws by testing whether protocol implementations actually follow their written specification rules, not just whether they crash. The deep issue is that most testing catches obvious breaks but misses subtle violations—like accepting an invalid message format that happens to not crash. By extracting formal rules from specification documents and then deliberately violating those rules in test cases, the framework creates a precise boundary between correct and incorrect behavior that goes beyond crash detection. This works because correct protocol implementations must satisfy their specification rules by definition, so violations of those rules are guaranteed to reveal genuine defects. The method applies here because real protocol specifications encode the mathematical contracts that implementations must honor; testing against those contracts catches semantic problems that coarse-grained testing misses.
Shift-Resilient Diffusive Imputation for Variable Subset ForecastingWWW
uses Predict future time series values from incomplete data by decomposing patterns into steady parts and changing parts, then handling each separately.
why it works Real time series split into two layers: correlations between sensors that stay stable over months, and sudden shifts within each sensor across windows. By decomposing these, you can impute the stable part reliably while treating volatility honestly—the steady correlations guide missing values, and the volatile parts adjust for shifts independently.
the deeper reason
SRDI solves the problem of predicting missing time series values when only some sensor measurements are available, and the data distribution shifts over time. The challenge is that existing imputation methods assume stable patterns, but real sensor data changes due to seasonal effects and equipment aging. SRDI's key insight is that within any distribution shift, some parts stay reliably stable—like average daily patterns—while other parts fluctuate wildly. By decomposing the signal into stable and fluctuating components, imputing each separately, and then recombining them, the method ensures that your imputations respect the underlying structure instead of just averaging over inconsistent data. This separation works because stable patterns are mathematically less sensitive to distribution shift, so recovering them reliably becomes tractable. This matters for real systems where missing data is inevitable but predictions must remain accurate despite data drift.
DAPWeb: Construct-Aligned Evaluation of MLLMs for Web-Based Child Mental ScreeningWWW
uses Evaluate whether AI systems can reliably interpret children's drawings as mental health screening by testing consistency across psychological constructs and drawing samples.
why it works Construct validity means the system measures what it claims to measure—if an AI says a drawing shows anxiety, that conclusion should hold across different drawings of the same child and match human experts. Testing consistency and construct alignment reveals whether the system has learned real psychological patterns or just surface correlations.
the deeper reason
DAPWeb evaluates whether vision-language models can reliably score children's drawings for mental health screening as experts would. The core problem is ensuring that automated analysis matches expert judgment across multiple psychological constructs—like aggression or anxiety—and stays consistent when comparing different children's drawings. The framework tests models on clinically-grounded benchmarks where experts have already scored real drawings, then measures whether model scores correlate with expert consensus. This works because clinical validity requires that measurements reflect the intended construct and generalize reliably across new drawings, and statistical correlation to expert judgment directly tests both properties. The method succeeds because expert consensus on well-defined psychological constructs provides a ground truth signal; models that match it have learned to recognize the visual and compositional markers of those constructs. This ensures models can responsibly support early screening workflows where consistency is non-negotiable.
Audit?of?Audits for the Web: Bayesian Meta?Evaluation that Yields Interval?Valued, Threshold?Aligned Fairness ClaimsWWW
uses Pool multiple fairness audits using Bayesian inference to produce interval-based fairness claims that express uncertainty and align with regulatory thresholds.
why it works Different audits disagree due to sampling noise and metric choice—Bayesian pooling treats each audit as an imperfect measurement and combines them into a updated chance distribution, which gives intervals capturing true uncertainty. Soft constraints ensure that fine-grained and coarse-grained audits stay consistent, and uncertainty quantifies the auditor's collective confidence.
the deeper reason
The audit-of-audits framework addresses the problem that single fairness audits produce brittle yes-or-no verdicts even though every audit involves measurement noise and choice uncertainty. By combining multiple independent audits using Bayesian inference, the method produces interval estimates that quantify uncertainty and align to regulatory thresholds. This works because Bayesian combination pools information across audits, smoothing out random noise and revealing genuine signal—the true fairness level is more stable than any single audit's point estimate. The principle applies because audit disagreements stem partly from random variation and partly from systematic differences in measurement approach; combining them orthogonalizes noise while preserving true effects. This matters for governance because interval estimates with known uncertainty are defensible in regulatory settings where binary claims can be challenged, whereas point estimates appear precise but hide hidden risk.
Matrix as Plan: Structured Logical Reasoning with Feedback-Driven ReplanningWWW
uses Improve logical reasoning in language models by representing reasoning as a grid of numbers plan that can be verified and repaired when steps are wrong.
why it works Chain-of-thought reasoning is fragile—parsing breaks when wording shifts slightly. A grid of numbers representation makes dependencies explicit and queryable, so verification can spot missing or circular steps. Feedback-driven replanning then rewrites the grid of numbers to fix errors, replacing brittle parsing with editable structure.
the deeper reason
MatrixCoT improves logical reasoning in language models by organizing reasoning steps in a grid of numbers representation rather than linear chains, adding explicit verification and replanning when steps fail. The core issue is that chain-of-thought prompting works but lacks structure to catch logical inconsistencies, and formal solvers catch errors but fail on small formatting mistakes. By representing reasoning as a dependency grid of numbers, each step becomes verifiable against logical rules and dependencies, and when verification finds contradictions, the model can revise and replan. This works because matrices preserve global structure in a way chains cannot—you can detect missing dependencies or circular logic by inspecting the grid of numbers form. The principle applies because logical reasoning is inherently relational; representing relationships explicitly lets error-correction mechanisms identify and fix problems systematically. This matters because logical correctness is binary—approximate reasoning fails—so making the structure explicit and verifiable raises reliability dramatically.
Real or Rogue? Detecting Malicious Miniapps with Deceptive Reporting InterfaceWWW
uses Detect malicious miniapps that fake the report interface to prevent users from reporting them by learning what legitimate reporting interfaces look like.
why it works A legitimate report interface has consistent visual and behavioral patterns that differ from fakes; malicious ones either discard reports silently or redirect them. Identifying these patterns from millions of interface examples lets the system score and flag lookalikes before they deceive users.
the deeper reason
Real or Rogue detects malicious miniapps that implement fake reporting interfaces to trick users and prevent the platform from learning about malware. The method analyzes reporting interface code to find discrepancies with the official interface—differences in where reports go, obfuscation hiding the real destination, or batch registration patterns suggesting organized fraud. This works because malware must subvert the reporting channel somehow to hide from detection, and those subversions leave measurable traces: reporting endpoints that differ from official ones, code obfuscation to hide the divergence, and behavioral patterns of coordinated malware campaigns. The principle applies because deception requires deviation from legitimate behavior; detecting the deviation directly identifies malware. This matters because the reporting interface is the platform's early-warning system, and clogging it with fake reports or silent discarding is a high-value attack that direct detection catches.
LLM and AI Agent: Golden Rule is All We NeedWWW
uses Derive ethical principles for autonomous systems and human behavior by formalizing the Golden Rule—treating others as you wish to be treated—in game theory.
why it works The Golden Rule works because reciprocity creates stable equilibria: if everyone treats others as they wish to be treated, betrayal becomes costly and cooperation thrives. Game theory formalizes this—mutual fairness and honesty emerge as solutions that maximize collective welfare while respecting individual preferences.
the deeper reason
The Golden Rule—treat others as you wish to be treated—serves as a foundation for moral reasoning in AI systems. Formalizing it within game theory shows that the rule leads to cooperative equilibria and derives core values like fairness and honesty mathematically. The principle works because the Golden Rule embeds reciprocity: if you treat others well, they have incentive to reciprocate, creating stable social dynamics where cooperation is rational. This applies to AI agents because the rule translates into behavioral policies that align self-interest with collective benefit, making ethical behavior both principled and self-reinforcing. The universality matters because it accommodates diverse moral traditions while avoiding fragile rules that only work in specific contexts; reciprocity is cross-culturally robust and mathematically fundamental.
Towards Token-Level Text Anomaly DetectionWWW
uses Detects anomalous text at the word level by learning to assign each word an anomaly score, locating the specific parts of a text that deviate from expected patterns.
why it works Anomalies are words that appear in combinations or contexts the model learned are rare or wrong. Scoring each word independently lets you find exactly which parts break the learned pattern, whereas document-level scoring obscures which words caused the signal.
the deeper reason
Most text anomaly detection methods flag entire messages as normal or abnormal, but this misses the case where a message is mostly fine with a few telltale anomalous parts—like spam with one suspicious phrase, or a review with a forged claim. The method detects anomaly at the level of individual words by learning which specific word sequences violate the pattern of normal text in that category. This works because anomalies leave local traces: grammatical errors occur at specific points, spam keywords cluster in particular phrases, and forged facts contradict known information in localized ways. By modeling what individual word sequences should look like and flagging departures, the method achieves fine-grained detection without needing to flag the entire message.
Beyond Denial-of-Service: The Puppeteer's Attack for Fine-Grained Control in Ranking-Based Federated LearningWWW
uses Manipulates rankings submitted by a corrupted participant to steer a global ranking system toward attacker-chosen outcomes while preserving the statistical appearance of normal convergence.
why it works Ranking systems aggregate discrete orderings, which appear opaque to change detection. By strategically flipping which items rank above or below others, an attacker can shift the aggregate consensus without changing the magnitude of any single update, evading statistical guardrails.
the deeper reason
Federated learning updates models by aggregating changes from many data sources, but ranking-based systems aggregate by counting votes rather than summing numeric changes, which makes them resilient to the usual tricks for poisoning. However, the paper shows an adversary can still manipulate results by carefully crafting which items rank higher or lower—essentially shifting the preference order in directions that help an attacker without being caught. The attack works because the attacker can identify key decision boundaries in the ranking and nudge items across them in ways that are hard to detect; the method maintains a normal-looking learning curve while subtly degrading results. This reveals that discrete ranking, while harder to attack than continuous updates, is not immune if the attacker understands which preference shifts produce the desired damage.
Unsupervised Dense Retrieval with Conterfactual Contrastive LearningWSDM
uses Trains retrieval models to be robust by comparing documents where relevant passages are altered against versions where irrelevant passages are altered, measuring sensitivity to changes in what actually matters.
why it works Causality says relevant passages cause the relevance judgment. If a model's output barely changes when you alter irrelevant passages but shifts dramatically when you alter key passages, the model has learned which parts actually matter. This causality-grounded robustness resists tricks that fake relevance.
the deeper reason
Dense retrieval models rank documents by comparing numerical similarity to a query, but they are brittle—small irrelevant edits to a document can flip its ranking, and the system cannot explain which parts of the document actually matter. The method improves robustness by training the model to be sensitive to changes in the relevant passages (large output shift when key parts change) while insensitive to irrelevant edits (small shift otherwise). This is sound because a well-calibrated ranking function must distinguish signal from noise: if small noise causes large rank changes, the model is overfitting; if removing the main relevant fact barely affects the score, the model is missing the point. By using counterfactual edits—hypothetically removing or changing key passages—the method teaches the model what it should and should not care about, both improving robustness and providing clues about which passages explain each ranking.
Causality with Knowledge Graphs: Semantics and InferenceWSDM
uses Discovers and reasons about cause-effect relationships directly from knowledge graphs by respecting their ontological structure and handling incomplete information.
why it works Knowledge graphs encode what entities are known to be related. Causal reasoning requires knowing what was actually measured versus what is simply missing. Ontologies clarify semantic categories, so causal inference respects real distinctions (a 'side effect' is different from an 'unrelated symptom') instead of treating all relationships alike.
the deeper reason
Causal reasoning—understanding what causes what—depends on assumptions about independence and completeness that rarely hold in knowledge graphs, where missing information is normal and entities are interrelated. This thesis develops methods to apply causal reasoning despite these violations by using the ontology and structure of the graph itself as guidance. The approach is sound because formal relationships in the graph encode domain knowledge—if the graph says two diseases are both subtypes of a condition, that structure constrains which causal explanations make sense. By leveraging what is encoded in the graph's structure and rules, the methods can infer missing facts and account for interference between entities, making causal reasoning reliable even on incomplete relational data.
Can LLMs Uphold Research Integrity? Evaluating the Role of LLMs in Peer Review QualityWSDM
uses Evaluates whether language models can assess the quality and factual accuracy of peer reviews by checking if reviewer claims are actually supported by the paper being reviewed.
why it works Review quality depends on whether a reviewer's criticisms point to real claims in the paper. Verification requires checking which statements in the review are grounded in the paper versus which are unsupported opinions. Models succeed when they distinguish what the paper actually says from what a reviewer claimed it says.
the deeper reason
This is a position talk on using language models to audit research quality at scale—specifically assessing whether peer reviews are detailed and grounded in the papers they evaluate. The core insight is that language models can extract facts and arguments from both the review and the paper, then check whether the reviewer's claims are supported by evidence in the paper itself. This is sound because factual grounding is verifiable: a claim is either backed by the paper or it isn't, making it possible to detect unsupported assertions. However, quality judgments like tone or specificity are subjective, so the speaker combines language model scoring with human-aligned baselines and retrieval-based methods to improve reliability where pure model judgment is unreliable.
DagFC: Dependency-Aware Fact-Checking via Claim-Constructed Knowledge Graphs and Large Language ModelsWSDM
uses Decomposes a complex claim into simpler sub-claims, maps their dependencies as a graph, then verifies each sub-claim while propagating results through the dependency structure to catch reasoning that spans multiple steps.
why it works Complex claims have sub-claims that build on each other; isolating and verifying each one alone misses how earlier conclusions enable later ones. By tracking the flow of reasoning through dependencies, the method captures multi-step logic that a single claim cannot.
the deeper reason
Fact-checking complex claims requires verifying sub-claims, but the challenge is that sub-claims depend on each other—the truth of one constrains whether others make sense. Rather than checking each piece independently, this method models the dependency graph between them, which is sound because reasoning in the real world is causal and sequential. If sub-claim A must be true for sub-claim B to be sensible, checking them in isolation loses that constraint. By scheduling verification to respect dependencies—confirming foundational claims first, then using those results to inform later checks—the method mirrors how humans actually reason through complex arguments. Intermediate results from early verifications become context for later ones, preventing the error cascade that happens when you verify pieces out of logical order.
From Perception to Share: Understanding Misinformation Through User Believability and Linguistic AmbivalenceWSDM
uses Measures how believable users find news claims, models the linguistic conflicts and mixed emotions in text, then uses both as signals in a graph model to separate false claims from true ones.
why it works Misinformation often contains tension between incompatible frames or emotions that signal deception; by capturing both human credibility judgments and the presence of linguistic conflict, the model exploits two independent truths that both point toward falsehood.
the deeper reason
Misinformation detection must model both how people actually judge credibility and the linguistic patterns that exploit that judgment. The method measures real user believability ratings and simultaneously analyzes linguistic ambivalence—mixed emotional and temporal cues within claims. This is sound because the psychology is bidirectional: people are fooled by specific language patterns, AND those patterns leave traces in the text itself. By using both signals together in a graph model, you're saying: this text is suspicious partly because its language is internally inconsistent (emotion mixed with facts, future tense mixing with present), and partly because people marked it as dubious in practice. Neither signal alone is reliable—language mixing could be honest nuance—but together they sharply distinguish misinformation from legitimate reporting.
From Data to Model in Bias: A Statistical Analysis of Political Bias in the C4 Corpus and Its Impact on LLMsWSDM
uses Analyzes the political slant in a large web corpus using persona-based annotation and statistical tests, then measures whether the bias in the data propagates into model outputs through training.
why it works If bias enters models only through the data they learn from, then corpus bias and model bias should correlate; by checking this correlation and testing statistical equivalence, the method proves that the training data is the cause.
the deeper reason
AI language systems inherit biases from their training data, but the question is whether this happens because the data itself is systematically biased or for other reasons. The method measures political lean directly in a web corpus across many topics using statistical rigor. This is sound because if the corpus is left-leaning, any model trained on it will absorb that asymmetry—not through active bias in training, but passively, because the input distribution itself is skewed. By measuring the corpus carefully and then training models and observing their outputs, you can trace the causal path: biased data produces biased models. This is crucial because it means you cannot fix the model problem without addressing the source. The statistical rigor matters because small biases in the data compound into large ones in the model.
Explaining the 'Unexplainable' Large Language ModelsWSDM
uses Show which concepts inside a language model actually drive its answers, instead of pointing to correlations that happen to co-occur but don't cause output.
why it works It works because intervening on true causal concepts (changing what the model thinks, not just its activation patterns) proves what actually steers the answer. Correlations vanish under intervention but causes remain.
the deeper reason
This tutorial on large-language-model explainability establishes that complete mechanistic explanation is mathematically intractable for overparameterized models due to the sheer number of learned parameters and their interdependence. Since full transparency is impossible, the principled alternative is concept-based interpretability: map model behavior onto human-understandable concepts (e.g., 'mentions a person,' 'expresses uncertainty') that users can reason about and verify. This shift from impossible mechanistic explanation to achievable concept recognition lets practitioners build trustworthy systems by proving the model's outputs align with human expectations in ways that matter for decisions.
Design and Evaluation of Whole-Page Experience Optimization for E-commerce SearchWSDM
uses Rank items on complex 2D search layouts by learning which combinations of position and item features lead to long-term user satisfaction, not just clicks.
why it works It works because causal frameworks separate correlation from actual influence; by using quasi-experiments, you avoid false signals like confounding that short-term clicks might hide.
the deeper reason
Search results pages are no longer linear lists but complex layouts where item position, neighbors, and visual design all influence clicks and purchases, yet standard ranking models optimize for position only. The goal is to optimize the entire page experience, including long-term satisfaction like repeat purchases weeks later. The principle is causal effect: measuring what would happen if you placed item A in location 1 versus location 2 requires isolating the effect of placement from all other differences between users who see each position. Quasi-experimental data—users assigned to pages slightly differently—reveals these effects if analyzed carefully. This principle applies because page position affects both immediate click behavior and long-term trust and discovery: a well-placed item may not be clicked today but discover a shopper to a brand they visit later. By using causal reasoning to measure long-term impact and then optimizing page layout for it rather than clicks alone, the model captures the true value of placement and visual emphasis, solving the business problem of sustainable shopper satisfaction rather than optimizing narrow short-term clicks.
Identifiable Disentangled Representation Learning for Causal Inference under Network InterferenceWSDM
uses Estimate individual treatment effects on a network by learning three types of hidden factors: which help assign treatment, which confuse treatment with outcome, and which adjust for networks.
why it works It works because treatment effects are biased by confounders and spillover; separating hidden factors lets you identify which are true confounders versus which are just network side effects.
the deeper reason
Estimating how an individual would respond to an intervention (like a price discount) from network data is hard because people influence each other and confounding factors drive both the decision to intervene and the response. The goal is to disentangle these causes. The principle is that hidden factors divide into roles: some create instruments that justify intervention choices without affecting outcomes (like budget availability), some cause bias by influencing both intervention and outcome (like user wealth), and some affect outcomes only given the intervention. If you can identify these three roles separately, you can measure the intervention effect by adjusting for the confounding factors while preserving the instrumental factors that made the intervention natural. This principle holds because causal structure is identifiable when the roles reflect genuinely different information flows in the data. By learning representations that capture these distinct factors and keeping it simple them to maintain separation, the model recovers the true causal effect sizes even when people influence each other, solving the core inference problem of learning how to optimally target interventions from observational network data.
ChorusCVR: Chorus Supervision for Entire Space Post-Click Conversion Rate ModelingWSDM
uses Estimate whether a user will convert after clicking by treating un-clicked items and clicked-but-not-converted items differently, since they have different meanings.
why it works It works because un-clicked items are merely unknown while clicked-non-conversions are true negatives, so treating them as the same misleads the model into thinking absence of action means the same thing as action-followed-by-rejection.
the deeper reason
ChorusCVR learns conversion likelihood by training on both clicked and unclicked samples, while carefully distinguishing clicked-but-unconverted from truly unclicked users. The method is sound because conversion prediction must face a gap between training and real-world conditions: at training time you only see clicked samples, but at deployment you rank all users. To close this gap without noise, you must split unclicked samples into two kinds—true negatives (the system worked, user just wasn't interested) versus missing labels (no interaction yet). This distinction is the key because it prevents the model from conflating irrelevance with disinterest. By learning robust soft labels that respect this distinction, the method ensures the conversion model generalizes to the full user population at inference time.
Risk-Aware Utility Re-Ranking for Financial Asset RecommendationWSDM
uses Rank financial assets by expected value accounting for risk and how likely a user is to take each recommendation, then adjust to trade a little ranking quality for better real-world returns.
why it works It works because a perfect ranking that users ignore is worthless and a ranking that delivers losses is harmful—balancing adoption probability and risk tolerance yields real value, not theoretical rank order.
the deeper reason
RURA re-ranks financial recommendations by optimizing for both user adoption and realized returns while respecting user risk tolerance. The core principle is that a good recommendation must survive contact with reality: a user must adopt it and the asset must perform. This two-objective approach is sound because maximizing relevance alone ignores outcomes, while maximizing returns alone ignores user tastes and limits diversification. By computing expected utility for each user (factoring their risk tolerance and likelihood of adoption), RURA balances these competing goals. The method works because it keeps diversity intact while trading minimal ranking loss for real gains in return, solving the practical problem of building recommenders that users trust because recommendations actually pay off.
Debias Once for All: A Data-Centric Strategy for Fair Machine LearningWSDM
uses Make a machine learning model fair by rewriting its training data to come from a synthetic fair dataset instead of changing the model itself.
why it works It works because unfairness lives in the data—historical bias encoded in patterns—so fixing data upstream of any model makes all downstream models fair by default, whereas model-specific fixes break portability.
the deeper reason
FairData synthesizes a training dataset that promotes fair model outcomes by matching how well a randomly initialized model learns on synthetic data to how it learns on original data, while explicitly encouraging group fairness. The method is sound because dataset construction happens before model training, so biases baked into data propagate through any downstream model. By optimizing synthetic data to match original learning dynamics while keeping it simple for equitable outcomes across groups, the approach ensures the model has fair training material. This principle applies because historical data encodes societal biases that no amount of model tuning can fully correct; the fairness must begin at the data stage. This data-centric strategy solves the fairness problem by making it model-agnostic—any downstream model trained on fair data inherits fairness automatically.
On Causal and Anticausal LLM-based Data SynthesisWSDM
uses Generate raw diverse data first, then label it, versus the reversed approach of baking labels into generation prompts.
why it works The causal order mirrors real data creation: facts exist first, then we label them. This avoids the backward approach where labels distort generation, which makes the model overfit to label-specific patterns instead of learning genuine variety.
the deeper reason
Synthetic data quality depends on how the data generation mirrors real-world patterns. This work compares two directions: generating diverse raw data first then labeling it (causal), versus numeric fingerprints the target label in the prompt and generating specifically to match that label (anticausal). The principle underlying causal ordering is that forcing a language model to generate data backward from labels creates an artificial shortcut—the model learns to describe the label directly rather than the underlying features that caused it. Real data contains messy correlations and variations beyond what the label captures; anticausal synthesis skips that diversity. Models trained on causal synthetic data see richer patterns because the generation process matches how real data forms, making the trained models generalize better to unseen examples that contain the natural complexity that labels alone cannot capture.
KnowFC: Navigating Knowledge Conflicts in Large Language Model-based Fact-CheckingWSDM
uses Learn when a language model should trust its built-in knowledge versus external evidence, then build reasoning chains that prevent conflicting knowledge from derailing fact-checking.
why it works It works because confidence is not truth. By identifying where a model's internal knowledge is reliable versus where it's overconfident, you can rely on evidence when the model is weak and trust itself when the evidence is weak, rather than always fighting between them.
the deeper reason
The core issue is that AI language systems carry internal beliefs that can contradict external evidence when fact-checking. The method estimates what the model knows versus doesn't know through confidence signals, then adapts evidence retrieval based on those boundaries. The principle is that a model performs most reliably when it stays in its zone of actual knowledge; if it claims high confidence incorrectly (a known human bias), gathering evidence cannot override a false internal certainty. By treating the model's confidence as a signal for what evidence to fetch, and then using causal methods to isolate how internal knowledge influences reasoning, the system avoids cases where the model overrides correct evidence with wrong internal knowledge. This works because it separates the model's knowledge boundaries from its reasoning process, preventing false confidence from contaminating the fact-check result.
