Joint Graph Learning for Robust Causal Inference over Knowledge GraphsWSDM
uses Fill in missing attributes and estimate treatment effects by modeling how entities influence each other in the knowledge graph structure.
why it works It works because missing data and causal effects are not independent problems. Using the relational structure to infer missing attributes helps the model understand connections between entities, which then allows it to account for how one entity's treatment ripples through related entities.
the deeper reason
The problem is estimating causal effects in knowledge graphs where data is incomplete and entities influence each other. The approach reformulates this as two linked prediction tasks: filling missing attributes and estimating treatment effects while accounting for interference between connected entities. The principle is that if you handle missing data and interference together through a unified learned representation, you can estimate effects that remain valid even when the data is sparse. Graph methods work here because they explicitly model which entities affect which others; by letting information flow through the graph structure during learning, the system discovers interference patterns that affect causality estimates. Missing attributes get filled consistently with these relational patterns, so the final causal estimates account for the true dependencies rather than treating each entity in isolation or naively ignoring missing information.
CelebCaption: A Benchmark Dataset for Identity-Sensitive Unlearning in Image CaptioningWSDM
uses Measure whether unlearning methods actually remove a specific person's influence from image captions or just hide it with false information.
why it works It works because true unlearning is different from obfuscation. If you test with varied captions, controlled presence and absence of names, and measure both generation quality and susceptibility to membership attacks, you can tell if the model genuinely forgot versus just learned to deny.
the deeper reason
Machine unlearning tries to remove a person's data from a trained model without retraining from scratch, which is important for privacy. The fundamental challenge is measuring whether the influence truly disappeared—most datasets designed for this lack enough identity-specific variations to catch when a model generates false information instead of actually forgetting. The method establishes three measurable criteria: reducing how often the model mentions a specific person, removing their identity from generated captions, and maintaining overall caption quality. By creating a large dataset with multiple captions per person (some naming them, some not, some detailed versus summary), the evaluation can quantitatively check each criterion. This works because it forces unlearning methods to prove they actually erased identity information rather than just pausing brief outputs; the varied captions reveal whether models truly forgot or merely suppressed certain patterns.
Planning Before Retrieval: A Constrained Planner–Executor Framework for Reliable and Efficient KG-Augmented ReasoningWSDM
uses Plan structured queries over a knowledge graph by reasoning about which constraints and connections matter for answering a question.
why it works Real-world knowledge is connected through relationships — knowing which relationships matter and in what order to follow them turns a chaotic search into a directed path. Planning first ensures you only retrieve what actually answers the question, filtering out coincidental connections.
the deeper reason
The core problem is retrieving facts from a knowledge graph reliably to answer questions. The soundness lies in treating retrieval as planned search, not heuristic guessing. By analyzing the question first to infer what paths through the graph matter, the system constrains exploration—it asks only the questions that matter and stops when constraints are satisfied. This works because knowledge graphs are structured: facts link in predictable ways, and knowing what to look for lets you avoid exploring dead ends. This transforms RAG from a fuzzy matching game into auditable reasoning, solving the real problem that current systems generate answers that look plausible but can't explain how they arrived there.
Geo-Personalization Bias in News Search: Analyzing Filter Bubbles in Search Engine Results with Multi-Perspective LLM AnnotationWSDM
uses Analyze search results across locations and time to measure how geographic personalization, local events, and topic traits shape filter bubbles.
why it works Filter bubbles aren't random — they're systematic patterns caused by specific factors. By controlling which factors vary (location one time, topic another time) and measuring the result each time, you isolate what actually causes each bubble, separating real effects from coincidence.
the deeper reason
Search engines show different results to different locations, creating filter bubbles where users see only local viewpoints. The analysis uses language models to annotate search results from multiple geographic perspectives, then compares what results users in different regions see. This works because language models can represent diverse interpretations of a topic—right-wing, left-wing, neutral—and label results accordingly. By applying multiple perspectives consistently, the analysis reveals whether personalization algorithms hide disagreement or surface it. This systematic comparison, repeated across locations and topics, builds evidence of where filter bubbles form. This exposes how search engines shape what people discover, solving the real problem that algorithmic curation is usually invisible.
Constructing Commonsense Knowledge Graph for Persona ConsistencyWSDM
uses Builds a commonsense graph encoding which statements agree or conflict with a persona, then identifies and rewrites AI responses that contradict the established persona.
why it works It works because persona conflicts are rooted in semantic meaning, not just surface text. A knowledge graph captures which ideas logically belong together; checking responses against it catches indirect contradictions that keyword matching misses.
the deeper reason
Conversational AI systems often contradict themselves implicitly—saying something now that conflicts with earlier statements or commonsense rules about a stated persona—but catching these requires understanding what should be true about a consistent character. Building a commonsense knowledge graph about personas creates an explicit map of which statements align with which personas. The method then recognizes responses that violate this map and rewrites them into consistency. The soundness principle is logical coherence: if a system's outputs all respect the same implicit rules, they will appear consistent. By making rules explicit and measurable, the system can detect and fix violations before they confuse users. This transforms persona consistency from an implicit hope into an explicit, verifiable property.
Bridge Breaking for Graph Neural NetworksWSDM
uses Identifies bridge nodes that connect unlike classes in networks, then aggregates their neighborhoods differently to prevent the smoothing that causes misclassification.
why it works It works because bridge nodes sit at boundaries where smoothing is wrong—averaging across different classes doesn't help. By detecting these critical nodes and treating them specially, you preserve the sharp distinctions that matter for classification.
the deeper reason
Graph systems that learn from examples assume connected nodes share similar properties (homophily), but real networks have bridge nodes—connectors between different groups—where neighbors have opposing properties, violating this assumption and breaking the model. The approach identifies these critical nodes and applies a different aggregation rule that prevents smoothing away important differences. The principle is that information smoothing, which works well among similar nodes, becomes harmful when neighbors actually disagree. By measuring which nodes are bridges using graph structure alone and treating them specially, the system avoids the mathematical pathology that sinks standard models. Preserving differences where they matter prevents the false consensus that kills performance on heterogeneous networks.
Enhanced Cold-Start Sequential Recommendation with Causal Diffusion Preference ModelingWSDM
uses Generates preference patterns for new users by identifying causal interactions in historical sequences, then using those patterns to initialize sequential recommendation models.
why it works It works because not all past interactions drive future behavior equally—some are noise. Causal analysis isolates the interactions that truly shape preference; generating representations from only those signals gives new users a head start grounded in real drivers.
the deeper reason
Cold-start sequential recommendation breaks when users lack history because models have no behavioral patterns to learn. The system first isolates the user's interactions most likely to reveal true preferences, filtering noise from accidental clicks. Then it uses causal inference to identify which factors actually drive purchasing behavior versus which just correlate, and conditions a diffusion model on these true drivers to generate realistic synthetic behavior. The guarantee from causal logic is that conditioning on causes, not mere correlations, produces realistic predictions because causes are the generative mechanism. By identifying true preference drivers and using them to seed behavior generation, the model creates believable cold-start user profiles. This transforms missing history into generated-but-grounded alternatives.
Uncertainty Quantification for Dynamical NetworksWSDM
uses Quantify uncertainty in network predictions by estimating how much unknown structure, noisy parameters, and random fluctuations change the system's future behavior.
why it works It works because real networks have hidden pieces and noise; uncertainty quantification asks 'how wrong could we be?' By measuring how sensitive predictions are to what we don't know, we learn which unknowns actually matter and build stronger forecasts.
the deeper reason
Dynamical networks are systems where the structure itself changes based on activity—edges form or fade, weights shift—making them inherently uncertain. Quantifying uncertainty means establishing bounds on how wrong predictions could be given incomplete information about the network's current state and parameters. The guarantee comes from rigorous probability accounting: if you measure the range of plausible network structures and their dynamics, you can compute which predictions remain valid across all possibilities and which break under some but not others. This matters because networks are fragile—small changes in topology can flip a system from stable synchronization to cascading failure—so knowing the range of outcomes prevents false confidence. For epidemiology or power grids, this framework transforms vague worry into actionable risk: you know how much room for surprise exists and can design safeguards accordingly.
Credibility Drift Attacks: LLM Crafted Adversarial Manipulations That Flip News BelievabilityWSDM
uses Make minimal, targeted edits to news stories that subtly change causal claims and qualifying facts, shifting perceived credibility while avoiding obvious tampering.
why it works It works because humans evaluate credibility through causal reasoning—does the evidence support the claim? Removing a qualifier or reversing causality breaks that chain invisibly. Small changes fool readers because they alter the logical structure beneath the surface, not the words themselves.
the deeper reason
News believability depends on subtle cues: causal language, qualifications, acknowledging counterevidence. The attack makes small, targeted edits—removing qualifiers, shifting causality, hiding caveats—that shift readers' trust in the story. This works because human judgment of credibility relies on these linguistic markers as heuristics; people subconsciously trust language that acknowledges complexity and doubt words that oversimplify. By making minimal, context-aware changes, the attack preserves the surface story so casual readers miss the manipulation, while the edits systematically weaken the linguistic signals of careful reporting. This exploits the gap between what a headline literally says and the tone of authority it conveys.
Self-Paced Fair Ranking with Loss as a Proxy for BiasWSDM
uses Score items to rank them, but learn to prioritize examples with low errors while gradually introducing harder cases, reducing gender bias without explicit demographic labels.
why it works It works because easier examples teach the model the right patterns first, and gradually adding harder cases prevents it from memorizing biased shortcuts. By filtering through how confidently the model scores each example, you can detect when gender bias is causing errors and correct it.
the deeper reason
The method computes a fairness score by monitoring how consistently a ranker assigns low loss to examples across demographic groups. The underlying principle is that loss magnitude serves as a reliable measure of data quality and encoding reliability — harder, more ambiguous examples naturally produce higher loss. By starting with only low-loss examples and gradually incorporating higher-loss ones, the model learns to rank reliably on clean cases before tackling noisy, bias-prone ones. This ordering prevents the model from absorbing societal biases that hide in harder cases, letting it solve the real problem: building fair rankings without needing explicit demographic labels.
Confounder-Aware Causal Graph Learning Framework for Multivariate Time Series AnalysisWSDM
uses Build causal relationships between time-series variables at two scales (whole sequences and local segments), modeling hidden confounders with dedicated variables rather than assuming all causes are observed.
why it works It works because real data has unmeasured causes affecting multiple variables at once. By explicitly representing these hidden causes with special variables, then solving for what they must be from the patterns you see, you can untangle which relationships are truly causal versus merely correlated.
the deeper reason
The method estimates true causal relationships among time-series variables by explicitly modeling hidden confounders that affect multiple measured quantities. The soundness comes from causal sufficiency: if all confounding factors are properly represented, the remaining dependence between variables reflects true causal influence. By separating confounders into persistent (slow-changing) and transient (fast-changing) types at multiple time scales, the model disentangles their different effects. This design lets researchers understand which variable actually caused which outcome, not just which were correlated, solving the critical problem in complex systems where hidden factors cloud every measurement.
Improving Interpretability of Cognitive Diagnosis Models with LLM-based Semantic AugmentationSIGIR
uses Predict student mastery by analyzing not just right or wrong, but which specific answer students chose, using language models to infer what misconception each wrong answer represents.
why it works It works because different wrong answers reveal different misconceptions. By mapping each answer to the specific idea gap it represents, you move from a crude right/wrong signal to precise diagnosis, enabling targeted teaching rather than generic feedback.
the deeper reason
The method infers student mastery by capturing which specific answer option was selected, not just whether it was correct, enabling the system to distinguish qualitatively different types of errors and misconceptions. The principle is that error type carries diagnostic information: a student choosing a particular wrong answer reveals a specific misconception, not just a generic knowledge gap. By semantically analyzing what each answer option represents, the model recovers this information. This solves the critical problem in education that binary correctness labels destroy the signal needed for interpretable diagnosis and personalized guidance.
Mitigating Adversarial Attacks by Transferring LLM-generated Narrative Reasoning for Robust Fake News DetectionSIGIR
uses Use a language model to spot consistent stories in how fake news spreads, then teach a graph algorithm to ignore isolated conflicting information and weight the coherent thread.
why it works Fake news attacks introduce noise meant to confuse the aggregator. By aligning everything to a consistent global narrative first, you make the aggregator robust to random noise.
the deeper reason
The core problem is detecting false news when the propagation network is deliberately corrupted by injected messages designed to mislead graph-aggregating models. The method works by using a trusted reasoning model to first understand what each news story should logically mean, then uses this expected meaning as an anchor to identify which nodes (users, messages) are inconsistent with the true narrative. This principle holds because true and false information require fundamentally different logical structures: false signals create internal contradictions when checked against sound reasoning, whereas genuine information maintains coherence. By anchoring to learned narratives rather than trusting the corrupted graph directly, the system filters out injected misinformation that would otherwise mislead node aggregation.
Diagnosing Identifiability in Two-Tower Models for Unbiased Learning to RankSIGIR
uses Test whether a model's ability to distinguish relevance from position bias is actually coming from the data by perturbing the parameters and checking if performance drops.
why it works A parameter that can be moved without hurting prediction is not constrained by the data; you cannot identify it. Measuring sensitivity reveals which parameters the data actually pins down.
the deeper reason
The core problem is distinguishing whether a ranking model can truly learn relevance and position bias separately from clicks, or whether the data lacks enough variation to identify both. The method works by testing whether each parameter is genuinely constrained by the data: shifting a parameter away from its optimal value and retraining—if click prediction suffers, the parameter was identified; if not, the data cannot uniquely determine it. This principle applies because identifiability is a property of data and model together: even if two parameter settings fit equally well, their different click predictions on new data reveal which one the current data actually determined. By measuring actual performance sensitivity to perturbations, the system diagnoses whether failure comes from model assumptions, limited data variation, or small sample sizes.
FollowTable: A Benchmark for Instruction-Following Table RetrievalSIGIR
uses Rank tables by relevance when users include both topic constraints and fine-grained schema requirements like column semantics and value ranges, not topic alone.
why it works It works because relevance is multidimensional: a table may be topically perfect but structurally wrong (wrong columns, wrong granularity). By ranking jointly on topic and schema satisfaction, the model distinguishes topical matches that are useless from those that actually fit the user's intent. Instructions reveal causal constraints, not coincidental patterns.
the deeper reason
Table retrieval instructions demand more than topical similarity: they specify content constraints like include-this-column-exclude-that-row and schema requirements like find-numeric-aggregations. Traditional relevance scoring ignores these because it only matches topics. The method works by treating instructions as explicit constraints that must be satisfied alongside relevance. Building a benchmark where instructions genuinely require different tables forces the model to learn to distinguish topically similar tables by their structural properties. The Instruction Responsiveness Score measures whether ranking changes appropriately when instructions change, directly testing instruction-sensitivity rather than just overall relevance. This metric-driven approach ensures models learn that instructions override topic similarity when they conflict. The core principle is that consistent instruction-following requires both understanding language constraints and knowing schema semantics—column types, value domains, granularity levels. By explicitly measuring these abilities, the method guarantees models develop instruction awareness rather than defaulting to topic matching.
Multi-Perspective Driven Expected Location Preferences for Next POI RecommendationsSIGIR
uses Predict next POI by modeling real preferences separately from contextual behaviors, and inferring where users actually intended versus settled for.
why it works It works because visit data mixes genuine preference with circumstance — work locations skew behavior — so filtering out external causes leaves true preferences to predict future choices accurately.
the deeper reason
MPDC models user preferences from two angles: what they actually choose (behavior) and where they intended to go (spatial intention). It then learns to distinguish which check-ins reflect true preference versus external pressure or practicality. The principle is that mixing signals reduces bias—when you measure both what happened and what the user likely wanted, the gap between them reveals confounding factors. Removing those confounders from the preference signal makes the learned model more predictive of future genuine choices, not just repeating past patterns that were partly forced.
Beyond Semantic Relevance: Counterfactual Risk Minimization for Robust Retrieval-Augmented GenerationSIGIR
uses Score retrieved documents by how well they steer a model toward correct answers even when queries are adversarially biased, using causal intervention to identify true evidence.
why it works It works because causal intervention reveals which documents genuinely cause correct answers versus which only happen to be similar. By testing documents against perturbed queries that contain cognitive biases, you identify evidence that works for the right reasons, not just cases where the bias and truth align.
the deeper reason
Semantic relevance-based retrieval fails when queries contain cognitive biases like false premises: the system retrieves documents matching the biased query, reinforcing hallucinations rather than correcting them. The core insight is that safety requires distinguishing relevance from robustness—a document may match the query but still be wrong if the query itself is flawed. The method works by simulating how queries break under adversarial perturbation (changing phrasing or correcting false premises), then learning which documents maintain correct answers despite these perturbations. This requires treating evidence strength differently: a document earns high evidence scores not by matching the original query, but by being sufficient to steer correct answers even when the query is corrupted. By training an evidence critic on this principle, the system learns to prioritize retrievals that are robust to user bias rather than sensitive to it, solving the robustness-utility tradeoff.
Decoding Multimodal Cues: Unveiling the Implicit Meaning Behind Hateful VideosSIGIR
uses Identify hateful content by weighing different harmful elements (images, words, sounds) together and explaining which parts caused the decision.
why it works It works because hate content is multimodal—harmful elements in different forms reinforce each other. By learning which elements matter and why, you separate genuine reasons for flagging from noise, and humans can verify your reasoning is sound.
the deeper reason
Hateful videos contain harmful meaning spread across sound, visuals, and text that must all be considered together. The method chains evidence from each modality into a unified explanation, showing how visual cues plus words plus tone combine to establish harm. Direct Preference Optimization steers the model toward reasoning chains that correctly combine this evidence and away from ones that miss it, penalizing contradictory conclusions. This works because the optimal reasoning path through multimodal evidence is the one that actually explains the decision correctly, and training on correct versus incorrect reasoning paths teaches the model to reliably follow sound logic.
OntoEL: Neuro-Symbolic Biomedical Entity Linking with Differentiable Fuzzy EL&#8869; ReasoningSIGIR
uses Match medical entity names to their true identities using learned nearness in a space, then recheck each match against logical rules that describe what's valid.
why it works It works because entity synonyms cluster together when you measure them as nearness; soft rule-checking then filters out candidates that logically contradict the context, eliminating ambiguity that pure similarity alone would miss.
the deeper reason
Medical entity linking must resolve ambiguous mentions using both surface similarity and ontological constraints—the formal rules that govern which concepts logically belong together. Fuzzy logic provides a mathematical bridge: it scores soft consistency between a candidate and the ontological rules without requiring the Boolean all-or-nothing match that breaks on real messy data. Classical reasoners handle the structural rules exactly, while soft evaluation captures grey cases. This works because the true entity is the one most consistent with both the learned surface representations and the logical constraints simultaneously; scoring both grounds the retrieval in real meaning, not just coincidental word overlap.
Hierarchical Denoising Entire Space Multi-Task Model for Post-Click Conversion Rate Prediction with Noisy LabelsSIGIR
uses Predict if a user will convert after clicking by fixing the mistakes that arise when training data is corrupted by noise from multiple stages.
why it works It works because noise compounds across stages: noisy clicks plus noisy conversions create a mess. Explicitly modeling and correcting for this hierarchical noise makes loss estimates honest again, so the model learns true patterns instead of noise.
the deeper reason
Conversion prediction must estimate user intent from noisy click labels feeding into noisier conversion labels stacked hierarchically. The method corrects the loss function mathematically by accounting for noise at each level, ensuring the optimizer receives an unbiased signal about true user preferences underneath the label corruption. Forward correction avoids numerical instability by working with the data as observed rather than trying to invert the noise model. This works because correcting for known bias sources makes each training step point toward the true decision boundary, even when the labels themselves are unreliable—the unbiased loss guarantees convergence to the right classifier.
Do Simulated Users Need to Remember? Analyzing the Impact of Memory Models in Conversational Search EvaluationSIGIR
uses Simulate users during multi-turn search to test systems, varying whether the simulator remembers past interactions or forgets them.
why it works It works because simulated user behavior must match real patterns to produce trustworthy rankings. Memory affects how queries change across turns; capturing the right memory model makes simulation predictions match what real users would do.
the deeper reason
Simulated search users must behave realistically enough that system rankings measured from simulation match those from real users. Long-term memory helps simulators track what they learned across an entire search session, so their later queries naturally build on earlier findings. Short-term memory of just the last action adds noise without helping the simulator reason about the search goal. This works because true system quality emerges from users who remember their search intent and adapt their queries, not from users forgetting constantly; simulators that remember align their behavior with actual user mental models.
SciCheck: Reasoning Distillation for Biomedical Claim VerificationSIGIR
uses Verify medical claims by adjust a small model on reasoning examples from a large model, trained to mimic correct reasoning paths only.
why it works It works because reasoning can be distilled. If you capture the reasoning steps that lead to correct verdicts and filter out wrong ones, a smaller model learns the decision rules without needing the original large model or perfect evidence.
the deeper reason
Biomedical claim verification requires sound reasoning chains backed by evidence, yet inference-time evidence is often incomplete and scaling AI language systems is expensive. Reasoning distillation transfers reasoning traces from a powerful model into a smaller one by teaching it to follow the same logical steps. The data pipeline filters for traces leading to correct answers and mixes web and gold evidence during training so the small model learns to reason robustly with imperfect sources. This works because reasoning is a learnable skill separable from model size—once reasoning steps are made explicit and filtered for correctness, a smaller model can internalize them and apply them efficiently to new claims.
An Epistemic Position-Based Click Model: From Interactions to Epistemic Distributions of Relevance and BiasSIGIR
uses Estimates ranges of uncertainty around click probabilities by modeling how strongly relevance and screen position each influence whether a user clicks.
why it works It works because observed clicks are shaped by two separate forces: how good the item really is and where it appeared on screen. Uncertainty ranges reveal which factors are well-understood versus which are guesses, making predictions more trustworthy.
the deeper reason
Click prediction models estimate whether a user will click a ranked item, but they typically output only a single probability, not a measure of how confident that estimate is. The key insight is that past click data contains both systematic signal—items ranked higher truly attract more clicks—and measurement noise and unknown confounders. A Bayesian approach generates a full distribution over uncertainty, capturing epistemic gap: what remains unknown about the mechanisms driving clicks. By representing relevance and position effects as probability distributions, the model quantifies when its estimates are unreliable, which matters for decision-making: should you rely on this prediction to rerank, or seek more information? This works because evidence quality varies; some clicks are robust across contexts while others are fluky, and distributions capture that spread of error. The practical value is better calibration: recommendation systems can now distinguish confident predictions from risky guesses, enabling safer ranking decisions.
Tokens to Types: Context Editing with Selective Entity Abstraction for Grounded GenerationSIGIR
uses Silences misleading background knowledge in language models by replacing entity names with abstract type labels before generation, so the model must rely on provided context rather than learned starting guess associations.
why it works It works because language models have strong learned associations between names and facts from training data, which can overpower new information. Replacing names with generic labels blocks those spurious lexical paths while preserving the relational structure needed to reason about the new scenario.
the deeper reason
Language models are trained on web-scale data that includes facts about entities like Paris, Cairo, and specific companies, and they're very good at retrieving those memorized facts. When a user provides context that contradicts training data—for example, defining Paris as a fictional city—the model's learned associations still fire, causing it to hallucinate facts from training rather than ground itself in the given context. By replacing entity names with abstract typed identifiers that carry no lexical association—City angle1 instead of Paris—the model loses the ability to match against memorized facts and must instead reason relationally using only the provided context. This works because lexical matching is a shortcut that competes with relational reasoning; removing the tempting shortcut forces deeper focus to structure. No model retraining is needed because the mechanism operates purely on input preprocessing; the model's underlying reasoning capability is unchanged. The practical result is that models now honor provided context even when it contradicts their training distribution, solving a critical failure mode in enterprise and counterfactual settings.
Mining Informative Interests via Latent Cross Reasoning for Search Enhanced RecommendationSIGIR
uses Identifies which past searches genuinely reveal recommendation intent by filtering noisy signals in a learned hidden space, then using only those reliable searches to recommend items.
why it works It works because users search for many things—some show true preference for item types, others are outdated or off-topic. By learning to recognize which signals align with genuine recommendation needs, it avoids spurious correlations that would degrade predictions.
the deeper reason
Search logs contain a mix of signals: some queries predict what a user will buy next, but others are exploratory or unrelated to their current purchasing intent. Naive joint modeling treats all search queries equally, allowing irrelevant searches to create spurious correlations that degrade recommendation accuracy. The core idea is to encode search and recommendation histories into a unified hidden representation capturing global interests, then iteratively filter that representation to amplify search signals correlated with item clicks. This works because contrastive learning finds features that are jointly present in positive pairs and absent in negative pairs; queries that co-occur with clicked items will be highlighted, while noisy queries will be suppressed. Each reasoning iteration refines the selection, progressively removing the influence of detrimental search behaviors. The result is a user model that learns when to trust search and when to ignore it, solving the fundamental problem that user behavior logs are heterogeneous and many signals are uninformative.
Mitigating Structural Overfitting: A Distribution-Aware Rectification Framework for Missing Feature ImputationSIGIR
uses Fills missing user features using learned feature patterns and graph structure, then corrects distribution shift at test time by projecting distorted features back onto the true learned pattern.
why it works It works because missing values can be inferred from neighbors and learned patterns, but the model may overfit to structural peculiarities during training. By learning the true underlying feature surface and realigning at test time, you recover natural semantic diversity and handle new graph structures correctly.
the deeper reason
Graph learning systems often encounter nodes with missing features, and existing methods impute values by propagating neighboring features through the graph. However, this approach assumes the graph structure itself is informative for the missing features, which fails when data is missing due to factors unrelated to graph position. More critically, when deploying to a new graph with different structure, the imputation distribution shifts, causing generalization failure. DART solves this by learning the true underlying feature distribution using masked autoencoding—recovering natural feature patterns even from partial, noisy data. Crucially, at test time on new graphs, it projects the structurally biased imputations back onto the learned distribution surface, removing the distribution shift. This works because the surface captures semantic regularity: what real features actually look like, independent of graph structure. Projecting back onto it filters out artifacts introduced by different graph topologies. The result is imputation that generalizes to unseen graph structures, solving a critical bottleneck in deploying graph models across domains.
Looking for the Bottleneck in Fine-grained Temporal Relation ClassificationSIGIR
uses Classifies relationships between events in text by first determining point relationships between time boundaries, then decoding those point relationships into interval relationships.
why it works It works because interval relationships are complex and rare in data, making direct learning hard. Point relationships between endpoints are simpler and more frequent, so learning those first provides reliable intermediate structure that combines naturally into the final answer.
the deeper reason
Temporal interval relations are complex: thirteen distinct interval types capture whether two events overlap, precede, follow, or contain each other. Directly classifying all thirteen types from text is difficult because the label space is large and many relations are rare. The insight is that intervals are defined by their endpoints; if you classify the temporal relation between all four endpoint pairs—start-to-start, start-to-end, end-to-start, end-to-end—you fully determine the interval relation. This works because point relations are simpler to learn: they're binary comparisons that appear more frequently in data and have clearer linguistic correlates. Once you know all point relations, the interval relation is deterministically derived, guaranteeing correctness. The decomposition reduces the learning problem to four simpler binary classifications that can each be trained on abundant data, exploiting structure in the task rather than brute-force label prediction. The result is more accurate temporal understanding with cleaner learning dynamics.
RES-MR: Risk-Aware Reasoning for Explainable and Safe Medication RecommendationSIGIR
uses Learns drug recommendations by reasoning through patient cases, then adjusts to balance cure likelihood against each person's individual drug risks.
why it works It works because showing the reasoning path grounds recommendations in clinical logic, and personalizing safety tolerances respects that different patients have different risk profiles that affect what counts as safe.
the deeper reason
Medication recommendations must be both justified (so doctors understand why) and safe (avoiding harmful drug combinations for each patient). The method uses two coupled stages: first, a reasoning distillation stage that trains the model to generate human-like reasoning about drug selection from patient data; second, a risk optimization stage that adjusts recommendations by learning which drug features to promote and which to avoid, customized to each patient's risk tolerance. This works because separating explanation from safety allows the model to reason transparently while still respecting individual variation in risk; the learned drug feature prototypes act as anchors that steer the model away from dangerous combinations by construction rather than relying on a single blanket constraint. This produces recommendations that are both interpretable and personalized to each patient's medical circumstances.
Inductive Subgraphs as Shortcuts: Causal Disentanglement for Heterophilic Graph LearningSIGIR
uses Identifies which connections between nodes in a graph are real causal relationships versus accidental correlations caused by misleading subpatterns.
why it works It works because some subgraph patterns appear frequently but mislead the model; explicitly tracing causal paths versus spurious paths lets you ignore the false correlations and learn only from genuine signal.
the deeper reason
Graph systems that learn from examples struggle on heterophilic graphs (where dissimilar nodes connect frequently) because they rely on the assumption that similar nodes cluster together; in heterophilic graphs this assumption breaks down. The work identifies that certain subgraph patterns systematically mislead the model by creating spurious correlations that feel predictive but aren't truly causal. By treating this as a causal problem and explicitly blocking the paths that create these misleading shortcuts, the model learns to ignore non-causal correlations and focus on genuine causal signals. This works because removing spurious paths forces the model to rely on true causal relationships in the data; when shortcuts are blocked, the only remaining learned patterns must reflect real dependencies rather than statistical flukes. This produces more robust and accurate predictions even in challenging heterophilic settings.
HCPRA: A Hierarchical Cognition-Perception-Reasoning Agent Framework for Emotion-Cause Pair Extraction in ConversationsSIGIR
uses Reconstructs why someone feels an emotion in conversation by tracking what the speaker knows, perceives, and reasons through.
why it works It works because emotions don't come from nowhere; modeling the speaker's knowledge and mental steps lets you trace the actual causal chain from situation to feeling.
the deeper reason
Extracting emotion-cause pairs in conversations requires reasoning about speakers' mental states and why those states arose. The method models this hierarchically by first reasoning about each speaker's personality and the scenario context, then simulating how emotions are perceived through the speaker's memory and past experience, then reasoning through multiple possible causal paths to find what triggered each emotion. This works because human emotion causation is genuinely hierarchical: personality shapes how we interpret events, memory shapes what we notice, and multiple different contextual factors can trigger the same emotion. By explicitly modeling each level rather than treating all utterances alike, the system captures interpretable reasoning that mirrors how people actually understand emotional causation in conversation. This produces more accurate and explainable emotion-cause links.
PurifAI: Detecting and Fixing Search-Induced Distortions in Web-Augmented LLMsSIGIR
uses Detects web search results that conflict with trusted internal knowledge and prevents them from overriding the verified facts.
why it works It works because truth has a source; when web content contradicts known-good internal sources, the contradiction itself signals danger, and blocking those results preserves accuracy.
the deeper reason
When an AI language systems is augmented with web search, conflicting information from the web can override an organization's verified internal knowledge base, creating a safety risk. The method generates diagnostic queries from trusted internal documents to test whether retrieved web content contradicts them, then blocks contradictory content before it reaches the model. The principle is that misalignment happens at the point where conflicting content enters the reasoning process; by detecting and removing conflicting information upstream, before the model sees it, the system prevents distortion at the source rather than trying to correct it after the fact. This works because the model can only be distorted by content it actually processes, so filtering content upstream preserves alignment with internal knowledge more reliably than post-hoc fact-checking. This is especially important in high-stakes domains where the internal knowledge base is the ground truth.
Exploration-and-Thinking: Agentic Reasoning over Knowledge Graphs via an LLM-RL Synergized FrameworkSIGIR
uses The system learns to explore knowledge graph paths efficiently while scoring which paths lead to correct answers, then discards paths that look right but actually contradict the facts.
why it works It works because reasoning is a search through possibilities. By coupling path exploration with learning what real evidence looks like and penalizing false leads, the system avoids following coincidental patterns and focuses on genuinely valid reasoning chains.
the deeper reason
The challenge is answering complicated questions by hopping through facts stored in a knowledge graph, using a language model to decide which facts to follow. The problem that ruins naive methods is computational waste and getting led astray by false paths. The fix works because it splits the job: first, use the language model to understand what the question means, then use a separate learned agent to do fast, focused exploration of the graph. Penalizing paths that contradict the graph's actual structure ensures the agent learns to trust the facts and not chase hallucinations, making reasoning both fast and accurate.
Debiased Recommendation Beyond the Positive Propensity AssumptionSIGIR
uses The method estimates how likely each product-user pair is to interact, then corrects for the fact that some pairs (like distant restaurants) were never shown to users and thus never clicked—deriving bounds on correct answer probabilities.
why it works It works because selection bias—the data only shows what was chosen to show—breaks standard probability estimates. By identifying unrealistic pairs and deriving upper bounds on what their true interaction rates could be, you can debiase the learning without complete information.
the deeper reason
Predicting whether a user will convert after clicking requires learning from clicks, but clicks come only from the users and items the ranking system chose to show. Some user-item pairs never appear at all, so the system has no way to know their true probabilities. Standard methods assume every pair has some chance, but in reality blockers exist: a restaurant ten kilometers away will never be shown. The fix is identifying these blocked pairs and bounding what you can learn about them, then teaching the model only the weaker constraint its data actually supports. This allows learning fairly even when the data itself has hard limits on what's observable.
Unified Entity Matching under Scarce Supervision via Meta-Rule Induction and RetrievalSIGIR
uses Extract matching rules from limited labeled examples, cluster rules into reusable patterns, then retrieve the most relevant pattern for each new entity pair to guide scoring.
why it works It works because explicit rules are more transferable than learned weights alone. Grouping rules by pattern lets you identify which rule actually applies to a new case, and rule-guided scoring is more robust than hoping adjust captured the right behavior from scarce data.
the deeper reason
Entity matching in the real world must handle multiple matching tasks (resolve duplicates, link names to knowledge bases, align records across databases) with very few labeled examples covering all scenarios. Instead of tuning model weights on scarce data—which leads to overfitting and brittle behavior—the method converts labeled examples into explicit rules in plain language, then groups similar rules together into reusable patterns. This is sound because rules are interpretable and reusable: if you learn 'people named Smith born in 1980 probably match across databases', that rule applies to new unseen data naturally without retraining. By grounding decisions on rules instead of implicit parameter updates, the system explains itself and generalizes to new scenarios. This principle holds because entity matching obeys recognizable patterns—certain attribute combinations are reliable signals—so formalizing those patterns lets them transfer. This enables systems to match entities accurately even with tiny labeled datasets, since explicit rules beat implicit patterns when data is scarce.
CoMCo: Consistency-Aware Multi-Agent Coordination for Zero-Shot Cross-Modal Entity MatchingSIGIR
uses Iteratively rank image-entity matches using multiple scoring signals, enforce that related entities get consistent matches, and only call expensive reasoning for ambiguous pairs.
why it works It works because global consistency (enforcing that related items match coherently) catches mistakes that local ranking would miss. The system exploits the constraint that if item A matches product X and item B is related to A, then B should relate to X too.
the deeper reason
Matching visual items to structured records is ambiguous: a single image might look like multiple database items, and local rankings might pick inconsistent matches (item A looks like B, B looks like C, C looks like A). The method uses a multi-stage refinement pipeline: start with fast vision-language similarity scores, enforce global consistency across related pairs, and only call a powerful reasoning model on genuinely hard cases. This is sound because consistency is a powerful constraint—if you insist that matched pairs form a globally coherent solution (not conflicting circles), most false leads disappear automatically. Reasoning models are expensive, so using them sparingly on hard cases preserves accuracy while cutting costs. The principle works because real-world matches should be consistent: if A matches B and B matches C, then A and C should be related, so systems can prune solutions that violate that logic. This lets large-scale matching systems produce globally coherent correspondences with cost-effective reasoning, rather than making independent noisy local decisions.
FairSpec: Expert Specialization for Fair LLM-based RecommendationSIGIR
uses Train separate expert models for recommendation quality and fairness, route each input to the appropriate expert via a learned router, and optimize both objectives jointly.
why it works It works because fairness and utility compete when baked into a single model, but separate experts let you suppress sensitive attributes in one expert without corrupting preference learning in the other. The router learns when to trust each expert.
the deeper reason
Language models amplify demographic biases when recommending: a user's age or gender can trigger stereotyped suggestions even for users with identical preferences, because model parameters encode both preference patterns and bias patterns together. Simply adjust to reduce bias harms recommendation quality because the model must unlearn preferences correlated with demographics. The method separates recommendation routing into specialist experts: some experts learn to predict good items (utility), others learn to predict and suppress demographic signals (fairness experts trained to fail at that task). A fair router decides which experts to use, and a joint optimization objective balances recommendation quality against fairness. This is sound because specialization isolates concerns: utility experts focus only on preferences, fairness experts directly oppose bias signals, and the router arbitrates. This principle works because demography and preference are entangled in training data but not in the underlying problem—real users of all demographics want good recommendations, so specialists can learn to serve both. This lets systems improve fairness without sacrificing recommendation accuracy.
How Far Are We from Automatically Identifying Violations of the Data Minimization Principle in Privacy Policies?SIGIR
uses Extract privacy practices from policy text, classify violations into types (inherent vs. contextual), then compare practices against patterns mined from compliant policies to flag anomalies.
why it works It works because compliance patterns from many compliant policies form a baseline of what practices typically match a stated purpose. Violations are contexts where a practice deviates significantly from the baseline or contradicts what the service needs, which becomes detectable when you have the pattern.
the deeper reason
Checking whether a privacy policy violates data minimization rules is hard because the rules are context-dependent (you might collect location data for navigation but not for ads) and policies are long unstructured documents mixing legal language with vague claims. The method first extracts what data practices the policy actually describes, then compares them against a compliance baseline built from both high-frequency patterns in real policies and expert knowledge of what data collection is genuinely justified. Some violations are obvious (collecting everything for any purpose), others need human judgment (is this purpose necessary?). By automating the obvious ones and flagging borderline cases for human review, the system reduces manual review workload while preserving accuracy. This is sound because data minimization violations fall into two categories—inherently unjustified (clear overreach) and contextually unjustified (unnecessary even if legitimate elsewhere)—and distinguishing them requires both pattern-matching and judgment. This principle works because privacy compliance is partly objective (does policy match law) and partly subjective (is this purpose legitimate), so human-AI language systems collaboration outperforms either alone. This enables large-scale auditing of privacy policies with human oversight where needed.
Towards Conflict-aware Selective Knowledge Unlearning for Continual Few-shot Knowledge Graph CompletionSIGIR
uses Forget which old facts conflict with new ones in a growing knowledge base, then update entity relationships by learning what changed.
why it works It works because removing contradictory knowledge lets the model update its internal state of what entities are like without getting stuck in old, wrong assumptions. The progressive unlearning prevents the model from averaging together conflicting beliefs.
the deeper reason
When learning new relationships with few examples, models over-rely on old knowledge, causing confusion. The insight is that not all starting guess knowledge helps—some directly contradicts new facts at structural or semantic levels. By identifying conflicting patterns and selectively forgetting them, the model's internal representations stay consistent and don't get pulled in opposite directions by old and new data simultaneously. This targeted forgetting works because removing contradictions unblocks the model to learn new patterns clearly with minimal examples.
Privacy Preserving Information Retrieval: Defining Privacy Research Pillars for a Future Research AgendaSIGIR
uses Define the research questions and safeguards needed so information access systems do not leak personal data when users search and retrieve.
why it works It works because thinking clearly about what each privacy threat means and where data flows makes interventions concrete and measurable rather than vague. The framework exposes gaps between what we think we're protecting and what we actually are.
the deeper reason
This is a position paper defining research pillars and gaps in privacy-preserving information retrieval. It surveys existing defenses and identifies where they fall short—data leakage through generation pipelines, incomplete protection across system stages, and evolving threat models. The paper's reasoning is that systematic gaps exist between what privacy mechanisms promise and what they actually protect, and closing these gaps requires grounding research in user needs, regulatory requirements, and end-to-end system design rather than isolated components.
Deletion Isn't Enough: Auditing RAG for Selective ForgettingSIGIR
uses Test whether removed facts still leak into generated answers even though the documents containing them were deleted from the retrieval system.
why it works It works because compliance looks at two separate channels: whether forbidden documents are retrieved, and whether their facts appear in answers anyway. Checking both reveals that deleting records is not enough if the model learned the fact during training.
the deeper reason
The problem is that record-level revocation (deleting documents) can appear to work while still disclosing the prohibited fact in generated answers—a compliance gap invisible to single metrics. The audit mechanism runs before-and-after comparisons and separates retrieval suppression from answer-level leakage, measuring both compliance and collateral damage to legitimate utility. This works because paired testing isolates whether revocation actually prevents disclosure in practice, revealing failures where individual metrics only measure fragments of compliance.
Evaluation Validity in Information RetrievalSIGIR
uses Decide whether metric improvements on benchmarks actually mean users experience better results in the real world.
why it works It works because not all measurement is valid: you can improve a metric while degrading the real experience if the metric measures the wrong thing. Checking that the metric correlates with what users actually want ensures progress is real, not statistical.
the deeper reason
Retrieval evaluation assumes that metric improvements correspond to real-world user benefit, but most evaluations drastically abstract from actual information seeking experience. The central question is validity: do observed metric gains predict actual effectiveness in practice? The paper argues for examining this assumption directly through user studies and alignment checks, because optimizing solely for current metrics can inadvertently degrade the actual experience. Validity matters because without it, benchmark improvements become decoupled from the goal of serving users well.
The Relevance of (Relevant) Entity PresenceSIGIR
uses Learn to rank documents by scoring how relevant entities are to the query, but detect when the model is secretly using knowledge it shouldn't have.
why it works Ranking by relevance score works because good scores put matching items first. But the deeper issue here is telling whether the score comes from the document text itself or from seeing which entities appear in known-relevant examples—separating the real signal from data leakage.
the deeper reason
The core problem is measuring whether named things mentioned in search results actually help users find what they want. The soundness rests on a simple principle: if the model learns which named things appear in documents that users already marked as helpful, it gains an unfair head start—it's memorizing the answer instead of learning to recognize it from text alone. This breaks down here because the method leaked information about which entities only appeared in pre-labeled good results, creating circular reasoning in the ranking pipeline. Without truly learning from document content, the system cannot work in the real world where it encounters new queries and documents it has never seen during training, making the approach impractical regardless of benchmark scores.
Mind the Metric: Reproducibility and Fair Benchmarking of Spectral Graph Models for Collaborative FilteringSIGIR
uses Use frequency-space filtering to separate true preferences from noise in user-item histories, then test if those improvements really hold under fair conditions.
why it works Frequency filtering works because user preferences and random noise occupy different frequency bands—high frequency = noise, low frequency = true preference patterns. But the study reveals some published results inflated this benefit through metric errors, showing the method only truly works in certain conditions.
the deeper reason
When recommender systems use graph techniques that work with frequency patterns to separate true user preferences from noise, they should outperform simpler classical methods—but reproducibility reveals this isn't consistent. The underlying principle that makes frequency-based separation sound is that real preference signals should occupy different frequency zones than noise, allowing filtering to preserve one while removing the other. This principle only holds if the frequency separation actually exists and if the method implements it correctly. The study found that implementation errors and metric miscalculations inflated results; when these are fixed and classical baselines are properly tuned, they remain surprisingly competitive, showing that the frequency principle isn't guaranteed to dominate in practice.
The Powerless Noise: How Experimental Settings Shape the Reported Power of NoiseSIGIR
uses Test whether adding random irrelevant text to retrieval-augmented generation actually helps question-answering, or whether the effect vanishes under different settings and model versions.
why it works The claimed benefit of noise hinges on specific prompt formats and decoding constraints in older models. Changing prompts or allowing longer outputs makes the effect disappear, showing the benefit wasn't a deep property of the retrieval-generation interaction but an artifact of those particular experimental choices.
the deeper reason
When search systems receive some irrelevant documents mixed with relevant ones, surprisingly they sometimes answer questions better, supposedly because the noise prevents the model from over-committing to wrong answers. The soundness of this benefit depends on the noise actually being random and disruptive to early wrong paths. However, reproducibility shows this effect is extremely fragile—changing the prompt or removing output length constraints causes the benefit to vanish entirely. The underlying principle assumes the model's errors are due to premature commitment, but error analysis reveals most failures come from truncation or malformed outputs from the language model itself, not from the retrieval input. Without robustness across conditions, the noise effect cannot be trusted as a general principle.
From Top-1 to Top-K: A Reproducibility Study and Benchmarking of Counterfactual Explanations for Recommender SystemsSIGIR
uses Explain a recommendation by finding the smallest changes to user-item history that would flip the recommendation, testing if these explanations hold across different recommender models.
why it works Counterfactual explanations work because they isolate causation: if changing X flips the outcome, then X is causal. Finding minimal changes avoids spurious correlations. Testing across model types reveals whether the explanation truly points to causes or just artifacts of one model's quirks.
the deeper reason
Explaining recommendations by finding minimal tweaks to user history that flip the recommendation is intuitive: if you change just one user-item interaction and the recommendation changes, that interaction must matter. The soundness rests on a key principle: simpler, smaller explanations (fewer tweaks) are more trustworthy than complex ones, because they isolate the true causal factors. However, this principle only holds if you measure explanations consistently—different studies assess item-level changes, list-level changes, and graph changes differently, making comparison impossible. The benchmarking study establishes unified metrics and finds that previous method comparisons depended heavily on which evaluation format was chosen, showing the principle works only when explanations are measured against the same standard.
KCC: Korean Civil Case Dataset for Legal Information RetrievalSIGIR
uses Rank legal cases by combining factual similarity to the query case with legal reasoning principles, using expert-annotated relevance judgments.
why it works It works because legal relevance depends on two separable things: does this case involve similar facts, and does the legal reasoning apply? Scoring each independently then combining them captures both the similarity that matters and the reasoning connection.
the deeper reason
The core problem is ranking legal cases by relevance when citation links are absent and civil law systems rely on implicit factual and reasoning connections. The mathematical principle is that expert human judgment of relevance creates a proxy for the true legal reasoning chain: when trained legal professionals agree that two cases are related, their agreement reveals what properties matter (factual overlap, similar legal principles, shared argumentation). This works because civil-law systems (unlike common-law) do not maintain explicit citation networks, forcing ranking systems to learn relevance from raw text alone. Building annotations where experts jointly evaluate factual similarity AND legal reasoning structure grounds any ranking method in what lawyers actually recognize as meaningful. This solves the fundamental evaluation problem: without such anchoring, machine-learned relevance measures drift from what jurists know matters.
GONets: A First-Look Into GitHub Organisation NetworksSIGIR
uses Represent open-source collaboration as a network of users connected to repositories; analyze patterns of contribution and code reuse diffusion through the network structure.
why it works It works because contribution patterns form a network where proximity (users in the same organization or sharing repos) predicts future collaboration. Information and code spread along edges; analyzing the network structure reveals how influence and reuse propagate.
the deeper reason
The core problem is understanding collaboration patterns and code reuse at the organizational level of GitHub, where individual projects are scattered across many groups. The mathematical principle is that a bipartite network (users on one side, repositories on the other, edges as contributions) precisely captures who does what: the structure itself reveals influence patterns, team formation, and dependency flow. This works because organizations operate as boundaries for governance and access control—studying them separately from raw user-repo pairs isolates the organizational effects (shared practices, internal standards, coordinated maintenance) that project-level analysis misses. By aggregating contributions at the organizational boundary and enriching edges with metadata (organization size, age, follower count), researchers can measure how organizational structure shapes collaboration itself. This network formulation solves the problem of understanding large-scale open-source as an ecosystem of interdependent groups, not just isolated projects.
The Alignment Gap: A Benchmark Demonstrating the Lack of Cross-Lingual Mapping in Dialect-Specialized Language Models - The Case of EhugboSIGIR
uses Measure how well language models align meanings across languages by placing Ehugbo queries and English documents in a shared space; compare global vs. regional models.
why it works It works because if two meanings are equivalent across languages, they should occupy the same region in a carefully trained space. Models trained on diverse language pairs learn this alignment; regional models, despite understanding each language well, lack the translation bridges to map between them.
the deeper reason
The core problem is retrieving information in a low-resource dialect (Ehugbo) when existing multilingual models show a surprising failure: regional models familiar with the language family underperform global models trained on translation pairs. The mathematical principle is that training through explicit translation supervision forces the model to learn a shared, language-agnostic representation where equivalent meanings map to the same location in the scoring space. This works because cross-lingual alignment is not automatic from linguistic similarity; it requires seeing examples where the same meaning appears in different languages and learning to ignore language-specific noise. Regional models, trained on in-language text alone, never encounter this supervisory signal. By diagnosing this alignment gap through visualization and error analysis, the work reveals that dialect coverage alone is insufficient—you need the constraint that sentences with identical meaning must score near each other, regardless of language. This principle solves the fundamental problem that low-resource language search requires not local expertise but global alignment supervision.
A Dataset of Cultural Heritage Manipulation on English Wikipedia in the Russo-Ukrainian ContextSIGIR
uses Analyze Wikipedia edit pairs to detect subtle narrative shifts in cultural attribution and agency; identify cumulative patterns of framing change.
why it works It works because comparing before-and-after text reveals intentional changes: what words were added, removed, or reframed. Subtle manipulation appears as consistent directional changes across many edits. Aggregating patterns across revisions exposes coordinated narrative shifts that individual edits might hide.
the deeper reason
The core problem is detecting subtle narrative manipulation of cultural heritage on Wikipedia, where edits appear individually legitimate but accumulate to reframe agency and legitimacy over time. The mathematical principle is that paired revisions (before-and-after versions plus editorial context) allow fine-grained analysis of what changed and why: cumulative analysis of small shifts reveals patterns that individual edits conceal. This works because manipulation of cultural narrative rarely happens as a single, obvious vandalism; instead, it emerges through incremental reframing: removing an attribution here, adding qualifying language there, shifting agency through pronoun choice. No single change triggers alarms, but the cascade changes meaning. By providing the revision history with consistent annotations, researchers can detect this drift through statistical and linguistic analysis that single-version snapshots cannot. This dataset design solves the problem that Wikipedia's transparency paradox (all edits are public) actually obscures manipulation because users cannot easily compare many versions or visualize trends.
RRE-GTC: A Geo-Temporal Cluster Dataset for Real-Estate Price Estimation and Market-Aware SearchSIGIR
uses Rank real-estate listings using geo-temporal price clusters combined with transport accessibility; use linear attribution to separate location value from intrinsic property quality.
why it works It works because real-estate price depends on separable factors: intrinsic property features and location premium. A linear model that explains price variation via these factors lets you isolate how much value comes from each. Ranking by combined features surfaces listings matching buyer preferences.
the deeper reason
The core problem is ranking real-estate listings when relevance depends simultaneously on location, time (markets shift), and intrinsic quality, and raw listing data is too sensitive to release publicly. The mathematical principle is that aggregating listings into geo-temporal clusters (geographic regions at specific time periods) and computing stratified statistical summaries (percentiles of price over time) preserves market structure while eliminating individual privacy risk. This works because a user searching for apartments cares about neighborhoods and neighborhoods are inherently aggregates—the typical price in a district, how it changes seasonally, what transportation connects it. By providing cluster-level features and a transport-isolated price signal (the value attributable to location alone, separated from building quality), the dataset reveals what portion of price comes from where you are versus what you own. This decomposition solves the practical problem that explainable ranking requires understanding which features drive ranking, which requires disentangling confounded factors. The geo-temporal structure captures the real complexity: market value is not static but evolves as neighborhoods change.
A Sensitivity-Aware Test Collection for Search Among Personal InformationSIGIR
uses Retrieve relevant emails while withholding ones marked as containing sensitive personal information.
why it works It works because relevance and sensitivity are two separate properties that must both be scored independently, and only returning results that rank high on relevance AND low on sensitivity lets you deliver useful information without exposing privacy.
the deeper reason
Sensitivity-Aware Search must jointly optimize two separate classification tasks: identifying relevance and identifying sensitivity, which requires models to learn that these properties are independent features, not correlated shortcuts. Training on both human and AI language systems-judged assessments works because it increases coverage of the distribution, but the key insight is that sensitivity must be explicitly labeled alongside relevance rather than treated as noise to ignore. This works because sensitivity detection is a genuine signal extraction problem—sensitive content is often relevant (the email discusses important business matters) but should be filtered, requiring the model to recognize patterns of sensitive language independently from relevance patterns. The dual evaluation (relevance and sensitivity performance) prevents models from gaming one metric at the expense of the other.
PeerPrism: Peer Evaluation Expertise vs Review-writing AISIGIR
uses Detect whether peer review text was written by a human, an AI, or came from a hybrid collaboration where ideas are human but writing is AI.
why it works It works because authorship has two sources—intellectual ideas and surface writing—and by treating them as separate features rather than a binary, detectors can score each independently and reveal when ideas are sound but expression is alien.
the deeper reason
PeerPrism disentangles idea provenance from text provenance because the two are orthogonal information sources: an AI language systems can beautifully articulate a human's core idea, or a human can clumsily express an AI-generated insight, and conflating these creates contradictory signals for detection methods. Existing binary detection treats this orthogonality as noise, but it is the signal itself: when detectors disagree under hybrid regimes, they're revealing that surface-text-based classifiers cannot infer intellectual contribution. The controlled generation regimes (fully human, fully synthetic, and hybrid transformations) expose this by showing that detectors trained on binary data systematically fail once ideas and surface text come from different sources. This proves that authorship must be modeled as multidimensional rather than collapsing to a single score.
From Single- to Cross-Document: Benchmarking Multi-Granularity Event Analysis of Large Language ModelsSIGIR
uses Predicts what event comes next in a story and infers which events cause which, tracing the path of one incident across multiple documents.
why it works It works because causality has structure: causes come before effects and appear in related documents, so showing how one event reliably triggers others reveals the true causal chain.
the deeper reason
Event analysis requires understanding information at multiple levels—from recognizing individual facts within a document to inferring relationships and narratives across many documents. The underlying principle is that no single task reveals all capability gaps; you need a progression from atomic details to global coherence. The authors design four ordered tasks—detection, relation, structure, induction—because each builds on the previous: if a model cannot find events, it cannot reason about their connections. By auto-annotating source data via a self-correcting framework and running models through this progression, they expose exactly where reasoning breaks down. This layered diagnosis lets the community understand what must improve for reliable event understanding at scale.
EVADE-Bench: Multimodal Benchmark for Evaluating and Enhancing Evasive Content DetectionSIGIR
uses Learns to detect when product text or images are trying to hide rule violations through disguise, scoring how likely each piece is hiding something.
why it works It works because intent leaves traces: words chosen to deceive follow patterns, and images cropped to hide things show consistent cropping marks; these patterns reveal what is intentionally obscured.
the deeper reason
E-commerce moderation requires detecting policy violations even when they are deliberately hidden through obfuscation—word splits, euphemisms, cropped images. The underlying principle is that rule understanding and intent inference are two separate capabilities that must both succeed; a model might know the rules but misread intent, or infer intent correctly but miss the rule. Evasive content defeats this by forcing both skills simultaneously: the system must decode the hidden meaning and recognize it violates a specific policy. By creating a multimodal benchmark with annotated text and images spanning six violation types, the authors establish a unified test where both reasoning and linguistic/visual comprehension are required. This prevents models from appearing to work when tested in isolation while actually failing in the real adversarial setting.
SimEval-IR: A Unified Toolkit and Benchmark Suite for Evaluating User Simulators and Search SessionsSIGIR
uses Tests fake users by how realistically they click on results and how accurately their behavior predicts which search system is better.
why it works It works because realistic behavior and valid system rankings are separate properties; resemblance to real clicks is only useful if it actually identifies which system truly works better.
the deeper reason
User simulators serve two distinct purposes—behaving like real people and producing valid system rankings—yet existing evaluation conflates them. The underlying principle is that these goals can conflict: a simulator might match real behavior statistics perfectly yet rank systems incorrectly if it emphasizes behaviors orthogonal to system quality. The toolkit establishes this distinction measurably by testing both objectives separately and correlating them. The key finding—that the standard 'human-likeness classifier' test has near-zero correlation with ranking validity—proves the distinction matters in practice. By providing validated benchmarks and showing which metrics (click-depth distance, Frechet distance over session patterns) actually predict ranking accuracy, the work enables practitioners to optimize simulators for their actual need: not realism for its own sake, but reliable system comparison.
Scalable K-Means Guided Partitioning for Block-based Sparse Document RetrievalSIGIR
uses Cluster sparse documents efficiently using a balanced K-means-guided bisection that groups similar lists of numbers together.
why it works It works because similar lists of numbers (measured by proximity in the sparse space) tend to be relevant for the same queries. Clustering groups these naturally-similar documents so retrieval only needs to search a few clusters instead of all documents, cutting search time dramatically.
the deeper reason
The core task is partitioning millions of documents into equal-sized groups such that similar documents fall into the same group, enabling faster retrieval. K-means clustering is the natural choice but becomes slow when creating thousands of groups. The proposed method uses balanced bisection: recursively split groups into two equal halves using K-means criteria, requiring logarithmically many splits instead of direct k-way clustering. This works because each binary split is inherently faster than k-way clustering, and logarithmic recursion only adds a small factor overhead. The key insight is that balanced bisection preserves clustering quality (documents stay grouped with similar documents) while achieving orders-of-magnitude speedup, because the method makes locally optimal split decisions that collectively build good global partitions.
