The algorithm scales because the number of operations is proportional to document-count times log of cluster-count, not cluster-count squared.
ExODRec: An Explainable Framework for Outlier Detection Model RecommendationSIGIR
uses Learn to predict how well each candidate model will perform on a new dataset by training on past datasets where we know both the model's success and the dataset's characteristics.
why it works This works because if different datasets have patterns in what makes them hard or easy, and models have consistent strengths and weaknesses, then studying past successes teaches you which model traits match which dataset traits. You never need to run the models—just predict from the patterns you've seen.
the deeper reason
The core challenge is predicting which outlier-detection model will work best on a new dataset without running all candidates. ExODRec learns this by first studying benchmark datasets and their meta-features, then extracting hidden traits that describe both how a model behaves and how difficult each dataset is. The soundness comes from a mathematical principle called item response theory, which says that when you measure how well different tools solve different problems, you can represent each tool and each problem by a single difficulty number. Because outlier-detection performance follows this pattern—some models are inherently harder to apply, some datasets are trickier—you can learn these hidden traits from history and predict new outcomes. This avoids the expensive step of actually running dozens of models on every dataset.
Attend to Fragments: How Key Information Affects Large Language Models for Factual Inconsistency DetectionSIGIR
uses Detect when a language model is checking a claim by identifying whether it's actually reading the relevant evidence or just fixating on repeated words, filtering unreliable detections.
why it works Language models often rely on keywords instead of logic. If shuffling sentence order breaks the model but the answer stays the same, it proves the model isn't reasoning from content. Filtering those cases improves accuracy because you eliminate decisions made for wrong reasons.
the deeper reason
AI language systems hallucinate—they write fluent text that contradicts the source document. To catch this, you can ask another language model whether the output logically follows from the input. However, the benchmark shows that models often identify the wrong parts of the input as supporting evidence, a phenomenon the work terms 'attend to fragments.' The underlying principle is that language models often take shortcuts based on keyword overlap; when they see certain high-frequency words, they assume relevance without properly reasoning through the logical structure. By carefully studying which parts of the source document the model actually uses, and filtering out predictions that relied on fragmented, unreliable reasoning, you remove false positives from the inconsistency detector. This works because inconsistency detection is brittle—you must trust every positive; filtering out weakly-reasoned cases improves overall reliability.
Towards Emotional Intelligence in Conversational AI: How Well Can LLMs Recognise Emotion in Conversations?SIGIR
uses Compare language model emotion labels to human annotations across conversation contexts, measuring agreement and studying which cases the model handles well or poorly.
why it works If language models are to replace annotators, they must match human judgment reliably. Measuring disagreement reveals whether the model is learning emotion recognition or just mimicking surface patterns. Context tests show whether the model understands emotional flow or treats each turn alone.
the deeper reason
To adjust a conversational AI model for emotion, you need labeled training data, but manual labeling is expensive. Using a language model to auto-label is faster, but creates a hidden risk: if you then use the same language model as a judge during evaluation, you have a circular test that inflates your results. The work measures how much language models agree with human annotators when labeling emotions in conversation. The soundness comes from a statistical principle: an evaluation is only valid if the test and the training data come from independent sources. When both come from the same model, you measure the model's consistency with itself, not its real-world correctness. By quantifying this drift between language-model labels and human labels, you expose how much circular evaluation has biased the field. This matters because it prevents practitioners from unknowingly publishing inflated claims.
Failing Forward: Understanding Query Failure in Retrieval, Judgment, and GenerationSIGIR
uses Measure which queries are hard to retrieve, hard to generate answers for, and hard to judge as correct, finding that the three difficulties are mostly independent.
why it works If difficulty came from just query semantics, the same queries would fail everywhere. But they don't—retrieval struggles with different queries than generation, and judgment struggles differently still. This tells you each task has its own biases, so you can't fix one by fixing another.
the deeper reason
When a query produces poor results, where did it fail? In retrieval, generation, or judgment? The work studies whether the same queries are hard across all three stages or only some. The underlying principle is that task difficulty depends on the interaction between query properties and each task's structure; a query hard to retrieve for might be easy to generate with because the tasks exploit different clues. By tracking overlap and instability across four years of benchmarks, the work shows that task-specific difficulty dominates, meaning that a hard query in retrieval does not automatically transfer to generation or judgment. This matters because it means practitioners cannot use retrieval difficulty as a predictor for downstream costs; each stage must be instrumented separately. The finding also suggests that conditioning generation on task-relevant cues can unlock gains, since the tasks have independent weak points.
Answer First, Evidence Second? Uncovering Hidden Risks in Well-Structured AI Search SummariesSIGIR
uses Measures when summaries match or contradict their cited sources by scoring agreement between summary content and source text similarities.
why it works If evidence truly supports a summary, the main ideas in both should be saying the same things and appearing in the same order. When you measure how much summaries and sources align point-by-point, mismatches reveal where claims drift from what the sources actually say.
the deeper reason
This paper audits whether search summaries with citations actually ground their claims in the sources they cite. The work reveals a mismatch: summaries look trustworthy by virtue of their structure and citations, but 32% are simply wrong—and this persists even when correct evidence sits in the cited sources. The finding matters because user trust follows appearance, not accuracy. Appearance comes cheap: good formatting and citing sources takes minimal effort but fools readers. Measuring the actual link between each claim and its source is what catches this gap and forces better practices.
Is a Busy Search Agent a Good One? Overthinking and Overretrieval at ScaleSIGIR
uses Counts excessive retrieval and reasoning steps in agent trajectories, then assigns penalty scores to discourage wasteful patterns and guide trajectories toward efficiency.
why it works By measuring exactly what kinds of steps lead to waste (redundant documents, circular reasoning), you can assign a cost that makes those choices less attractive. Agents optimize what you measure; measuring waste directly makes them optimize it away.
the deeper reason
Search agents that can iteratively fetch documents and reason often retrieve redundant information and take excessive reasoning steps, wasting cost. The paper formalizes these inefficiencies and studies how they scale with model size. By measuring how much retrieval is wasted and how many reasoning steps loop unproductively, the work identifies the precise behaviors to target. It then proposes feedback signals that convert these measurements into rewards, giving the agent explicit guidance to prune wasteful steps. This grounds cost control in measurement rather than guesswork.
Pretraining Exposure Explains Popularity Judgments in Large Language ModelsSIGIR
uses Measures how many times entities appear in training data (exposure) and compares it to both real-world popularity and the model's stated preferences, showing they align more with exposure than ground truth.
why it works Models learn what the training data emphasizes. If an entity appears frequently in pretraining, the model learns strong associations with it regardless of reality. Exposure captures what's statistically regular in data; aligning to exposure means the model is doing exactly what training shaped it to do.
the deeper reason
Language models favor well-known entities, and this paper asks: is it real-world popularity or just exposure during pretraining? Using an open model with its full training corpus, they measure how many times each entity appeared during training and compare to Wikipedia popularity. Pretraining exposure and real popularity correlate strongly, but model preferences align more tightly with exposure. This matters because it shows that model bias is not a separate phenomenon—it is the direct imprint of training data. What seems like a model flaw is actually accurate calibration to what it has seen.
When RAG Disagrees: Detecting Latent Epistemic Conflict via Logit InteractionsSIGIR
uses Compute a score from model's internal confidence and semantic overlap with retrieved context to predict whether retrieval will help or hurt output.
why it works A model's internal raw scores reveal true confidence separate from text it produces. When retrieved context aligns semantically with raw scores confidence, the model genuinely trusts the context. When they diverge, the model is torn—a sign that retrieval contradicts its learned knowledge. This internal signal detects conflict faster than checking the output.
the deeper reason
AI language systems contain internal parametric knowledge from pretraining, but retrieval augmentation brings external evidence; when these conflict, the model is uncertain which to follow. Instead of running expensive supervised probes, this method detects conflict by measuring how confident the model's internal raw scores are about its parametric answer versus how much that answer aligns semantrically with the retrieved context. When conflict exists, raw scores and semantic alignment diverge—high raw scores confidence but low alignment signals tension. This works because the model's decision computation, revealed through raw scores, becomes a reliable indicator of internal disagreement before the model generates any text, enabling fast conflict prediction.
Numerical Hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Detection and AnalysisSIGIR
uses Detect when retrieval-augmented answers invent numbers by checking if generated numbers appear in retrieved documents, flagging fabrications.
why it works Numbers are discrete and traceable—either they're in the source or they're made up. This is different from text hallucinations, which can be paraphrases or rephrasing. A simple check for number presence catches pure fabrication with perfect recall because a made-up number leaves no shadow in the source.
the deeper reason
Language models sometimes fabricate numbers that sound plausible but have no grounding in retrieved documents, a failure mode that standard similarity-based and AI language systems-judge methods miss because they focus on overall semantic match. A number-aware heuristic checks whether the actual numbers in the generated output appear explicitly or can be directly computed from numbers in the source documents. This works because hallucinated numbers almost never appear in sources—fabrication means the model invented a number—while correctly grounded numbers by definition originate in or flow from source text. Detecting the absence of this source grounding is far simpler and more reliable than judging semantic correctness.
uses Use historical pre-promotion behavior to predict which customers will buy during a promotion, accounting for the fact that pre-purchase browsing shifts to buying later.
why it works Pre-promotion and promotion periods have different user behaviors—before the sale, people add to carts but don't buy. On sale day, they convert. This is a distribution shift that previous models ignore. By learning from historical pre-promotion data that captures this exact shift pattern, the model learns when cart-adding signals future conversion, not immediate purchase.
the deeper reason
Before promotional events, users browse and add items to carts, then convert on the promotion day—a delayed conversion pattern absent from regular time periods. Converting rates appear low before the promotion because the delayed conversions haven't occurred yet, not because the pre-promotion phase is fundamentally different. Using counterfactual reasoning, the method learns from pre-promotion data what users are likely to convert later, accounting for the shifted distribution where delayed conversions cluster on a single future date rather than spreading across the continuous period. This works because counterfactual logic lets the model predict future conversion outcomes for pre-promotion behavior by disentangling the actual behavior from when conversion happens to occur.
Separating Wheat from Chaff: Fine-Grained Defenses Against Poisoning in Multi-Perspective RAGSIGIR
uses When retrieving for multi-perspective generation, model how different opinions relate as clusters of agreement so you can tell the difference between a real disagreement and an attack designed to bias the system.
why it works It works because real perspectives on an issue form clusters where many documents agree, while an attack tries to inject a document with hidden bias that stands alone; seeing which documents naturally cluster together reveals the true topology of legitimate disagreement.
the deeper reason
When a system retrieves information to generate multiple viewpoints, adversaries can inject biased documents to steer the output toward one perspective. The defense models how perspectives connect and conflict as a graph structure, preserving diversity by grouping similar viewpoints together rather than filtering out disagreements. This works because the core mistake of existing defenses is treating all contradictions as bad, but perspective disagreement is legitimate while inserted bias is not. By clustering perspectives and identifying fine-grained contradiction patterns, the system can distinguish genuine debate from manipulation. The graph structure captures which perspective disagreements are natural (both supported by real knowledge) versus which are signs of poisoning, letting the system keep diverse legitimate viewpoints while rejecting artificial distortion.
CSMAD: Hallucination Detection via Multi-Agent Debate with NLI-Verified Contradictory StatementsSIGIR
uses Multiple independent judges evaluate both a claim and a deliberately constructed opposite claim, then compare their reasoning to decide what is actually true.
why it works It works because disagreement forces each judge to defend their position against direct contradictions, revealing which arguments hold up under scrutiny. When both versions are rejected or both accepted, exchanging reasoning uncovers flawed shared assumptions that isolated judges would miss.
the deeper reason
The method generates a claim that directly contradicts the input and asks separate judges to evaluate both, which forces independent reasoning paths rather than shared overconfidence. Because true claims usually defeat false contradictions while false claims often fall to legitimate contradictions, disagreement between judges signals unreliability. The system only updates judgments when it can exchange specific counterarguments, making corrections evidence-based. This works because contradiction creates asymmetry: truth stands when challenged but fiction often crumbles when forced to defend against direct opposition.
Effective Offline LLM and DNN based Matching, Filtering and Ranking for Search Ads Retrieval in E-CommerceSIGIR
uses Ads are ranked offline using language models to filter by relevance and systems that learn from examples to rank by conversion, ensuring only high-quality candidates reach online systems.
why it works It works because online systems have strict latency limits, so only a tiny fraction of candidates can be scored; offline scoring with powerful models has no speed constraint and can eliminate irrelevant noise beforehand. This frees online systems to focus ranking effort on the best candidates.
the deeper reason
The system retrieves a large pool of candidate ads offline using numeric fingerprints and then filters them with a language model to identify truly relevant ones, keeping only the strongest for the online ranking stage. Because online latency constraints prevent running a powerful model on all candidates, pre-filtering offline lets the online system spend its limited compute budget on the hardest decisions. This works because precision earlier in the pipeline compounds: removing clearly irrelevant ads before ranking ensures the ranker only compares genuinely competitive candidates.
Constraint Persistence in Conversational Product SearchSIGIR
uses Constraints users state in conversation are classified (identity, contextual, session) and their relevance is scored when users switch product categories, preserving only the ones that still apply.
why it works It works because not all constraints are equally sticky; an ingredient preference (identity) transfers across product changes, but a temporal one (needed today) doesn't. Scoring relevance per constraint type prevents over-constrained queries (zero results) while respecting user intent.
the deeper reason
The system classifies each user constraint as identity-based, contextual, or session-level, then decides which constraints stay valid when the user switches to a different product category. Because carryover constraints often become impossible to satisfy across categories, keeping the wrong ones leads to zero results; the system learns which constraints genuinely apply across boundaries. This works because constraint lifecycle is a classification task: whether a price filter makes sense for laptops after searching phones, or whether a room-count preference applies to flight hotels, depends on semantic compatibility that the model can learn from reasoning examples.
LLM-Click Agreement: Harmonizing Implicit Feedback and Semantic Judgments for Enterprise SearchSIGIR
uses Supervision for search ranking only uses query-result pairs where both click signals and language model judgments agree, filtering out pairs where they disagree.
why it works It works because clicks are behavioral (people are biased, multitasking) while language model judgments are semantic (pure relevance); agreement means the pair is genuinely good by both lenses. Disagreement often signals label noise, so keeping only agreements trains cleaner models despite having fewer examples.
the deeper reason
The system labels a query-result pair as relevant only when both click-based signals and language model judgment agree it is, filtering out noisy labels where one signal contradicts the other. Because clicks can be misleading due to position bias or fast clicks on non-relevant results, requiring agreement with semantic judgment removes that noise; the result is supervision that reflects true relevance rather than clickthrough noise. This works because agreement acts as a conservative filter: only labels with genuine evidence from two independent sources survive, making the training data cleaner and more reliable.
SID-Coord: Coordinating Semantic IDs for ID-based Ranking in Short-Video SearchSIGIR
uses Scores videos using both exact ID memorization and semantic meaning, with a learned gate that decides which to trust based on whether the item is popular or rare.
why it works It works because memorization excels on frequent items (you've seen them often) while semantic similarity helps on rare items (you see patterns instead). The gate learns when each approach is trustworthy. For rare items, semantic patterns are reliable; for common ones, exact history is.
the deeper reason
The system simultaneously scores memorization (whether someone who saw an item before will interact again) and generalization (whether someone who never saw an item will like it based on semantic similarity). The principle is that these two abilities require different modeling paths: raw co-occurrence counts are powerful for frequent items but fail on rare ones, while semantic structure generalizes well to the unseen but can be weak on popular items. By gating between them adaptively per prediction, the model lets each mechanism do what it does best. The gating mechanism works because it conditions on the specific item: when predicting for a popular, frequently-seen video, memorization dominates, but for a new or rare video, semantic similarity takes over. This balancing solves the memorization-generalization tradeoff that has plagued ranking systems serving both mainstream and long-tail content.
Enhancing Multi-Valued Treatment Uplift Modeling with Knowledge Sharing and RCT DataSIGIR
uses Learns how treatments affect different people by sharing knowledge across treatment groups and anchoring the representations to stabilize learning.
why it works It works because sharing signals between treatment groups borrows strength when data is sparse. Anchoring representations prevents them from drifting differently per mini-batch. Using RCT data adds unbiased ground truth, which pulls the model toward correct causal effects.
the deeper reason
The system estimates how much each person benefits from each of several treatment options—say, different discount levels in a marketing offer. The core challenge is data sparsity: with ten treatment groups, each person's data fragments into small pieces. The principle is that when data is sparse across many groups, shared structure—learning what works across groups together—stabilizes estimates far better than fitting each group alone. The system discovers and uses this shared structure through two mechanisms: anchoring representations to stable points during training so predictions align across groups, and having one treatment's success inform predictions about similar treatments. This sharing works because the underlying reasons someone responds to a discount are often similar across discount levels—their purchase tendencies don't reinvent themselves for each option. Pooling evidence across treatments lets the system make reliable recommendations even for treatments with sparse direct data.
Bridging the Topology-Semantic Gap: A Benchmark and Framework for Power Grid Work Ticket GenerationSIGIR
uses Combines semantic search with power-grid topology: uses semantic retrieval but constrains it to respect electrical system physical laws, with explicit reasoning chains.
why it works It works because power grids have rigid physical constraints that pure semantic matching misses. Symbolic patterns match abstract intentions to technical entities, while subgraph encoding ensures physical feasibility. The two together prevent hallucinations that violate safety rules.
the deeper reason
The system generates work tickets for power grid operations—instructions for technicians—using retrieval-augmented generation, but constrained by the power grid's strict physical laws. The core challenge is that semantic search alone retrieves components that match in meaning but violate electrical rules—for instance, suggesting work on two parts of the grid that physically can't interact. The principle is that topological structure—the physical wiring and connectivity of the grid—imposes hard constraints that semantic search must respect. By fusing semantic understanding with physical graph structure, encoding what components can actually interact, and guiding generation to follow topology-aware reasoning chains, the system produces technically valid instructions. This works because the topology acts as a filter: even if semantics and physics both point to an item, it only matters if the topology allows it. Respecting physics simultaneously makes the system safer, narrowing hallucinations to only those that could theoretically work.
TRACE: A Conversational Framework for Sustainable Tourism Recommendation with Agentic Counterfactual ExplanationsSIGIR
uses Recommendations balance relevance with environmental impact by eliciting user sustainability preferences through conversation and generating counterfactual explanations showing greener alternatives.
why it works Users often default to popular choices without considering impact. By extracting hidden sustainability preferences through conversation, the system learns what users actually value, not just what they initially ask for. Counterfactual explanations show what would change if they chose greener alternatives, helping users see the causal link between choices and outcomes.
the deeper reason
The core problem is recommending travel without reinforcing overcrowded, carbon-intensive destinations, but nudging toward sustainability risks feeling coercive and harming user satisfaction. The underlying principle is that agentic counterfactual explanations—showing users what greener alternatives exist and what tradeoffs they'd face—let users make informed choices rather than being pushed, preserving agency while surfacing the sustainability features they may not have considered. This principle applies because humans resist being told what to do but embrace new options when they understand the reasoning; showing a user a sustainable beach resort they genuinely like (not a preachy worse option) is persuasion through evidence, not coercion. Eliciting hidden preferences through conversation ensures the system learns what users actually value. This solves the practical goal: scaling sustainable tourism by numeric fingerprints environmental impact into recommendations without sacrificing the user experience that makes recommendations valuable.
Peerispect: Claim Verification in Scientific Peer ReviewsSIGIR
uses Extract claims from reviews, find evidence in the paper, and check if the evidence supports each claim using natural language reasoning.
why it works It works because written claims and supporting evidence, when found, should align in meaning; failing to align signals the claim is unsupported or incorrect, isolating reviewers' subjective opinions from factual statements.
the deeper reason
Peer review quality suffers when reviewers make claims that are subjective, rhetorical, or unsupported by the paper being reviewed. The system extracts check-worthy claims from reviews and then verifies them by retrieving manuscript evidence and applying logical inference—asking whether the claim follows from what the paper actually says. This works because claims are factual statements with truth conditions; if you can locate the relevant passage in the paper and reason about it, you can identify when a review makes unsupported assertions. The method is sound because it grounds verification in the primary source (the manuscript) rather than external knowledge, isolating the specific claim-evidence relationship that matters for fairness. By making verification rapid and visual, it enables program committees to detect unfair review statements at scale.
MuseKG: An Interactive Knowledge Graph Over Museum CollectionsSIGIR
uses Organize museum objects and metadata into a typed network, then answer questions by finding entities related to the question and retrieving their connected evidence.
why it works It works because museum data is inherently relational—objects connect through people, events, and places; representing these connections explicitly lets similarity become reachability, so finding related objects becomes following edges in the graph.
the deeper reason
Museum collections span structured records, images, and unstructured text that museums struggle to integrate into a single queryable form. A knowledge graph unifies these by extracting entities and relations into a typed structure where objects, people, organizations, and images all have places and explicit links. This works because knowledge graphs organize information by identity and relationship rather than by source format—when you resolve all references to 'Creator A' to a single entity node regardless of whether they appeared in a catalog record or an image description, you enable exploration across sources. Natural-language queries can be grounded to these entities, and compact neighborhoods of the graph provide evidence for answers. The method is sound because it treats heterogeneous data as expressions of the same underlying entities and relations, making unified query and discovery possible.
SLeDoC: System for Legal Document ComparisonSIGIR
uses Compare legal document paragraphs by semantic meaning rather than word-level matching to detect inconsistencies, rewrites, and paraphrased contradictions.
why it works It works because paraphrased text has the same meaning even with different words; semantic comparison groups paragraphs by what they actually say, so contradictions that survive paraphrasing become detectable without character-level fragility.
the deeper reason
Legal documents undergo frequent revision but character-level or words-level comparison tools miss paraphrases and semantic shifts—two phrasings that mean different things but look similar lexically. The system combines information retrieval techniques with language models to perform span-aware semantic comparison, moving beyond surface matching to meaning. This is sound because paraphrases are semantically equivalent, but semantic shifts change meaning; a system that reasons about meaning—not just character sequences—can distinguish them. Language models encode semantic understanding, so asking them to judge whether two spans mean the same thing after retrieving relevant context is more reliable than string matching. The reason this works is that legal documents are precise about meaning, and humans reviewing them need to spot where revisions inadvertently changed obligations, permissions, or constraints. Semantic comparison catches those shifts where syntactic diffs miss them.
FactOWL: A Cost-Efficient Tool for Long-Form Factuality EvaluationSIGIR
uses Extract atomic facts from long text, search multiple sources to find supporting evidence, aggregate evidence across sources, then estimate what fraction of facts are correct.
why it works It works because hallucinations stand out when facts are broken into small claims checked against real sources; multi-source aggregation amplifies signals from true facts while errors in one source are contradicted by others, revealing the true factuality rate.
the deeper reason
AI language systems generate long-form responses that may contain hallucinated facts, and evaluating factuality is slow and expensive with existing tools. FactOWL addresses this by extracting atomic facts from the response, retrieving supporting evidence from multiple Wikipedia sources and Wikidata triples, and aggregating across sources to handle ambiguity and incomplete contexts. This is sound because a fact's truth can be established through evidence from authoritative sources—if multiple sources support a claim, it's reliable; if none do, it's suspicious. Aggregating across multiple sources handles the problem that any single source may be incomplete or outdated. The reason multi-source aggregation works is that no single source is perfect, but consensus across sources is trustworthy. By using open, real-time data sources and efficient retrieval, the system makes factuality evaluation cheap and fast enough to be practical for researchers and applications.
PatentMerit: A Holistic System for In-depth Technology UnderstandingSIGIR
uses Score patents by disruptive potential and evolution using network citation patterns and clustering to surface high-impact technologies.
why it works Citation networks reveal which patents influence others; grouping patents by topic shows where breakthroughs cluster. Combining these separates genuinely transformative work from one-off contributions.
the deeper reason
PatentMerit scores individual patents and clusters of patents by analyzing how technologies build on and diverge from each other using citation networks and language meaning. The soundness rests on a basic truth: if many other patents cite a patent and extend its ideas in diverse directions, that patent likely unlocked something valuable. By treating patents as nodes in a network and tracing flow through citations, the system computes influence scores that reflect genuine technical momentum, not just filing volume or age. Combining network flow with topic extraction lets the system spot when a patent introduces a genuinely new technical direction versus incremental refinement. This approach surfaces real innovation signals buried in bibliographic noise, letting R&D teams focus on patents that actually shaped a field's evolution.
Detectability and Evaluation Risks of LLM-Generated Answers in Low-Resource Swahili Agricultural Information RetrievalSIGIR
uses Score text patterns to distinguish AI language systems-generated agricultural answers from human-authored ones.
why it works AI language systems produce consistent patterns (length, diversity, similarity) that differ from human text; scoring and classification separate true signal from noise, revealing detectability as a diagnostic for evaluating generated content.
the deeper reason
This study trains a text classifier to distinguish AI language systems-generated answers from human-written answers on agricultural questions in Swahili. The method works because language models generate text with consistent statistical properties: longer sequences, lower word-diversity patterns, and measurable similarity to their training data all appear reliably in generated text. A logistic regression classifier learns these patterns and achieves 0.98 accuracy, proving the patterns are strong and learnable. The 0.98 accuracy signals that generated answers exhibit fingerprints of their origin. This detectability matters for IR system evaluation: when answers come from language models, knowing which ones are generated versus human-expert answers lets evaluators adjust their trust and audit output quality. In low-resource agricultural settings where misinformation spreads rapidly and farmer welfare depends on answer reliability, detectability becomes a diagnostic tool for assurance.
Towards Evidence-Aware Retrieval and Verification for Scientific Fact-CheckingSIGIR
uses Rank scientific papers by whether they actually support or refute a claim, not just by word similarity; distinguish supporting evidence from coincidental mentions.
why it works It works because simply finding papers with overlapping words misses the distinction between papers that actually address the claim versus papers that mention related terms by chance. Scoring based on evidence structure—whether the paper's logic actually connects to the claim—separates true support from false positives.
the deeper reason
Scientific fact-checking requires finding evidence that either confirms or refutes a specific claim. The core principle is that evidence for verification and evidence for general relevance are not the same thing: a paper might mention the same topic but contradict the claim or be irrelevant to judging it. This principle applies because verification is a contrastive task—the retriever must find papers that could possibly weigh in on the claim, whether supporting or opposing, not merely papers topically similar. Standard ranking systems treat all relevant papers equally, but for fact-checking, a paper that takes an opposite stance is as useful as one that agrees, and both matter more than a tangentially related paper. By designing retrieval specifically for the verification task, rather than generic similarity, the system ensures downstream models receive the right evidence to reason about claim truth, solving the core bottleneck: poor evidence makes verification impossible no matter how good the verification model is.
Faithful LLM-Assisted Question Answering for Technical and Academic SearchSIGIR
uses Ground AI answers in retrieved evidence and learn to distinguish citations that actually support the answer from fabricated or unsupported claims.
why it works It works because models learn spurious correlations when trained on data containing hallucinations. By explicitly training on task of separating supported claims from unsupported ones, the model learns the structure of genuine logical support versus plausible-sounding fabrication.
the deeper reason
When an AI language systems answers a question, users need to trust that the answer is grounded in real evidence and faithful to sources cited. The core principle is that generation without verification is unreliable: AI language systems can produce plausible-sounding but false information, and they sometimes cite sources that do not actually support what they claim. This principle applies because language models are trained to predict next words based on statistical patterns, not to verify truth; they have no built-in mechanism to check whether their own outputs match reality. By requiring the system to explicitly retrieve evidence before generating an answer, check that retrieved evidence actually supports each claim, and surface uncertainty when evidence is sparse or conflicting, the system builds verification into the pipeline. This solves the decision-making problem: technical and scientific decision-makers need confidence that answers are truthful, not just confident-sounding, and explicit evidence checking is the only way to provide that.
Characterising the Effects of Social Conformity on Information Seeking in Mixed Human-AI EnvironmentsSIGIR
uses Learn how human information-seeking changes when AI agents participate in discussions; distinguish AI influence from natural social conformity effects.
why it works It works because social conformity and AI effects both influence behavior, but untangling them requires controlled observation. By measuring behavior in mixed and unmixed settings and modeling the interaction, you isolate AI's true causal effect from confounding social mechanisms.
the deeper reason
In online discussions mixing human and AI participants, people adjust their judgments to match what others think—a tendency called conformity. The core principle is that social conformity emerges from comparison: individuals look to others' views as evidence and adjust toward the majority. This principle applies because groups create implicit pressure; when most people accept an idea, questioning it feels risky, and when AI agents align with human consensus, they appear more trustworthy. The presence and positioning of AI agents in the group alters conformity dynamics: people may conform more to a majority that includes AI, or differently if the AI disagrees with the human majority. By studying how conformity operates in mixed groups, the research reveals whether AI participation changes how trustworthy information judgments become, solving a critical concern: as AI-generated content permeates discussions, understanding whether AI presence increases or decreases collective judgment quality helps predict real-world information consequences.
MANILA26: SIGIR 2026 Tutorial on Information Retrieval for Climate Change ImpactSIGIR
uses Finding relevant documents from scientific literature by ranking them by how closely their content matches climate evidence, accounting for geographic and temporal context.
why it works It works because when you treat documents as locations in a space where similar topics sit near each other, you can find what you need by measuring distance. Adding weights for geography and time ensures the most relevant evidence ranks first, filtering out noise and bias.
the deeper reason
Climate change evidence synthesis requires finding relevant scientific papers across disconnected databases and domains, then combining findings into a coherent picture. The core task is matching complex information needs to scattered sources while detecting when retrieval fails silently. The mathematical principle at work is that structured provenance tracking—recording not just what documents say but where claims came from, who verified them, and what gaps remain—creates verifiable chains of reasoning that human experts can audit. This works because disagreements about evidence quality, geographic applicability, and methodological soundness cannot be resolved by statistical similarity alone; they require explicit documentation that humans can inspect. By building unified pipelines that integrate geographic data, time-series measurements, and bibliographic sources with this provenance layer, systems can transparently show where human judgment must override automated ranking, addressing the real problem that climate policy decisions demand justification visible to skeptics.
Verifiable User Simulation for Search and Recommendation SystemsSIGIR
uses Simulating user behavior by learning structured profiles and checking whether simulated choices match the real people they represent, to test if search and recommendation systems are fair.
why it works A simulator is only trustworthy if you can trace why it made each choice and verify that choice reflects the user it claims to represent, not the model's hidden biases. Auditing each component—profile, contract, execution, feedback—catches bias before it harms real users.
the deeper reason
Evaluating search and recommendation systems using simulated users avoids the cost of recruiting humans, but the risk is that a simulator may make choices inconsistent with its declared profile or may harbor biases against certain demographic groups. The core computational task is predicting what choice a user would make given their profile, task context, and the system's output. The soundness principle is that if you decompose the simulator into auditable, interpretable components—a persona with explicit attributes, task-level contracts that specify expected behavior, execution traces that record why each choice was made, and verification checks that confirm choices match the persona—then you can detect inconsistencies and biases by inspecting this trail. This principle works because simulated choices are functions of these components; if you can see the components and the choices they produced, you can reverse-engineer whether the simulator behaves as intended. By adding a refinement loop that updates personas and contracts based on detected inconsistencies, the framework becomes verifiable rather than opaque. This matters because biased simulators can systematically disadvantage minority groups in evaluation, leading to deployed systems that seem to perform well but actually discriminate.
Second Workshop on Explainability in Information RetrievalSIGIR
uses Explaining why a search result or recommendation was shown by identifying which input features influenced the score most and measuring whether the explanation helps humans trust the system.
why it works An explanation is trustworthy only if it points to the real reasons, not post-hoc rationalizations. Measuring cause—which features actually moved the score—requires methods that isolate each feature's effect. Information theory measures how much the explanation reduces uncertainty about the system's decision.
the deeper reason
As ranking and recommendation systems become more complex and consequential, users deserve to understand how systems made their decisions. Explainability requires systems to expose their reasoning in human-interpretable form, creating accountability. The core problem is that modern systems use many distributed signals—learned representations, statistical patterns, multiple ranking stages—making it hard to point to a single reason for an outcome. The principle enabling explainability is that if you decompose the system into interpretable stages and measure the contribution of each stage to the final ranking, you can construct explanations that show which factors mattered most. This principle works because ranking is compositional: documents pass through multiple filters and scoring stages, and by measuring the impact of each stage you can trace how a high-ranked item rose in the ranking. By building transparency and explainability into system design rather than bolting it on afterward, systems become auditable: users can detect whether rankings reflect their interests or the system's biases, and designers can identify and fix failure modes before deployment. This addresses the societal need: as systems make decisions affecting access to opportunities, users and regulators must be able to verify those decisions are sound.
SynthIR: The First Workshop on Synthetic Content in Information Retrieval EcosystemsSIGIR
uses Evaluating search and recommendation systems in an environment where some content is made by AI, distinguishing real information from generated content, and measuring whether users can tell the difference.
why it works Mixed environments of real and synthetic content break traditional metrics because a system might rank generated garbage highly if it happens to match keywords. Measuring whether users trust the result requires auditing whether retrieved content is verifiable. When you know which content is synthetic, you can catch ranking failures.
the deeper reason
Information ecosystems now contain both human-authored and AI-generated content, but retrieval systems were designed assuming corpora contain only human text. The core problem is that AI-generated content may contain hallucinations or be weakly grounded, yet ranking systems cannot easily distinguish it from human content, potentially ranking false or misleading information high. The principle at work is that evaluation metrics designed for human corpora measure different properties than those designed for synthetic content: metrics like relevance to a query work for both, but metrics like factual accuracy or credibility require measuring whether claims are grounded in external evidence. This principle applies because synthetic content poses new risks: a hallucinated but plausible-sounding answer might rank high because it is fluent and mentions relevant terms, even if false. By explicitly studying the properties of AI-generated content and redesigning evaluation to measure both quality and provenance, systems can more fairly rank mixed content and alert users to reliability concerns. This addresses emerging challenges: as synthetic content proliferates, systems that ignore its distinctive properties will inadvertently promote misinformation; evaluation frameworks must evolve to handle mixed corpora where human judgment about credibility is essential.
Justice, Emancipation, Democracy, and Information Access (JEDI): The SIGIR Workshop on Resisting Corporate and Authoritarian Capture of Information Access PlatformsSIGIR
uses Designing search systems that resist corporate control and support democracy by auditing whose voices get amplified, which information sources are suppressed, and how ranking choices entrench or reduce power imbalances.
why it works Search is political because ranking chooses whose information reaches whom. Separating truth from manipulation requires auditing the choices: which stories rise, which stay buried. Weighting voices fairly—by merit, not profit—is a design choice, not an accident. Measuring whose interests a system serves exposes whose freedom it supports or restricts.
the deeper reason
Information retrieval systems embody choices about whose information is made visible, whose voice is amplified, and how access is mediated, making them political tools. The core problem is that IR researchers have typically treated their systems as neutral technical artifacts, ignoring how design choices affect power and access. The principle at work is that systems designed without explicit focus to social justice and democratic values will tend to reinforce existing inequalities: algorithms amplify trends in training data, platforms favor content that attracts engagement over truth, and corporate control of search platforms concentrates power over information access. This principle applies because information is fundamental to participation and freedom: communities without access to information cannot advocate for themselves, and communities whose perspectives are systematically downranked have less influence over shared decisions. By explicitly centering questions of emancipation and democratic values in system design, researchers can ask whether their choices serve oppressive or liberatory aims and redesign toward more equitable alternatives. This addresses fundamental needs: societies depend on accessible, trustworthy information systems for democracy to function, so IR research that ignores justice concerns is complicit in systems of oppression.
VulGen: Workshop on Vulnerabilities in Generative Systems for Information RetrievalSIGIR
uses Identifying and measuring failure modes in generative systems used for information retrieval.
why it works It works because vulnerabilities are patterns that emerge when you actually run the system against adversarial or biased inputs—testing whether the system's behavior matches its intended function reveals when it fails.
the deeper reason
The core task is identifying and cataloging failure modes in systems that generate text for search. The soundness rests on this principle: when many independent researchers study the same systems from different angles—adversarial, behavioral, fairness—they uncover different slices of real harm that no single perspective catches. This works because generative systems fail in surprising, non-obvious ways that only become visible when you combine attack intuition, empirical testing, and domain knowledge from security and social science. By synthesizing these views, the community builds a shared map of what can go wrong, which is essential for preventing deployment disasters where an untested vulnerability leads to user harm at scale.
59 papers

Measuring surprise and information

Underneath search and compression sits a way to measure how surprising an outcome is, and therefore how much information it carries — a rare event tells you a lot, a certain one tells you nothing.

Why it works — the principle

It works because information has a natural, hard-to-cheat measure: the more unlikely a message, the more it narrows down the possibilities, and the fewer bits you need on average to send common things and more for rare ones. Systems that spend effort in proportion to surprise put their attention exactly where the uncertainty — and the payoff — actually is.

D-Models and E-Models: Diversity-Stability Trade-offs in the Sampling Behavior of Large Language ModelsWWW
uses Measure whether a language model's next-word probabilities match the true probabilities that matter for a task, revealing a trade-off between variety and stability.
why it works When a model samples the next word, it uses learned probabilities. If those probabilities are stable (don't bounce around) they match task requirements better. If they vary wildly, the model produces diverse outputs but unreliable ones. The math works because sampling is controlled by these probabilities, so their accuracy directly controls output quality.
the deeper reason
The core task is deciding whether a language model's words-by-words probability scores reflect real-world outcome likelihoods, like whether item relevance or purchase chance. The method works by comparing two things: what the model predicts at each step versus what actually happens in the real task. If they align, the model is trustworthy for that application; if they diverge, the model is overconfident or underconfident. This comparison reveals two model types: some prioritize exploring varied options at each step, creating noisy, less predictable sequences; others stay stable and focused, matching reality better. This principle holds because real tasks like shopping or code writing have genuine target distributions—some items are objectively more relevant than others—and a model aligned with that distribution will make better practical choices. The distinction matters because exploratory tasks need diversity while critical tasks like safety need stability; using the right model type for your goal prevents a system from either hedging bets too much or missing important options.
MoE-LC: General-Purpose Lossless Compression for Multi-modal Data via Entropy-Aware Multi-ExpertsWWW
uses Estimate how hard each batch of data is to compress, then assign more experts to hard batches and simpler experts to easy ones, routing each piece to the expert best suited to it.
why it works It works because different data has different complexity (one video is simple, another is intricate). Matching expert capacity to complexity improves efficiency: simple data doesn't waste resources, hard data gets the focus it needs. Surprise (how much surprise) measures complexity directly, so it naturally tells you which expert to use.
the deeper reason
Different modalities and batches have vastly different compressibility: a uniform color field compresses easily, a noisy photograph compresses poorly. A single compression expert designed for average conditions wastes computation on easy inputs and fails on hard ones. The system measures each batch's actual complexity (how much surprise), then allocates the right number of specialized compressors—easy data uses one simple expert, hard data gets multiple. This works because compression difficulty is measurable in the data itself: you can estimate how many bits any given stream needs without building a compressor. By routing adaptively based on measured how much surprise and applying high-precision work only where it matters, the system balances resource use across heterogeneous, shifting distributions without sacrificing compression quality.
Digital Skin, Digital Bias: Uncovering Tone-Based Biases in LLMs and Emoji EmbeddingsWWW
uses Measure whether emojis with different skin tones sit close together in the model's inner representation space, and whether they carry different sentiment scores even when the base emoji is identical.
why it works It works because if a model truly treats a smiling face emoji equally regardless of skin tone, they should sit at equal distances in the model's learned space and carry the same sentiment. Large distances or sentiment gaps reveal the model has learned to encode skin tone as distinct and meaningful in ways that shouldn't matter, exposing where bias is baked in.
the deeper reason
numeric fingerprints—learned numeric representations of emoji—capture statistical patterns from training data faithfully. If training data associates positive language with light-skin emoji and negative language with dark-skin emoji (reflecting societal bias), the numeric fingerprints will encode those associations structurally: positive sentiment words will sit closer in numeric fingerprints space to light-skin emojis than dark-skin ones. By measuring numeric fingerprints similarities, sentiment scores, and representational geometry across skin tones, the study exposes these hidden biases. This works because geometry in numeric fingerprints space is not random—distances and clusters reflect learned associations. Even when bias is invisible in the raw text, it materializes in the learned representation. Finding skewed sentiment and inconsistent meaning across skin tones is not about judgment but mathematical measurement of the model's learned statistics, revealing that the model has internalized the very disparities it should not perpetuate.
Rhythm of Opinion: Interpretable Hawkes-Graph Networks for Hierarchical Opinion PropagationWWW
uses Model opinion propagation as a point process where opinions flow at rates determined by emotional context and hierarchical position.
why it works Opinion spreads in bursts when emotions align, modeled as time-clustered events; the rates reveal how hierarchy and feeling drive adoption. This captures that propagation speed depends on both content and audience readiness.
the deeper reason
Opinion spread follows temporal patterns where emotions and hierarchical depth interact—some sentiments propagate faster at reply level versus root comments, and earlier posts create memory effects on later ones. The method models this using Hawkes processes combined with graph networks: a Hawkes process quantifies how past events increase the likelihood of future similar events, parameterized by emotional and structural features. The framework works because Hawkes processes have interpretable rate parameters that directly represent propagation strength and temporal decay, and graph networks add structure by only allowing influence along comment hierarchies. By decomposing propagation into these interpretable pieces, they can measure the actual mechanisms driving opinion spread rather than just predicting outcomes.
Do You Think What I Think? A Qualitative Study for Maximising User Engagement through Latent Visual PropertiesWWW
uses Identify visual design choices—color, layout, symbolic encoding—that do not directly represent data yet improve insight and engagement.
why it works Visual properties work because they exploit how humans process information: color evokes emotion, layout guides focus, symbols encode meaning. These channels communicate beyond the numbers alone.
the deeper reason
Static data visualizations convey facts but miss hidden visual properties that trigger insight and creativity—things like cognitive patterns, color emotional associations, or design space that viewers can reinterpret. The study reveals that engagement grows when designers explicitly craft these hidden properties: ignorance mapping signals what you do not know to reduce cognitive overload, creative unblocking uses filtering and interactivity to encourage exploration, and symbolic representation uses color or shape to evoke emotion and empathy. These properties work because they address how humans actually interpret visualizations—not just as literal data encodings, but as tools for sense-making and reflection.
Toward Graph-Tokenizing Large Language Models with Reconstructive Graph Instruction TuningWWW
uses An AI language systems learns graph-to-text alignment by reconstructing graph structure from its internal words outputs, adding explicit graph supervision to language-only instruction tuning.
why it works It works because text-only supervision creates asymmetry where language dominates and graph context is underutilized; by requiring reconstruction of the original graph, you force the model to preserve all information, making alignment bidirectional rather than text-biased.
the deeper reason
Teaching language models to handle graphs faces a fundamental problem: just encoding graphs into sequences and supervising with text leaves the language model dominant, barely using graph structure. The method addresses this by adding explicit graph reconstruction: the model not only predicts text words aligned with the input graph, but also reconstructs the graph itself from those words. This works because reconstruction is a stronger constraint—it forces the model to preserve graph information end-to-end. Information theory guarantees that maximizing the mutual information between input graphs and learned representations lets both graph and text supervision pull in aligned directions. Reconstruction adds graph supervision directly, improving this upper bound on alignment. The model learns words sequences that capture both semantic meaning (text alignment) and structural correctness (graph reconstruction), preventing the text signal from drowning out graph signal.
Early Recall Estimation and Stopping in Technology-Assisted Reviews via Ranker-Sampler FusionWWW
uses Combines a ranking model's scores with a probability sample of documents to estimate true recall without judging the entire corpus, enabling early stopping decisions.
why it works It works because the ranker's scores act as an informative starting guess about which documents are likely relevant; updating that starting guess with random samples gives unbiased estimates, and confidence bounds tell you when additional sampling won't substantially improve the estimate.
the deeper reason
In document review workflows, knowing when to stop requires estimating true recall without examining every document—prohibitively expensive at low prevalence. The method fuses two sources of information: a ranking model that scores documents (telling you which documents are most likely relevant) and a random sample of truly judged documents (giving you an unbiased ground truth signal). The ranking model acts as an informed starting guess: if it assigns high scores to many documents, you'd expect high recall; a small sample refines this belief. The model-assisted estimator corrects ranker bias by combining its calibrated scores with design-based sampling weights from classical statistics. This works because the two sources have complementary strengths: the ranker has no sampling error but may be biased; the sample has no model bias but high sampling spread of error. Combining them statistically reduces both errors. Conservative lower bounds then guarantee stopping rules won't overestimate and miss relevant documents.
Spectral Disentanglement and Enhancement: A Dual-domain Contrastive Framework for Representation LearningWWW
uses Partition high-dimensional features into strong signals, weak signals, and noise using decomposition, then amplify the strong signals that carry task-relevant meaning.
why it works It works because features collapse into narrow cones, wasting features. By sorting features by importance (how much they vary), you focus on the true pattern and ignore noise, which improves generalization because real knowledge fits simpler than noise does.
the deeper reason
High-dimensional feature spaces often suffer from an imbalance where a few features carry signal while most are noise, causing models to generalize poorly. This method uses spectral decomposition to separate the strong, medium, and weak features, then amplifies the strong ones according to a schedule that keeps training stable. The principle: if you can identify and amplify the subspace where task-relevant patterns actually live, you reduce the confusion from noise without breaking the model's learning trajectory. The dual loss—comparing features both as usual and also in their spectral profile—ensures the model learns to represent the world in a cleaner, more organized way, making predictions on fresh data more reliable.
Evaluating LLM Recommendations Under StressWWW
uses Test models on five tasks of rising difficulty and measure how much their accuracy drops, then compute a sensitivity score to rank robustness under stress.
why it works It works because stress reveals true robustness: a model that works on easy tasks but fails on hard ones is fragile. The drop in performance is the right signal—you're seeing what breaks first, which tells you where the model is weakest and most likely to fail in deployment.
the deeper reason
Language models are evaluated in relaxed, open-ended settings, but real deployment involves time pressure, incomplete information, and strict constraints—conditions where models often fail. This paper stress-tests three models across escalating difficulty and measures a Stress Sensitivity Index: how much each model's performance drops as pressure increases. The principle: robustness cannot be measured in comfortable conditions because degradation only emerges under load. By deliberately creating realistic stress scenarios and measuring the slope of degradation, practitioners can predict which model will remain reliable in production, and researchers can identify failure modes that comfortable benchmarks miss.
Towards Better Evaluation Metrics for Text-to-Motion GenerationWWW
uses Match text descriptions to motion using optimal transport, then measure discrepancy without assuming a fixed shape of distribution, to evaluate generation quality.
why it works It works because optimal transport finds the most efficient coupling between text and motion—the minimum cost to transform one into the other. This captures global matching better than local methods. And avoiding the Gaussian assumption catches real data that's spiky or multimodal.
the deeper reason
Metrics like FID and R-Precision for motion-generation are biased: FID assumes a Gaussian distribution when motion is not, and R-Precision ignores the global alignment. This work proposes Optimal Transport Matching (treating text-motion pairs as an assignment problem to find the best global pairing) and Maximum Mean Discrepancy (measuring distributional distance without assuming any shape). The principle: when comparing distributions, if you avoid restrictive shape assumptions and focus on true alignment between text and motion, you get evaluations that correlate with human perception. By grounding metrics in transport theory and empirical divergence rather than Gaussianity, the evaluation becomes an honest reflection of whether the generated motions actually match the requests.
A Prompt-Aware Structuring Framework for Reliable Reuse of AI-Generated Content in the Agentic WebWWW
uses Attaches confidence scores and metadata recording how the content was generated, with verifiable credentials to estimate reliability when the same content is reused.
why it works It works because reusing untracked content causes errors to compound and spread. By measuring and recording confidence at generation, any downstream user can estimate the true reliability of what they're reusing, stopping bad information before it chains into hallucinations.
the deeper reason
AI-generated content becomes reusable when its provenance is transparent—what model, prompt, and settings produced it, plus confidence in the output. This metadata enables downstream agents to assess whether reusing content is safe by checking if conditions match their own context and verifying credentials. The soundness rests on the principle that identical inputs from the same model with the same settings will produce similar outputs. By attaching this structured context envelope, the framework makes content reliability assessable without requiring re-execution, preventing chained hallucinations where bad outputs are propagated through agent pipelines.
Blind-QEM: A Privacy-Preserving Framework for Quantum Error Mitigation via Zero-Knowledge ProofsWWW
uses The system verifies quantum computation results using zero-knowledge proof protocols that confirm correctness without revealing the circuit's structure or proprietary noise models.
why it works Zero-knowledge proofs work because the verifier can check a commitment matches an execution without ever seeing the secret. Here, the quantum provider can prove the result follows from the submitted circuit without exposing that circuit, protecting intellectual property on both sides.
the deeper reason
Quantum computers solve problems by running circuits through noisy hardware, but circuits and calibration data are often proprietary IP; central error mitigation requires visibility into both, creating a privacy-utility dilemma. Blind-QEM solves this using zero-knowledge proofs: a service provider can certify that it applied correct noise-mitigation statistics without ever seeing the client's circuit, by verifying a commitment to the circuit and checking that the statistics are consistent with that (hidden) circuit. This works because zero-knowledge proofs are a mathematical gadget: the prover can convince a verifier that a statement is true without revealing why. Applied here, the provider proves it aggregated correct statistics over committed circuits without learning the circuits themselves. The soundness rests on cryptographic binding: QPU-signed logs and circuit commitments lock both parties into consistent claims, so neither can later change their story about what was run or what was mitigated.
Active Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Conflict-Fused Uncertainty QuantificationWWW
uses Combine three uncertainty signals at each step to decide when to fetch external information, triggering retrieval for multi-hop reasoning.
why it works It works because uncertainty has multiple sources: the model's internal confusion, disagreement across multiple runs, and conflict between different signals. Fusing all three captures the true ambiguity better than any single signal, so retrieval triggers precisely when needed.
the deeper reason
Language models generate text step-by-step, but deciding when to stop and retrieve external knowledge is hard because uncertainty comes from multiple sources: disagreement about what word comes next, and disagreement between different sampling attempts at the same step. The method quantifies both sources separately using how much surprise within a local window and consensus across multiple samples, then combines them into a single score using information divergence. This works because real uncertainty has structure—local how much surprise captures what the model's immediate confidence is, consensus captures whether running the model again gives the same answer—and fusion of both signals provides a more complete picture than either alone.
Trust in One Round: Confidence Estimation for Large Language Models via Structural SignalsWWW
uses Score model confidence by analyzing patterns in the internal hidden states across multiple scales, without needing extra computations.
why it works It works because a model's internal layers show stability and coherence patterns before the model produces its final answer. These patterns correlate with correctness better than surface-level signals like likelihood or similarity, and they cost nothing extra to compute.
the deeper reason
Existing confidence scores for language model outputs use single signals like words probability or similarity to reference answers, but these fail under distribution shift because the model's internal behavior changes. The method instead examines structural patterns in the model's internal state trajectory—shapes and oscillations in hidden layers—which capture how stable the computation was. This works because confidence should reflect whether the model executed a consistent computation, not just the probability of the final words. Structural features are model-agnostic because any model learning the same task develops consistent internal patterns for correct versus incorrect reasoning, making these patterns robust across different architectures and domains.
Data Degrades with UseWWW
uses Measure how much information each data use leaks and account for cumulative privacy loss across repeated queries.
why it works Privacy loss is proportional to information revealed; repeated uses amplify individual leaks because each query constrains future possibilities. Aggregating these bounds prevents privacy guarantees from degrading as data is reused.
the deeper reason
The talk argues data is consumable rather than infinitely reusable, grounded in privacy mathematics. The core principle is that any meaningful public release of data about real people necessarily leaks some information about those individuals, and these leaks accumulate each time the dataset is shared or queried. This is sound because information is additive: if analysis A reveals something about person X, and analysis B reveals something about person X, an observer seeing both results learns more than from either alone. The legal concept of mosaic effect reinforces this—seemingly harmless facts combine into intimate portraits. This matters because it means data use itself has limits: if ten analyses each leak 0.01 of privacy, the total loss is real. Treating data use as a rival good implies governance systems where access is budgeted and monitored.
SMART: A Social Movement Analysis & Reasoning Tool with Case Studies on #MeToo and #BlackLivesMatterWWW
uses Extract emotion distributions from social media posts and forecast their intensity and volume in future posts.
why it works Emotions have inertia and respond predictably to external events; modeling past sequences as a mixture of emotions lets you forecast when sentiment will shift, enabling early detection of discourse changes.
the deeper reason
Social movements generate emotional signals across platforms, and journalists need early warning when discourse shifts, especially around external events like elections. SMART combines data collection with a learned language systems-based forecasting model that predicts future emotional intensity. The method works because emotions on social media respond to external events with predictable delays: trauma discussions spike after news of injustice, then decay; the learned language systems learns these temporal patterns and can forecast when the next spike will occur or intensity drop. This is sound because human emotional response to events is non-random: communities process news synchronously, producing correlated posting patterns that compress into learnable dynamics. By detecting when predicted emotion diverges from actual emotion, journalists spot when discourse has shifted course—an early signal something unexpected happened.
Understanding the Consequences of VTuber ReincarnationWWW
uses Measure the quantitative impact of reincarnation on audience size, revenue, harassment, and industry ripple effects using 728K livestream sessions.
why it works Aggregate statistics across many events reveal patterns that single cases cannot. The volume of data allows real effects to emerge from noise, showing how individual career transitions translate into measurable shifts in audience behavior and creator welfare.
the deeper reason
VTuber reincarnation—when a performer leaves an agency and debuts with a new persona—causes measurable damage to careers and revenue. This paper quantifies that damage empirically by analyzing 728K livestreams and 4.5B viewer interactions around 12 major reincarnation events. The study documents audience decline, financial loss, and harassment increases using observable quantities: viewer counts, subscription churn, payment volume, and comment negativity. The strength of this approach is that it grounds abstract industry problems (burnout, instability, precarious labor) in concrete, measurable outcomes. The mathematical principle is that aggregating large-scale behavioral traces reveals population-level effects that individual accounts miss. By analyzing when and how the audience changes relative to the reincarnation event, researchers can attribute causality: the timing shows the reincarnation is the shock that triggers audience departure, not confounding factors. This quantification matters because it transforms a subjective narrative (reincarnation is harmful) into data-driven evidence. When agency executives and performers see numerical evidence of audience loss and its magnitude, the argument for reforming industry structure becomes harder to dismiss.
Prediction Guardian: A Distribution-based Real-time Anomaly Detection and Mitigation Framework for Online AdvertisingWWW
uses Monitor the shape of ad-ranking prediction scores over time; when the distribution shifts (fewer high bids, more low bids, or suddenly extreme values), flag it and smooth outliers.
why it works Healthy systems produce predictable, repeatable distributions of predictions; a sudden shift means the training data or real-world behavior has changed. By comparing today's distribution to historical baselines using divergence metrics, you catch silent failures before they ripple downstream into billing or user experience.
the deeper reason
Advertising prediction models compute expected values that drive real business logic, so a single corrupted prediction can cause cascading harm in pricing and delivery. The system monitors whether current predictions match the statistical shape of healthy historical predictions—typically a log-normal distribution with a predictable tail. The core principle is that distribution shifts have detectable signatures: if corruption pushes predictions systematically higher or lower, or swells the tail, the aggregate distribution departs from the baseline. By comparing real-time distributions to historical ones using robust distance metrics, the system identifies when something has gone wrong without needing to pinpoint the exact failure. Once anomaly detection signals a problem, targeted mitigations (smoothing outliers, zeroing corrupted values) restore predictions to a healthy shape before they propagate into pricing and ranking decisions.
RobustReviewAI: A Robustness Evaluation System for AI-Powered Peer ReviewWWW
uses Measures how a review system's decisions change when text, tables, and formulas are altered, revealing weak points.
why it works It works because small changes that don't affect true meaning (perturbations) expose whether the model is truly understanding the paper or relying on brittle patterns. If decisions flip under these changes, the system isn't robust.
the deeper reason
The core challenge is measuring how reliably an AI review system makes the same judgment when content is slightly altered—like when formulas or tables are changed. The method works because perturbations applied to different parts of a paper (text, tables, formulas) reveal which kinds of information the reviewer actually relies on; if the system gives wildly different scores after a small table change, that signals fragility. By systematically testing across all content types rather than just text, they capture whether the reviewer truly understands the full work or has fooled itself by finding shortcuts in readable prose alone. This matters for deploying AI reviewers in conferences, since a fragile reviewer might recommend papers it doesn't actually understand.
Additively Competitive SecretariesWWW
uses Minimize the worst-case gap between what an optimal decision-maker in hindsight could have achieved and what a decision-making policy achieves on average when hiring from a random-order stream.
why it works This works because the regret metric penalizes both being too conservative and too aggressive in the right way: policies that miss good candidates (high regret) and policies that hire bad ones (high regret) must balance the two, which naturally finds strategies that capture most of what's possible without requiring perfect timing. The additive gap is also robust—it scales fairly across different problem sizes.
the deeper reason
The paper computes the worst-case additive distance between what an online policy achieves and what an oracle could do with perfect foresight. The soundness rests on measuring regret under full knowledge of values in [0,1]—this creates a bounded problem space where no policy can exceed 1 unit of loss.
