Pseudo-Relevance Feedback improves search by reusing top results to find better terms, but it sometimes makes queries worse—query drift—with asymmetric harm across different search intents. The paper asks the crucial question: does this harm actually affect real users? By deploying a careful grid-based study where users chose between original and refined results without bias, they found that harm avoidance beats harm amplification two-to-one. This matters because offline metrics miss what users genuinely prefer; participatory measurement with real queries grounds research in actual experience.
Targeted Parameter Selection for Rank-Biased MeasurementSIGIR
uses Selects decay weights for ranking comparisons using power-law distributions, choosing parameters so top results receive emphasis matching experimental goals.
why it works Comparisons only need to order results correctly, not score them truly. A carefully chosen decay weight can boost top items while ignoring tail differences. Finding the right weight shape means top-ranking results dominate the signal while irrelevant details stay quiet.
the deeper reason
Rank-biased metrics weight early results more heavily to match user focus, using a geometric decay. This paper proposes a two-parameter weighting scheme with both decay strength and shape, allowing inverse power-law functions beyond geometric. More parameters bring more flexibility to match different experimental goals and user behaviors. The principle is that human focus does not follow a single universal curve; different retrieval contexts have different decay patterns. Providing principled ways to select parameters lets researchers match their measurement to their actual user model.
G-CoS: An Interpretable Gain-Cost Framework for User Satisfaction Estimation in Generative Information RetrievalSIGIR
uses Model satisfaction as a balance between response quality and interaction cost, where users trade off better answers against effort spent.
why it works Users want good answers but also want to spend minimal time and effort. These trade off—a perfect answer that takes five searches is worse than a good answer that takes one. By measuring both quality gain and cost together, you capture what users actually optimize for in their behavior.
the deeper reason
User satisfaction in generative IR results from balancing response quality against the cognitive effort and cost to obtain it—a user values a good answer but not if they spend excessive time reformulating queries or parsing lengthy interactions. Rather than using an external judge, this method models satisfaction as a direct trade-off between measured response quality and measurable interaction costs, learning how each contributes to satisfaction from actual user data. This works because satisfaction is fundamentally about subjective utility, and utility theory teaches that choices reflect trade-offs between desirable attributes; by quantifying both gain and cost, the model captures how users actually weight these features in practice.
BeLink: Biomedical Entity Linking Meets Generative Re-RankingSIGIR
uses Instruct-tune an open model to rank candidate entities for biomedical linking, treating multiple candidates as a set to choose from.
why it works Large pretrained models work well at ranking when you teach them what ranking means through instruction tuning. Set-wise tuning lets the model see multiple candidates together, so it can compare them directly. This is faster and more accurate than scoring them independently.
the deeper reason
Biomedical entity linking involves linking mentions in text to correct medical entities, a problem where many candidate entities could match a mention. Re-ranking candidates with a generative model works because the model can reason about which candidate best fits the full context of the mention and surrounding text. Instruction-tuning teaches the model to score candidates as a set rather than individually, exploiting the fact that comparing multiple candidates together often makes the correct one obvious—context that disambiguates one mention often eliminates wrong candidates immediately. This approach is faster than dense ranking because set-wise selection is more efficient than pairwise comparisons.
DisCoRec: Disentangled Conformity-aware Recommendation with LLM-Guided Multi-View LearningSIGIR
uses Score each user-item pair using a learned model that weights different factors—genuine interest vs social influence—differently for each one.
why it works By learning to separate what users actually want from what they're doing because others do it, you can score predictions more accurately. Weighting the true factors more heavily pushes good recommendations to the top.
the deeper reason
The paper separates two conflicting forces shaping what users click: their true preferences and their tendency to follow the crowd. The underlying principle is that these two sources of signal can be isolated if you model them in separate views and then learn which view to trust in each situation. This works because genuine preference and social conformity produce distinguishable patterns in behavior—one person might always click popular items regardless of personal taste, while another ignores trends. By having language understanding examine each view independently and then using a gate to decide which view matters most for each user, the system avoids the false confidence that comes from naive focus. This lets recommendations become truly personalized rather than averaging out into what everyone buys.
HE-DeepFM: An FHE Inference System for CTR Prediction with Efficient FM InteractionsSIGIR
uses Score click-through likelihood using encrypted computation that computes feature interactions efficiently without ever exposing the raw data.
why it works The math works inside the encrypted domain by packing related calculations together so you can do pairwise interactions without the expensive quadratic blowup. The ranking stays accurate because the core scoring formula is unchanged.
the deeper reason
The core challenge is computing pairwise feature interactions for CTR scoring while keeping data encrypted. Factorization Machines normally require O(F squared) operations to combine every pair of features, which becomes prohibitively slow under encryption. The solution exploits SIMD packing: encrypting multiple feature values into one ciphertext slot and computing them in parallel. When these packed slots are multiplied, the mathematics automatically computes all the pairwise products you need in a single encrypted operation, collapsing what would be quadratic work into near-linear work. By redesigning the FM operator to pack features strategically, the system can predict ad clicks on sensitive data without decrypting it, unlocking privacy-preserving personalization.
One-Pass Decoding for Generative Recommendation with WFST-Constrained A* SearchSIGIR
uses Score all possible next item identifiers in a single forward pass, then use A* search through the space of valid sequences to find the best recommendation without backtracking.
why it works Computing scores once instead of iteratively avoids error propagation from early greedy choices. A* search guarantees you find the optimal sequence because it explores only valid paths, weighted by one-pass scores that are consistent across all positions.
the deeper reason
Generative recommendation predicts the next item by generating item identifiers, but iterative decoding forces locally greedy choices that lead to suboptimal sequences. The solution computes all position-wise item scores in one forward pass and searches over them using A* guided by a finite-state machine that enforces valid item sequences. This works because the finite-state machine encodes constraints—items must follow valid transitions in the user's purchase history—and A* uses these constraints to prune impossible branches. Computing scores in a single pass means no early decision can trap later choices, and A* guarantees that the path found is optimal under the constraint. The result is globally coherent item sequences instead of locally greedy predictions.
LLM-based Semantic and ID Representations for Sequential RecommendationSIGIR
uses Score items in sequences by learning textual and collaborative features together, then rank the items with highest scores.
why it works It works because combining multiple sources of understanding (what the item is semantically and who interacts with it) captures user preference more accurately than any single signal alone. Learning from the data teaches the scoring function to weight signals appropriately.
the deeper reason
The core problem is learning user preferences when item interactions are sparse. The method works by combining two complementary signals: ID-based collaborative patterns, which reveal what people frequently bought together in dense regions of the catalog, and semantic features from a language model, which generalize across items using world knowledge. Where ID signals fade because an item is new or rarely purchased, semantic features carry meaning forward; where collaboration is strong and reliable, ID patterns are more trustworthy. Blending both sources lets the system use frequency signals where they're strongest and reasoning signals where data is thin, improving recommendations for both popular and novel items.
GraphSynthQA: Knowledge-Graph-Guided Query Synthesis and Step-Level Preference Optimization for Web AgentsSIGIR
uses Rank web-search steps by comparing successful paths to failed attempts, training the model to prefer actions that lead downstream to correct answers.
why it works It works because comparing success-and-failure pairs teaches the model which decisions matter most. By contrasting paths that work against those that don't on the same query, you isolate the causal steps that move toward truth, without needing to explore all possibilities expensively.
the deeper reason
The core challenge is training web agents to browse and answer questions when real training data is scarce. The method works by generating questions from a knowledge graph grounded in actual web-verifiable evidence chains, then training with step-level feedback. Each reasoning step gets feedback based on whether that action led to eventual success, providing dense process supervision instead of just terminal outcomes. Because every intermediate choice is evaluated, the agent learns which actions tend to cascade toward answers, without the expense and brittleness of online trial-and-error. This dense feedback is mathematically sound because it directly optimizes for actions that correlate with success.
Rank-R1: Enhancing Reasoning in LLM-based Document Rerankers via Reinforcement LearningSIGIR
uses Improve ranking by first reasoning about why a document is relevant, using reward signals from correct rankings to strengthen that reasoning.
why it works It works because humans rank by thinking first, so teaching the model to reason before ranking lets it discover what details actually distinguish better answers. The ranking feedback tells the model which reasoning patterns led to good decisions.
the deeper reason
The core problem is ranking documents by relevance when the criteria are complex and implicit. The method works by learning to write an intermediate reasoning step before the ranking decision. Relevance is not purely syntactic matching; human judges apply tacit knowledge about why a document answers a question. Reinforcement learning discovers reasoning patterns that correlate with high relevance scores, allowing the model to articulate the logic before committing to a ranking. This works because reasoning steps that predict ground-truth relevance must capture genuine criteria, making the ranking itself more robust to distribution shift and out-of-domain queries.
Beyond Semantic Similarity: Explicit Intent Modeling for Query-Product MatchingSIGIR
uses Score query-product matches by scoring individual attributes separately then combining them, focusing on attributes the query explicitly mentions.
why it works It works because buyers specify attributes (color, size, brand) that are non-negotiable, not soft preferences. By scoring each attribute independently you catch when a product violates one hard constraint, then combining ensures all attributes are satisfied. Weighting mentioned attributes heavily ensures they dominate.
the deeper reason
The core problem is matching query intent to products when users specify explicit attribute constraints like brand and color. Overall semantic similarity can mismatch these constraints; a product may be topically related but violate key attributes. The method works by resolving attributes in both query and products, then matching at the aspect level before aggregating. This fine-grained matching catches attribute violations that whole-item similarity misses. The system remains efficient because aspect resolution and matching reuse sparse, structured data; this preserves two-tower retrieval speed while gaining attribute awareness.
LLM Agents Factory: Retrieval of Domain-Specific LLM AgentsSIGIR
uses Retrieve pre-built agent profiles matching a user query from a large repository, scoring semantic similarity to find the most appropriate agent.
why it works It works because good agents for a domain already exist or follow patterns. Instead of designing each agent on-the-fly (expensive and unstable), retrieving from a known set reuses proven templates. Semantic matching finds agents similar to the current task, and they transfer because agents in the same domain share structure.
the deeper reason
The core problem is deploying language model agents efficiently when designing them on-the-fly for each request is expensive and unstable. The method works by retrieving pre-built agent profiles from a repository of twenty thousand proven agents instead of generating agents dynamically. Retrieval is fast and deterministic; each profile is vetted and reusable. For speed-critical systems, a small model can be trained to predict which agent to use directly. This approach works because agent construction is a retrieval problem not a generation problem—most queries benefit from one of the existing agents rather than a bespoke one.
BERT-Based Cross-Encoder for Large-Scale Engagement Prediction and Re-ranking in Walmart Search EngineSIGIR
uses Score engagement by learning from query-item text pairs labeled with actual user engagement, capturing what buyers truly prefer.
why it works It works because user intent is hidden in language patterns, not historical clickrate statistics. Learning directly from text and true engagement labels teaches the model to recognize the language features that signal what will actually get added to cart. This works even on tail queries where statistical patterns don't exist.
the deeper reason
The core problem is predicting which products users find engaging for a given query when historical engagement data is noisy and sparse for tail queries. The method works by learning directly from query-product text pairs labeled with actual engagement, rather than relying on historical statistics. Text pairs capture the real semantic match between what users asked for and what they found; this direct coupling removes noise from visibility bias and other confounds. Because the training signal is the actual semantic query-item relationship, not indirect engagement history, the model learns genuine preference signals that generalize to both sparse tail queries and broad intent discovery.
MMRM: A Multiplex Multimodal Representation Model for Product Ranking in E-commerce SearchSIGIR
uses The system learns a single rich description of each product using multiple signals at once, then uses that description to rank items and understand users.
why it works Products have multiple facets—their image, text, and how users interact with them—and a single shared model can learn from all these signals together. One complete description is more efficient and more accurate than treating each signal separately, because shared understanding reveals patterns no single signal shows alone.
the deeper reason
When ranking products in search, using multiple types of user signals at once—clicks, purchases, engagement time—is more powerful than using them separately because they measure different aspects of satisfaction. The system learns a shared visual and textual representation of each product by training on all these signals together, then derives task-specific user profiles for each signal type using search behavior sequences. This works because the underlying multimodal product features (image, title, price, reviews) genuinely affect different behaviors in predictable ways, so modeling them once with signal-specific output heads captures those dependencies more efficiently and accurately than fitting separate models.
Population-Guided Intent-Aware Query Rewriting for Web SearchSIGIR
uses A system learns to rewrite search queries to match mainstream search intents, scoring rewrites by how well they align with what populations search for.
why it works It works because population-level patterns reveal what most people actually want to find; by learning this intent from search logs, rewrites naturally align with real user goals. The learned rewriter improves on fixed rules because it discovers patterns that static templates miss.
the deeper reason
The system learns to rewrite queries by clustering what the general population searches for, capturing the dominant intent shared across millions of users. Because the most common search pattern reflects what works best in the system's ranking model, aligning a query toward this popular center makes it more likely to match results the ranking system considers high-quality. This works mathematically because high-volume queries have already been optimized: the system has learned which results satisfy them. When an unusual or ambiguous query gets rewritten to resemble a popular intent, it drops into a well-worn path where the ranking system is confident.
Calibrate Your Items! Train CTR Models in Two Steps for Robust RecommendationsSIGIR
uses A neural model learns to predict click rates while being trained to also predict whether its scores fairly represent different groups of items.
why it works It works because calibration (predicting fairness alongside predictions) prevents the model from relying on shortcuts that work for frequent items but fail for rare ones. When scoring is constrained to be honest across all groups, downstream systems that multiply scores by other factors (like auction bids) work correctly.
the deeper reason
The system trains models to predict click-through rate with equal accuracy across all items, not just overall accuracy. When predicted rates match actual rates item-by-item, the model faithfully represents how each item will perform when combined downstream with bids or other multipliers. This works because miscalibration compounds: if a low-value item gets overestimated, it steals ranking position from a high-value item that was underestimated, breaking the final scoring. Forcing the model to be honest about every single item prevents these distortions from stacking up.
MedNQS: Medical State-Aware Dual-Stage Next-Turn Question Suggestion for Online Medical ConsultationsSIGIR
uses A system tracks the medical conversation state, retrieves question candidates filtered by what makes sense given that state, then ranks them using data on which questions users actually chose.
why it works It works because medical consultations follow patterns; knowing the dialogue state (what was discussed, what condition) narrows possibilities to relevant ones. Ranking by real user preferences (not guesses) ensures suggested questions actually help the conversation.
the deeper reason
The system tracks the medical conversation state so it knows what has already been discussed, then retrieves follow-up questions tuned to the current situation rather than generic questions for the topic. Because medical reasoning builds sequentially, a good follow-up question depends critically on context; asking an off-state question wastes the doctor and patient's time. The system ranks these context-aware candidates using preference judgments from real consultations, aligning the model with actual medical workflows rather than static quality scores.
PCANet: Price Change Aware Framework for Mitigating Inconsistencies in Large-Scale Ranking SystemsSIGIR
uses Flight rankings are scored using both relevance and user sensitivity to price changes, dynamically adjusting which flights rank high based on whether a person will tolerate fare surprises.
why it works It works because two people finding the same flight relevant does not mean showing both will convert equally; one might abandon if the price jumps, the other won't. Scoring by relevance times sensitivity per individual prevents wasted ranking effort on flights that will shock away price-sensitive users.
the deeper reason
The system maintains a cache of prices but detects when inventory changes might make those prices stale, using live inventory signals to flag which prices need rechecking. Because stale prices cause trust erosion and failed bookings, alerting the ranking model to price volatility lets it avoid showing deals that will break by checkout time. This works by treating price consistency as a real constraint: when the model knows a price is uncertain, it can deprioritize that option in favor of more stable choices, preventing the experience cliff that users see between listing and payment.
SkyDistill: Navigating Fuzzy Flight Search Ranking via Precise Intent DistillationSIGIR
uses Knowledge learned from precise flight searches is transferred to a smaller model for fuzzy searches using three layers of hints: feature alignment, confidence-weighted transfer, and ranking order preservation.
why it works It works because fuzzy search data is sparse but precise search is rich; precise search fundamentals (what makes a flight attractive) are reusable. The three alignment layers ensure the smaller model doesn't just copy rules but learns to adapt: features map correctly, weak confidence signals are filtered out, and relative preferences stay consistent.
the deeper reason
The system trains a precise-search model on exact itineraries where intent is clear, then distills that knowledge into a model for fuzzy searches where intent is ambiguous. Because fuzzy queries mix competing goals while precise queries solve single goals, the precise model has learned a cleaner signal; teaching the fuzzy model to mimic that signal helps it navigate the messier case. This works because the fuzzy model now inherits structures and feature relationships that the precise model discovered, giving it a head start on the much harder fuzzy problem.
A Cost-Efficient AI Copilot for High-Volume E-commerce Customer SupportSIGIR
uses A copilot rewrites each customer message into a complete, standalone question, retrieves relevant policies and procedures, then generates a draft response based on all three.
why it works It works because customer messages alone are ambiguous—rewriting makes them self-contained so context is never lost. Ranking relevant policies ensures responses align with actual company practice. The draft+edit model lets humans verify that automation hasn't hallucinated while cutting the time they spend on routine reasoning.
the deeper reason
The system writes draft responses grounded in the company's procedures and order history so human agents can review and refine them in seconds rather than reconstructing context from memory. Because agents spend energy rebuilding context on each message, providing a policy-consistent draft front-loaded saves cognitive load at the moment of decision. This works because the system externalizes the mechanical parts of response composition: retrieving procedures, factoring in order state, matching tone. When agents only edit and approve, they focus purely on judgment, not memory.
PersonaPlugin: A Multi-Source Persona Framework for LLM Personalization in TelecommunicationsSIGIR
uses Telecom user signals (calls, app usage, location) are converted into structured personas that are then injected into language model responses to personalize answers.
why it works It works because raw signals (call duration, app opens, location) are noisy; structuring them into personas (preferences, constraints, context) gives the language model semantically meaningful input. Personas act as filters: instead of the model guessing what matters, it gets explicit signals about the person it's addressing.
the deeper reason
The system builds a description of each user from call transcripts, app behavior, and location patterns, then injects this profile into the language model so it tailors responses to that person's situation. Because users have different needs and preferences that appear across their data traces, building a unified profile lets the model reason about them coherently. This works because the model can now condition on concrete facts about the user rather than generic defaults; personalization works when the system has actual signals to condition on.
Building a Production Shopping Agent at ScaleSIGIR
uses Routes customer requests to specialized retrieval, reasoning, and tool-calling systems, optimizing for accuracy, speed, cost, and reliability at massive scale.
why it works It works because each subtask (product search, Q&A, actions) has different optimal strategies. Routing to specialized components lets each solve its problem cheaply and accurately. Production constraints force this modularity rather than a single end-to-end model.
the deeper reason
The system deploys a reasoning agent for shopping at Amazon's scale, where latency, accuracy, and cost are all strict requirements. The core insight is that combining three capabilities—reasoning about what the customer wants, retrieving relevant products quickly without searching the entire catalog, and orchestrating multiple tools to take action—creates a system that achieves production quality despite the inherent difficulty of question-answering and discovery. The principle is that specialized components for retrieval and tools are more efficient and reliable than trying to make the agent solve everything end-to-end. This architecture works because each piece can be optimized independently for its specific job: retrieval systems are fast at narrowing possibilities, tools are reliable at structured actions, and reasoning focuses on connecting them. The combination lets the system handle product discovery, answer questions, and take actions within real-time constraints while maintaining accuracy that customers trust.
When Search Is Not Enough: Ranking Content for Query-Less Browse SurfacesSIGIR
uses Learns to rank content within browse categories using actual user browsing session data instead of treating the category name as a search query.
why it works It works because browsing is different from searching: users explore without clear intent. Category names are imperfect proxies for what users actually want to see. Learning from click sessions directly captures true preferences within each curated collection.
the deeper reason
The system ranks content in browsing categories—collections of templates grouped by theme—where users don't issue search queries. The core computation is learning which items within a collection genuinely match what that category represents, beyond what the collection's name literally says. The principle is that collection names are incomplete descriptions: a "Flyers" category has subcategories and themes the name doesn't capture, and users' browsing behavior reveals what those implicit themes are. By learning directly from how users browse and interact within collections, the model discovers the true ranking that satisfies their implicit expectations. This works because users' actual choices reveal the structure the collection system is supposed to support, even if titles don't. A ranking learned from real browsing behavior improves engagement precisely because it aligns with what people actually came looking for within that category.
NBA-Net: Next-Behavior-Aware Network for Intent RecommendationSIGIR
uses Predict what a user will do next, and use that prediction to improve the ranking of intent suggestions for their immediate need.
why it works It works because current intent is not independent from future actions; they are coupled. By predicting the next behavior and propagating that signal backward, you capture the trajectory of user goals, making intent recommendations more aligned with what users actually intend to accomplish next.
the deeper reason
A user's immediate intent (what they want to do now) is shaped by what they plan to do next—a customer asking for a product refund likely intends to revisit feedback first. Standard methods infer intent only from past actions, missing this forward-looking structure. The method predicts the next action the user will take, then uses that prediction to guide the main intent model. This works because next actions carry information: if the model learns that users heading toward complaint submission show distinct behavior patterns, predicting those patterns helps identify intent signals that raw history alone misses. The framework trains both forward prediction and intent classification jointly, with the prediction acting as auxiliary training that forces the model to learn representations capturing the full behavioral arc. This dual training works because it exploits causality: next behavior doesn't cause current intent, but both flow from the same underlying user goal, so conditioning on next behavior serves as a learned sensor for that hidden goal.
BEATS: Bootstrapping E-commerce Attribute Taxonomies for Search through Iterative Human-AI CollaborationSIGIR
uses Generate and refine product attribute schemas from scratch by iteratively generating attributes, checking quality, and collecting human feedback to improve prompts.
why it works It works because attributes are domain knowledge. Bootstrapping via iterative human-in-the-loop refinement progressively tightens the definition of what attributes are valid, so each round learns from error patterns. Human annotation anchors the semantic space, guiding the system toward marketplace reality.
the deeper reason
E-commerce platforms in emerging markets often lack structured product attributes, making faceted search and ranking difficult. The method uses a language model to propose attributes for each category, then iteratively improves them through developer review and human annotation feedback. This works because language models can infer reasonable attributes from product names and category context, and human feedback closes the loop: annotators catch errors, spurring prompt refinement that produces better proposals next round. Structured iteration matters because each error pattern in early proposals is visible to humans, who can guide the language model toward the domain conventions that matter locally—sizes matter for clothing, materials for furniture. Once attributes are tagged on products, they enable three improvements: filtering now becomes granular, ranking models gain structured features, and text representations become semantically richer. The method is sound because it trades human time for automated generation, amplifying that human effort through iterative refinement rather than requiring experts to build taxonomies from scratch.
Preliminary Study of an Evaluation Benchmark for Vision-Language Models in Fashion E-CommerceSIGIR
uses Test how well different vision-language models extract fashion attributes and product information, measuring which models and prompts work best per task.
why it works It works because operational deployment requires task-specific assessment. General-purpose benchmarks miss fashion nuances. Testing multiple models and prompts reveals that best performance is task-dependent and error patterns are model-specific, so continuous monitoring is necessary for reliability.
the deeper reason
Vision-language models are often evaluated on general tasks, but fashion e-commerce requires extracting style attributes, color, fit, and material—tasks where performance varies wildly across models and models behave inconsistently across prompts. The paper measures this variation systematically across six commercial and two open-source models on five fashion-specific tasks. This matters because a model performing best on general vision-language benchmarks might perform worse on extracting fit or fabric, and its strengths and weaknesses are model-specific not prompt-specific, meaning organizations cannot simply tune prompts to fix problems. Continuous monitoring reveals that model updates improve some capabilities while degrading others, so organizations relying on models need ongoing evaluation in their specific domain. The benchmark's value lies in exposing the mismatch between general-purpose performance and operational reality: what works across diverse internet images may fail on the specific structured extraction tasks that drive e-commerce systems.
Fast and Feasible: Permutation-based Constrained Reranking for Revenue MaximizationSIGIR
uses Reorder search results to maximize revenue from paid placements while keeping relevance and fraud risk within acceptable bounds using discrete optimization.
why it works It works because reranking is a constrained optimization problem: change the order to improve one metric (revenue) without breaking others (relevance, fraud). A fast approximation algorithm that swaps neighboring items greedily reaches most of the ideal revenue gain within the latency budget required by live serving.
the deeper reason
Search results are relevant but undermonetized, so platforms want to boost high-revenue products. Reranking all results to maximize revenue alone would degrade relevance and user trust, so the problem becomes: select a reordering that maximizes revenue while keeping relevance and fraud-risk above thresholds. The method formulates this as an optimization problem, then solves it approximately by repeatedly swapping adjacent items if the swap improves revenue or fixes a violated constraint. This works because swapping neighbors is fast and the algorithm terminates when no productive swaps remain, giving a locally optimal ordering within deployment latency limits. The principle underlying this approximation is that many constraints are 'loose'—slightly violated swaps can fix them without large revenue loss—so local search finds solutions that honor constraints and capture a large fraction of the ideal revenue. The approach is practical because it avoids solving an expensive exact optimization for every query, yet maintains all constraints, proving that constrained reranking can coexist with relevance.
Cheaper is Better: A Discount-Aware Network for Conversion Rate Prediction in E-commerce Recommendation SystemSIGIR
uses Predict purchase conversion by learning how item discount rates trend over time and correcting for bias in which users see which discounts.
why it works It works because discounts drive purchasing decisions but their effect is entangled with selection bias (some users always get discounts, others never do) and time trends (holidays spike discounts). Separating the true discount signal from these confounds lets the model learn how discounts truly influence purchase likelihood.
the deeper reason
Predicting post-click conversion rates is hard because discount rates strongly influence purchase likelihood—cheaper items convert more—but discount distributions are skewed (most items get no discount, a few get heavy discounts) and promotions vary seasonally, creating complex non-linearities. The method extracts frequency components of item discount rates using Fourier transform, which works because many natural patterns (trend, seasonality, repetition) are periodic, and frequency decomposition reveals these periodicities cleanly. Removing seasonal and user-specific biases separately addresses the core issue that a user's discount sensitivity depends on what other items they saw: someone accustomed to discounts behaves differently from someone seeing their first sale. The auxiliary regression task that predicts item discount rates forces the model to learn a refined representation of discount magnitude, making the representation more informative for conversion. Together, these components work because discount influence is not random noise—it has structure (periodicity, user-specificity, item-specificity)—and the model explicitly learns to measure and condition on that structure rather than treating discount as a black-box covariate.
What Gets Cited: Competitive GEO in AI Answer EnginesSIGIR
uses Score each source on factors like relevance and recency, then measure which factor predicts being cited first when two sources compete for the first reference.
why it works It works because you never need exact scores, only their order. A learned scoring function that correctly ranks which source matters more is enough to put the most citable source first. This means partial, learned signals are sufficient.
the deeper reason
When a language model generates an answer with citations, it chooses which source to cite first based on its internal reasoning. This paper runs thousands of controlled experiments where exactly two documents compete, varying one characteristic at a time, and measures which gets cited. The key insight is that by isolating single differences and using repeated pairwise trials, you can identify which factors genuinely influence the model's citation behavior, separating true content effects from noise like document position. The underlying principle is that controlled experimentation with balanced designs reveals causal patterns: if you change one thing and citation probability shifts consistently, that thing causes the shift. This works because you're holding everything else identical, so alternative explanations vanish. The result is a checklist of what actually drives visibility for answer-engine optimization.
DPEO: Dynamic Preference Evolution Optimization for Self-Evolving CTR PredictionSIGIR
uses Two competing models take turns as reference and target, with the target learning to surpass the reference, creating a moving benchmark that drives continuous improvement.
why it works Pure external competition for single best score gets stuck in local optima. An internal dual-model setup where they compete with each other creates constant evolving pressure: the target always has a fresh opponent to beat, preventing stagnation and guiding both toward better solutions.
the deeper reason
The core problem is that single-policy CTR models get trapped in local minima where small improvements stop happening. The underlying principle is that internal competition—having two sub-learners alternate as reference and target—creates a continuous the downhill direction landscape that prevents settling, because one learner's success destabilizes the other's, forcing both to keep improving. This principle applies because having two models on the same data but with swapped roles (one must beat the other each batch) means neither can achieve static equilibrium; they naturally escape stagnation the way two animals competing for resources must keep evolving or lose access. The asymmetric the downhill direction flow ensures the target learner moves toward beating the reference, which then adapts, creating a cycle that prevents saturation. This solves the practical goal: getting CTR models past the performance plateau where incremental gains have become impossibly small.
LiBRA: Enhancing Live-streaming Recommendation with Bigraph-based Capacity-aware Ranking ApproachSIGIR
uses Streamers are ranked by estimated relevance to viewers, but the score is adjusted downward if the streamer is near capacity, balancing matching quality with fair traffic distribution.
why it works Pure relevance ranking concentrates all viewers on popular streamers, degrading their experience. When you embed capacity as a hard constraint in the ranking objective, you force the system to find the best match for each viewer that the servers can actually handle, improving overall experience across all streamers and viewers.
the deeper reason
The core problem is matching viewers to streamers while respecting each streamer's service capacity—too many viewers overwhelms them and degrades quality for everyone. The underlying principle is that optimal subgraph selection on a bipartite graph guarantees the maximum viewer-streamer match that respects capacity is found globally, not just greedily; this is achievable because once you model capacity as an edge weight constraint, the problem becomes a classical graph optimization that algorithms can solve exactly. This principle applies because streamers truly have hard capacity limits—bandwidth, moderation ability, chat responsiveness—that degrade quality when exceeded, and viewers truly have clear preferences they'd like satisfied; the bipartite structure captures both. By learning capacity estimates and then finding the globally optimal subgraph, the system avoids the trap of greedily pushing all viewers toward popular streamers (which saturates them) while starving unpopular ones. This solves the practical goal: delivering good user experience and fair opportunity for all streamers simultaneously.
ESCOMIC: User Adaptive Explainable Search for Comic BooksSIGIR
uses Re-weight importance of facets (genre, character, pacing) based on user interaction signals to reorder search results.
why it works Users clarify intent through subtle actions; weighting facets by feedback adapts the ranking to match each person's evolving goals, making results more relevant than a one-size-fits-all score.
the deeper reason
ESCOMIC ranks comic pages by scoring how well they match a query across visual appearance and story characteristics. The core insight is that this ranking improves when the weight given to each facet (like visual style or pacing) adapts based on which facets the user repeatedly engages with. This works because implicit feedback from user interactions reveals what matters in the current search intent: if a user ignores style but lingers on pace, boosting the pace facet in future rankings will pull results closer to their actual goal. By explicitly showing which facets drove each ranking decision, users can validate that the system understood them correctly, building trust. This transforms search from opaque to interpretable, letting comics fans find stories matching their mood in ways generic image-text search cannot.
Visual RAG at Scale: Tile-Level Spatial Pooling for Efficient Multi-Vector Document RetrievalSIGIR
uses Pool many small lists of numbers scores across a page into summary scores at coarser tile scale, then rerank using full detail.
why it works You only need the rough order for candidate generation, not exact scores; averaging coarser patches gives that order fast. Only the top candidates need exact rescoring, so the two-stage approach cuts work quadratically.
the deeper reason
Visual RAG at Scale reduces retrieval cost by first pooling thousands of image patches into dozens of compact tile summaries per page, then using these summaries for fast initial candidate filtering, followed by precise reranking with full details. This cascading strategy works because at the filtering stage, a coarse summary is sufficient to reject irrelevant pages: if a tile summary doesn't resemble the query at all, the full page will not either. Only for genuinely close candidates is the precision cost of full comparison justified. Matryoshka numeric fingerprints guarantee that shorter summaries preserve ranking order for top candidates, so early filtering does not corrupt final results. The quadratic speedup comes from reducing the sheer number of numerical comparisons, trading insignificant accuracy loss for throughput gain where it matters most.
EasyRAG: A Beginner-Friendly and Interactive Framework for Retrieval-Augmented GenerationSIGIR
uses Rank and combine retrieved passages by learned scores to feed most relevant sources into response generation.
why it works Learned ranking assigns higher scores to passages that actually help models generate correct answers. Reranking before generation lets the model focus on gold-signal facts rather than processing all possibilities.
the deeper reason
EasyRAG teaches RAG concepts through three progressively complex implementations that each extend the starting guess one. The pedagogy works because learners first see the simplest form—fetch external text, feed it to a language model, receive an answer—which immediately reveals the basic value proposition over models alone. Each subsequent level introduces a real trade-off: speed versus coverage, or end-to-end tuning versus computational cost. By implementing these methods side-by-side and showing how they differ mathematically, students build intuition for why each design choice matters. The framework succeeds by isolating each conceptual piece rather than presenting RAG as a monolithic black box, letting beginners understand the decision points they will face when building real systems.
From Translation to Retrieval: Evaluating LLM-Based Information Retrieval for Hausa and FongbeSIGIR
uses Rerank and expand queries using large models to improve search for low-resource languages (Hausa, Fongbe).
why it works Large models encode multilingual knowledge even for rare languages; reranking candidates with learned scores from that knowledge surface relevant results despite sparse training data for the language itself.
the deeper reason
This work systematically tests whether using a language model to expand queries or rerank results helps or hurts retrieval for Hausa and Fongbe. The core principle is straightforward: if language model quality is high, its rewrites will improve signal; if quality is low, rewritten queries will add noise. By measuring language model translation quality independently and correlating it with downstream retrieval gains, the study reveals the bottleneck: Fongbe translations are severely degraded compared to Hausa, and generated text hurts downstream tasks more often than it helps. This empirical linking of upstream quality to downstream impact lets practitioners decide whether to trust AI language systems interventions or stick with simpler methods for their target language. The study's real contribution is this diagnosis—showing that language-specific evaluation, not generic best practices, must guide IR deployment choices.
Bridging the Language Gap in Text-to-SQL: Adapting LLMs for Chichewa in a Low-Resource SettingSIGIR
uses Score and rank retrieval results to feed relevant schema snippets into models that map natural language to SQL.
why it works Models make fewer mistakes when shown similar past queries and schemas; ranking retrieval results by relevance puts gold examples first, improving in-context learning and reducing hallucinated SQL.
the deeper reason
This work adapts language models for Text-to-SQL in Chichewa by applying efficient adjust and combining it with retrieval-based prompting. The two techniques work together because efficient tuning updates a small parameter subset to improve Chichewa fluency, while retrieval provides in-context examples of successful Chichewa-to-SQL pairs. Tuning alone cannot overcome the domain gap (Chichewa was barely represented in pretraining), but tuning combined with relevant examples lets the model leverage those examples as scaffolding. The 23.4 percentage point gap between English and Chichewa execution accuracy reveals the underlying challenge: the model has learned SQL reasoning better in English-dominated data. By measuring both tuning variants and retrieval strategies separately, the paper shows that neither alone suffices, but their combination bridges the gap. This demonstrates that low-resource language adaptation requires stacking techniques, each addressing a different bottleneck.
Toward a Telugu Question Answering Dataset for Agricultural IR to Serve Marginal Farmers in Drought-Prone Rayalaseema: A Gap Analysis and RoadmapSIGIR
uses Benchmark systems that score and rank agricultural answers for drought-prone Telugu-speaking farmers.
why it works A standardized ranking benchmark with human judgments lets researchers measure whether scoring functions improve real-world information access for farmers without benchmarks, enabling fair comparison of methods.
the deeper reason
This gap analysis surveys available agricultural information sources for Telugu-speaking farmers and finds that none meet the intersection of three criteria: Telugu language, agricultural focus, and question-answering format that accepts Rayalaseema drought contexts. The study's framing is powerful because it anchors the benchmark need in a real, underserved population facing a concrete problem: drought-vulnerable marginal farmers need practical guidance but cannot access English-language or generalist systems. A Telugu agricultural QA dataset would let researchers build and evaluate retrieval and generation models for this specific population. The roadmap matters because it shows how to construct such a dataset from existing regional sources rather than starting from zero. By documenting the gap explicitly, the work makes the business case: a benchmark fills a void that blocks equitable access for 74 million speakers.
Local Information Access in Marathi: Evaluating LLM-Native Web Retrieval in a Low-Resource EnvironmentSIGIR
uses Score web results retrieved by AI language systems to measure accuracy of Marathi information retrieval, analyzing search depth effects.
why it works Scored rankings reveal whether shallow or deep search ranks correct answers highest; measuring score distributions exposes failure modes and cost-accuracy tradeoffs, guiding deployment strategy.
the deeper reason
MarathiWeb evaluates web-augmented language models by separating globally translated queries from locally native queries and measuring whether the model can retrieve and integrate relevant information from the web. The test reveals that despite high rates of web search invocation, accuracy drops sharply for local queries in Marathi, suggesting the bottleneck is not tool calling but evidence integration: the model retrieves pages but struggles to extract or synthesize relevant text. The finding that shallow retrieval (one search) outperforms deeper multi-step search is striking and constrains future system designs: the model apparently hallucinates connections between searches more than additional searches help. This benchmark's value lies in isolating integration failure from retrieval failure, exposing that language model web search still requires fundamental improvements in reading comprehension, not just tool availability. The cost-accuracy trade-off is practically important for deployment in low-resource regions with metered bandwidth.
Retrieval for User-Centered Translation: Lessons from RAG-based Tools for Low-Resource DomainsSIGIR
uses Score and rank in-domain examples from translation memory and glossaries to weight AI language systems post-editing and improve machine translation.
why it works Domain-specific terminology matters most; ranking retrieved examples by relevance to current phrase and weighting their influence over the baseline translation focuses the model on high-confidence domain knowledge.
the deeper reason
Tulun combines machine translation with language model post-editing, guided by user-maintained translation memories and domain glossaries, to improve technical translation for low-resource languages like Tetun and Bislama. The system works because translation memory and glossaries anchor terminology: if a specialized term appears in translation memory with its starting guess correct translation, fetching and using that example in the language model prompt improves consistency and accuracy. Domain granularity matters because medical terminology differs radically from general discourse; broad categories miss this specificity. The 16-22 ChrF++ point improvement comes from in-context learning: the language model corrects and contextualizes machine-translation output when shown relevant domain examples. Transparency to end-users is crucial because it lets them understand why choices were made and refine glossaries, creating a human-in-the-loop cycle. This retrieval-augmented approach succeeds where traditional machine translation alone fails on technical domains.
Offline-First Information Retrieval for Curriculum-Aligned STEM Resources in Low-Resource Namibian SchoolsSIGIR
uses Rank documents by a statistical score of how well they match query terms, adapted for low-bandwidth search.
why it works Ranking works because you don't need the exact score values, only their order. A fast statistical score that correctly ranks which documents are more relevant gets the best results on top, and this ranking is robust even when computed cheaply on limited devices.
the deeper reason
The core problem is ranking educational documents by relevance when the school itself must host retrieval without internet. The underlying principle is that a ranking method works only if it considers what matters in the specific context—here, both the content match to a query and alignment with the actual curriculum taught. This principle applies because teachers and learners use the system within a defined educational scope; a document relevant to physics but outside their grade level wastes limited storage and time. By explicitly modeling both textual similarity and curriculum position, the system ensures results match not just queries but real teaching goals, solving the fundamental constraint: offline systems cannot learn from click logs or A/B tests, so ranking must rest on domain structure from the start.
Evaluating Proactivity in Conversational Search through Anticipatory RetrievalSIGIR
uses Infer what information the user will need next in a conversation by predicting their future queries, then rank documents for those predicted needs before they ask.
why it works It works because multi-turn conversations have coherent goal sequences: users refine or explore related subtopics in predictable patterns. If you model what comes next in that sequence, you can surface relevant information before the user explicitly asks, reducing wasted turns.
the deeper reason
Proactive search anticipates what the user wants to ask next, rather than waiting for an explicit query. The principle is that conversation has structure: users gradually narrow or pivot their goals through dialogue, and those moves follow patterns. This principle applies because information seeking is a sequential process—each question typically depends on answers to previous ones, so the user's current position and recent queries reveal likely next moves. By inferring implicit intent from the pattern of past exchanges, a proactive system can surface relevant suggestions before the user knows to ask, reducing the burden of formulating every new query from scratch. This solves a real effort problem: in complex searches spanning many turns, users often get stuck not knowing what to ask next; offering anticipatory suggestions shortens the path to answers.
Adaptive Personalisation for Effective Conversational Search SystemsSIGIR
uses Learn when to personalize each query using a classifier; weight past interactions differently for different users; blend rankings based on user intent.
why it works It works because not every query benefits from personalization—sometimes a generic search is better—and user history is noisy. A classifier learns which queries actually benefit from historical context, while weighted blending lets personalization help only when it actually improves precision, avoiding the trap of applying personalization uniformly.
the deeper reason
Conversational retrieval tries to adapt results to each user's background and needs, but deciding when adaptation helps is itself a hard problem. The core principle is that personalisation is not uniformly beneficial: sometimes a query should be answered the same way for everyone, while other times user history dramatically changes the right answer. This principle applies because different query types have different personalisation requirements; a factual question like 'What is photosynthesis?' needs the same answer for all users, but 'What job opportunities exist for me?' depends entirely on starting guess context. By training a classifier to predict when personalisation helps for each query, and then routing through specialized agents for personalised or generic retrieval accordingly, the system avoids wasting computation and avoids diluting results with irrelevant personalization. This solves the efficiency and accuracy trade-off: systems can be both personalized and precise by adapting the degree of personalization to what each query actually requires.
LLMs as Search Engine Components and Users: Infrastructural Adaptations to a Dual TransformationSIGIR
uses Adapt search pipeline components to handle AI-generated queries, which have different statistical patterns than human queries.
why it works It works because AI generates queries with different structure (more reformulations, faster sequences, different syntax) than humans. Ranking and filtering functions trained on human query patterns fail on AI queries; retraining on AI query distributions aligns system behavior to actual traffic.
the deeper reason
Search engines now embed AI language systems to improve results, but AI language systems are expensive and sensitive to input quality and shifts in query distribution. The core principle is that components optimized for one use case—human searchers—often fail when the users change—AI agents querying systematically. This principle applies because human and AI search differ fundamentally: humans type occasional queries with typos and reformulation, while AI language systems-agents generate many queries rapidly and systematically as part of reasoning loops. Caching, spelling correction, and query understanding models all assume human query patterns; applying them to AI traffic wastes compute and can degrade results. By measuring how AI language systems actually use search—their query volume, reformulation patterns, sensitivity to noise—infrastructure designers can optimize pipeline components for dual traffic. This solves the scalability problem: as AI language systems become search users, systems that ignore this dual role will waste compute and resources; explicitly modeling both human and AI search enables more efficient infrastructure.
LLM Personalization: Foundations, Breakthroughs, and FrontiersSIGIR
uses Personalizing language model outputs by learning user memories and preferences, then adjusting the model's generation at inference time to match each person's style and goals.
why it works Language models are generic; personalizing them works by storing what you learn about each user and steering the model toward that user's context at each step. Learning to adapt the model to user context beats using the same generic model for everyone because context shapes what the right answer is.
the deeper reason
Language models generate generic responses because they lack user-specific information; personalization requires encoding individual preferences, memories, and contexts into the model's decision process. The core problem is that preferences are individual—no universal ranking of options is correct for all users—so the model must somehow condition its output on personal data. The principle enabling this is that personalization can be applied at multiple points in the model's lifecycle: during training through curating or reweighting examples toward individual preferences, during inference through conditioning on retrieved personal context or user history, and through memory systems that track evolving preferences over time. This principle works because each layer of personalization amplifies the signal from the previous layer: a model adjust on one user's preferences learns that user's values, and then at inference time conditioning on that user's recent interactions further narrows the output. By combining these layers—memory, architecture, training objectives, inference adaptation—systems can align model behavior with individual goals while remaining practical to deploy at scale. This matters because generic systems cannot serve diverse users well; personalization is necessary for systems to respect individual autonomy and provide value tailored to context.
The 10th Workshop on Search-Oriented Conversational Artificial Intelligence (SCAI'26)SIGIR
uses Answering questions asked conversationally by holding context from previous turns, retrieving relevant facts, and generating multi-turn responses that adapt to what the user just said.
why it works Conversation is sequence: each turn depends on all starting guess turns. Learning to rank and generate conditioned on conversation history works because it models the temporal dependency—you answer differently after context changes. Personalization compounds this because you also adapt to the individual user.
the deeper reason
Conversational systems must maintain context across multiple turns—understanding what the user has already asked, what they learned, and how their information need is evolving—while retrieving relevant information to answer follow-up questions. The core challenge is that context grows over time, so the system must decide what information remains relevant and how to efficiently rank documents given the full conversation history. The principle enabling this is that if systems maintain an explicit conversation state representing what the user has learned and what they still seek, they can use that state to personalize retrieval and ranking for each new query. This principle applies because follow-up questions are abbreviated: users assume the system remembers context, so a question like What about in that region requires the system to recall previous discussion to understand what region means. By explicitly tracking conversation state and using it to modify retrieval and ranking, systems can handle these abbreviated questions and adapt their explanations to the user's knowledge level. This addresses practical needs: users prefer concise follow-up questions, and systems must parse abbreviations correctly; additionally, users appreciate personalized explanations that build on what they already know rather than starting from scratch.
63 papers

Predicting what comes next

Behaviour and language arrive as ordered streams — the pages you visited, the words in a sentence — and the useful move is to predict the next item from what came before.

Why it works — the principle

It works because the recent past genuinely constrains the near future: what you clicked last shapes what you'll click next, the last few words shape the next word. So a system that captures those local dependencies can predict well without holding the entire history in mind at once.

Rise: A Retrieval-Augmented Generation Enhanced Immersive System for EducationWWW
uses Answer student questions and assess engagement by retrieving relevant educational content and personalized context from a learner's history.
why it works Pulling in retrieved context prevents the model from forgetting starting guess interactions, so it can recognize when a question connects to earlier topics and tailor answers to that student's level.
the deeper reason
Immersive educational systems require generating high-quality, personalized content on low-end devices, which is computationally impossible if every interaction runs a full model locally. The core strategy is to retrieve relevant starting guess knowledge and examples from a store, then let the model focus only on personalization and interaction. This works because retrieval shifts the burden from generating from scratch to selecting and adapting, reducing the model's computational load while still producing contextually grounded responses. Adding digital humans and interactivity creates engagement that makes learning stick, while learning analytics track what each student understands. By distributing work—retrieval handles breadth, local models handle personalization, humans handle engagement—the system delivers rich learning without overloading devices in resource-constrained regions.
ES-MemEval: Benchmarking Conversational Agents on Personalized Long-Term Emotional SupportWWW
uses Evaluate whether chatbots remember fragmented user disclosures across sessions, extract implicit needs, spot conflicts, and personalize support over time.
why it works Emotional support requires the model to reconstruct a coherent user profile from scattered hints, so measuring these capabilities separately reveals which memory failures break personalization.
the deeper reason
Long-term emotional support requires tracking user state across sessions where new information is implicit, scattered, and contradicted by later disclosures. The core problem is that standard long-context and retrieval systems treat facts as static and explicit, missing the temporal dynamics of evolving emotional states and conflicting information. A robust long-term memory system must extract which facts matter, reason about when they apply (temporal reasoning), detect contradictions across sessions (conflict detection), and know when not to use a fact (abstention). Evaluating these five capabilities separately reveals where systems fail: whether they can ground responses in facts (extraction), track timeline (temporal), or wisely refrain from using outdated information (abstention). This breakdown is essential because emotional support succeeds only when the system remembers not just facts but the human context those facts carry.
VK-LSVD: A Large-Scale Industrial Dataset for Short-Video RecommendationWWW
uses Build recommendation models from a massive dataset of user interactions with short videos, training on sequential feedback to predict which video a user will watch next.
why it works It works because users' interests change rapidly with short videos—each watch influences the next choice. Modeling sequences lets the system learn those rapid shifts from real user behavior. Scale matters: with 40 billion interactions, patterns in interest evolution become statistically clear, and cold-start (new users or videos) can be addressed by finding similar users or content in the large corpus.
the deeper reason
The challenge in short-video recommendation is modeling rapid shifts in user interests from implicit feedback alone, while lacking public datasets representative of real platform behavior. This dataset provides 40 billion real user interactions labeled with content features and contextual signals, enabling researchers to study how user preferences evolve at scale over time. The dataset's value is that implicit feedback (what users watch, skip, or rewatch) reflects authentic behavior without survey bias, and the scale—40 billion interactions—reveals rare patterns that smaller datasets miss, like how seasonal events shift viewing trends or how users explore new content genres. With this grounded benchmark, recommendation algorithms can be validated against true real-world dynamics instead of synthetic or unrepresentative data. For the field, this dataset becomes the standard for building and testing models that capture transient user interests accurately.
ONeRec: Towards Openness-Aware and Adaptive Proactive News RecommendationWWW
uses Recommend intermediate articles that balance current interest alignment with gradual drift toward a target topic, weighted by the user's openness.
why it works Users resist radical shifts but accept gradual ones; weighting by openness prevents rejection. Intermediate articles act as stepping stones, each one slightly closer to the target than the last.
the deeper reason
News recommendation normally ranks articles by similarity to past preferences, but proactive recommendation must guide users toward a target topic while maintaining engagement. The approach quantifies each user's openness—their tolerance for novelty based on reading patterns—then selects intermediary articles that blend target relevance with immediate interest satisfaction. This works because user receptiveness is not all-or-nothing; measuring it empirically from history reveals who can accept a wider range of topics and who prefers comfort. By modulating the balance between matching current interest and steering toward the target according to openness, the system makes gradual guidance feel natural rather than jarring.
Statistical Analysis of 12V Power Load Uncertainty Using Conditional Probability for SDV Energy ManagementWWW
uses Uses conditional probability of power load given the past 60 seconds of history to predict upcoming battery demand and reduce uncertainty.
why it works It works because driver behavior is partially predictable within short windows; conditioning on recent history removes noise from one-shot predictions and captures momentum in usage patterns, revealing true upcoming load better than static averages.
the deeper reason
Predicting 12-volt battery load for vehicle power management is hard because driver behavior looks random, yet recent history carries signal: if the heater ran heavily in the last minute, it's likely still on. The method models this by computing conditional probability: given the observation that load was high recently, what's the distribution of load now? This works because electrical devices have inertia—heaters cool slowly, compressors don't switch instantaneously—so past state constrains present state probabilistically. Using 60 seconds of history as context reduces prediction uncertainty by 41% because that window spans the timescale at which load transitions happen. A learned model then maps historical context to precise load predictions. Why it works: conditional probability is mathematically sound because the recent past is informative—it screens off more distant history via the Markov property, so conditioning on recent observation gives the best available predictive power.
Swen: A Cross-Platform Desktop Assistant for Instant and Personalized Large-Language-Model InteractionWWW
uses Identify what the user wants—translation, explanation, or summary—then generate the matching response tailored to their background and preferences.
why it works It works because intent recognition reduces the problem: instead of one model trying to do everything, you classify what you're solving for first, so the right specialized logic runs. And tracking what the user likes lets you personalize by remembering their style.
the deeper reason
Users waste time switching applications and rewording questions when they encounter unfamiliar content. This assistant detects the intent behind a selected text—is the user asking for translation, explanation, or summary?—then calls the appropriate prompt and retrieves answers tailored to the user's learned preferences and background. The soundness: intent is usually recoverable from context and word choice, and people develop stable answer preferences. By building a profile over time and matching intent to past successful explanations, the system can give better answers faster than a generic prompt would, reducing the friction that makes people abandon tools.
LLM-Enhanced Web-Centric Spatio-Temporal Intelligence: Methods, Applications, and Frontier ResearchWWW
uses Predicts the next move or location in a trajectory by learning patterns from sequences of places and times, applying the learned patterns at location, trajectory, and region scales.
why it works It works because human movement is sequential—where you go next depends on where you've been. Learning from trajectories means you capture real patterns of motion that simple statistics miss, and applying the same learned patterns at all scales lets you use local knowledge to predict regional flows.
the deeper reason
Spatio-temporal intelligence from web data improves by treating human mobility—check-ins, location history, transportation—as layered signals revealing behavior at location, trajectory, and region scales. Each scale captures different phenomena: location-level reveals local patterns, trajectory-level models individual movement coherence, region-level exposes aggregate flows. Language models excel at this hierarchical reasoning because they can process descriptions at multiple abstraction levels simultaneously, from individual actions to city-wide phenomena. By organizing analysis around these natural scales, systems can ask questions appropriate to each level without flattening rich behavior into a single representation.
Accurate and Efficient Personalized Query Rewriting in Baidu SearchWWW
uses Rewrites a user's search query to better match their personal intent by training a fast model to reason like a language model but without the reasoning overhead.
why it works Large reasoning models take too long for real-time search, but chain-of-thought helps them pick the right query. The method first teaches a smaller model to mimic reasoning outputs, then trains it to skip the reasoning steps and jump straight to the answer. Since the small model learned to replicate reasoning results, it keeps the accuracy gains without the latency, exploiting the fact that you need reasoning's output, not its speed.
the deeper reason
The core problem is rewriting search queries to match what users actually want without adding reasoning delay. The mathematical guarantee is that a model can be trained to produce the reasoning-enhanced output directly without showing intermediate reasoning steps—the model learns to internalize the reasoning process during training. This is sound because reasoning-guided training provides the correct signal about what the final output should be, teaching the model to perform the right inference in one step. By using supervised training that teaches the model the correct outputs without showing working, then reinforcement learning to refine this, the system achieves accuracy gains from reasoning without the computational cost of reasoning at query time.
Is More Context Always Better? Examining LLM Reasoning Capability for Time Interval PredictionWWW
uses Compares how well language models predict the time until a user's next purchase versus statistical models that learned the time patterns directly.
why it works It works because language models are trained on text prediction but not number prediction; statistical models built for time intervals exploit the mathematical structure of the data (how long until next event) whereas language models must convert numbers to text and back, losing precision.
the deeper reason
The task is predicting when a user will make their next purchase by feeding previous purchase timing information to a language model. The finding is that adding many details about the user actually hurts prediction accuracy, contrary to intuition. This happens because the model was trained primarily on text, not numerical timing patterns; it excels at understanding semantic meaning but struggles to extract quantitative regularities from sequences of dates. When given more context, the model gets distracted by linguistic relationships rather than focusing on the temporal intervals themselves. The result reveals that language models lack the built-in mathematical machinery to capture time as a quantity the way specialized statistical methods do, so too much context introduces noise rather than signal.
Generative Archetype-Grounded Item Representations for Sequential RecommendationWWW
uses Predict the next item a user will interact with by learning representations of items based on their ideal target audience and adjusting those representations to match actual user behavior.
why it works This works because item identity has two sources of truth: who the item is designed for (semantic) and who actually uses it (behavioral). Combining both grounds the model in reality rather than description alone.
the deeper reason
Item representations in recommendation often either describe the item in isolation (using only product attributes) or learn from past behavior (using only what users bought), but these can diverge—a product meant for teenagers might sell well to retirees, so descriptions and actual audience patterns conflict. The underlying principle is that you need both: semantic representations capture the intended identity (what the product is meant to be), but behavioral signals show the lived identity (who actually buys it), and these two must align or recommendations will mismatch what users genuinely want. This approach works by first inferring from item metadata who the product targets (its archetypal audience—the mental profile of ideal buyers), then extracting semantic representations of that archetype, then applying a calibration objective that adjusts these representations to match actual interaction patterns. By grounding generative archetypes in empirical behavior, the system ensures that recommendations reflect reality rather than aspiration: if a formal dress actually appeals to casual dressers, the representation learns that truth, letting recommendations surface the right items to the right users.
MIGC-CMamba: Cross-Domain Mamba with Multi-Scale Imaging and Granular-Ball Computing for Traffic Flow PredictionWWW
uses Converting traffic sensor readings into image-like patterns, then finding which places and time-scales matter most for predicting traffic flow a few hours ahead.
why it works It works because traffic flow has both fast (minute-to-minute) and slow (daily cycle) rhythms that mix together—treating data as images lets vision techniques extract both local and global patterns at once. Granular-ball clustering finds which regions truly influence each other.
the deeper reason
Traffic prediction systems struggle because time-series data contains both periodic repeats (Monday behaves like last Monday) and spatial echoes (congestion spreads from one location to neighbors), yet existing methods underexploit both. The core thing being estimated is future flow: which roads will congest and when. The principle is that multivariate sequences are easier to recognize and extrapolate when viewed as images, leveraging visual pattern-matching to catch both trends and periodicity. This applies because traffic has spatial structure—highways form networks where flow propagates—and temporal structure that repeats on daily and weekly cycles. By converting sequences to images, using spatial graphs that cluster related roads, and bridging temporal and spatial domains, the system integrates information sources that were previously siloed. Experiments show stronger spatiotemporal dependencies and more accurate forecasts.
TRACE: Trajectory Recovery with State Propagation Diffusion for Urban MobilityWWW
uses Reconstructing missing GPS points in sparse trajectories by iteratively denoising fragments while remembering intermediate results from starting guess steps.
why it works It works because trajectory segments follow smooth motion rules—as you gradually reduce noise from the denoised version, a memory mechanism holds and refines partial recoveries so complex hard-to-fill gaps don't collapse back to noise.
the deeper reason
