By building a single ontology that defines PFAS hierarchically and links to authoritative identifiers from the EPA, researchers can map their data to standardized entity references. When a dataset says 'DTXSID 1234', every other system immediately knows what chemical is meant, enabling queries and integration across sources that would otherwise be impossible to reconcile.
Pattern Discovery with Wide-Lens Analysis and Sharp-Focus ValidationWWW
uses Zooms out to find clusters of similar patterns in unstructured data, then zooms in to verify which patterns are real and build consistent categories.
why it works It works because pattern discovery has two parts: finding candidates (wide view) and confirming they are consistent (close inspection). Cycling between these discovers what actually recurs in data without needing ground truth labels. Rough candidates guide where to look closely; detailed validation confirms which candidates truly repeat.
the deeper reason
Discovering patterns in unfamiliar data without labels is hard because rough patterns look plausible but may not be extractable or real. Pattern Insights Explorer alternates between wide-lens views (where do similar examples cluster?) and sharp-focus views (can we precisely extract that pattern consistently?). This works because width reveals where signal concentrates, but signal needs precision to be actionable; iterating between these perspectives ensures that discovered patterns are both frequent and actually measurable.
Class-Domain Incremental Learning on Graphs via Disentangled Knowledge DistillationWWW
uses Split node features into task-specific patterns and task-agnostic background noise, then teach new classes while protecting old knowledge.
why it works Separating signal from noise lets the model learn what truly changes between tasks versus what is stable; distilling old knowledge preserves learned patterns, preventing the model from erasing starting guess insights when new classes arrive.
the deeper reason
The core challenge is learning from graphs that evolve over time, where new node types appear and visual styles shift, forcing a model to simultaneously learn new classes and forget old ones without collapsing its earlier knowledge. The method disentangles node representations into two separate channels: semantic factors that carry the class-identity signal, and style factors that capture the surface appearance variations caused by changing feature styles or edges. This separation works because it isolates what must transfer across time (the decision boundary for classification) from what changes (cosmetic visual patterns). By freezing one channel while updating another, and by replaying remembered examples from early tasks, the model can absorb new information without overwriting previous patterns. This structured forgetting—keeping semantics stable while letting style adjust—is mathematically sounder than monolithic retraining because it explicitly names and controls where catastrophic interference occurs.
Hierarchical Prompt Contrastive Learning for Weakly Supervised Histopathology SegmentationWWW
uses Learn to segment tissue regions by comparing image features to text descriptions and category prompts at multiple levels.
why it works Text prompts ground visual features to semantic meaning; comparing multi-layer features to those prompts forces the model to align images with concepts it understands, and hierarchy lets it learn both fine detail and broad category at once.
the deeper reason
Segmenting histopathology images using only image-level labels (not pixel-level truth) is hard because classes appear similar (inter-class homogeneity) and images of the same class look different (intra-class variation). The method constructs text descriptions for each category at multiple levels of specificity and trains the model to align visual features from different layers of the image encoder to these text descriptions. This works because text prompts create a stable, semantic anchor outside the visual domain—words like 'benign tissue' carry consistent meaning regardless of staining variation. By hierarchically organizing these prompts (whole-class prompts and sub-class prompts), the model learns to separate what is truly diagnostic from what is mere visual noise. The contrastive alignment principle ensures that visual and textual representations of the same concept pull together while mismatches repel, gradually sharpening the boundary between classes despite sparse labels.
RaDAR: Relation-aware Diffusion-Asymmetric Graph Contrastive Learning for RecommendationWWW
uses Generate diverse views of user-item interaction graphs using both generative models and learned edge refinement, then train by comparing views.
why it works Random perturbations destroy critical signals; generating views smartly with both global structure and relation-aware edge weights preserves semantic meaning, so comparing them teaches robust user-item relationships even under sparse data.
the deeper reason
Recommendation systems using graph systems that learn from examples suffer when random edge perturbations are used to generate training views, because removing real edges can destroy important signals (what users actually bought together), undermining the contrastive learning objective. The method proposes two complementary strategies: a generative model to construct new plausible graph structure capturing global patterns, and a denoising model to refine existing edges by suppressing likely false positives. This works because generative views preserve semantic structure while being statistically different from the original, and denoising removes noise rather than erasing signal. By using asymmetric contrastive learning—where negative samples are globally informed rather than purely local—and diffusion-guided refinement (progressive noise injection and recovery), the system learns robust representations even when data is sparse and noisy. The principle is that augmentations should modify the graph in semantically meaningful ways, not arbitrarily, so that the learned patterns reflect real collaborative patterns rather than artifacts of random corruption.
Adaptive Contrastive Learning in Sequential Recommendation based on Perturbation and Restoration NetworksWWW
uses Learn to adapt how you perturb and restore user sequences for comparison so augmentation preserves user intent.
why it works Hard-coded perturbations destroy the sequences users actually care about; learning what noise preserves meaning ensures augmented views still capture real preference patterns, so contrastive learning finds stable user interest structure.
the deeper reason
Sequential recommendation learns user preferences from the order of past interactions, but standard data augmentation techniques like random dropout or noise injection can obscure user intent by destroying meaningful patterns. The method proposes learnable perturbation and restoration networks that adaptively corrupt and repair user sequences in a semantically consistent manner. This works because it bypasses the assumption that all corruption strategies are equally valid; instead, the model learns what kinds of sequence changes preserve user intent and what changes constitute true augmentation. The contrastive learning objective then teaches the model that two semantically similar sequences should produce similar preference predictions while dissimilar sequences diverge. By automating augmentation selection, the approach ensures that positive examples in the contrastive pair are actually related to the same user intent, not just similar by accident. This adaptive principle is sounder than fixed augmentation because it lets the model discover which distortions reveal robust patterns versus which destroy real signal.
PAGE: Progressive Anomaly Generation Network for Semi-supervised Graph Anomaly DetectionWWW
uses Generate artificial anomalies by step-wise corruption of node attributes and connections, then train to separate real anomalies from progressively degraded normal nodes.
why it works Works because anomalies of different severity levels exist in the real world, so training on a spectrum from mild to extreme makes the model recognize subtle deviations that a single-step method would miss. The progressive constraint forces learned scores to rank corruption levels properly.
the deeper reason
PAGE generates increasingly severe fake anomalies by first adding noise to node features, then progressively disrupting graph connections. The core insight is that real anomalies live on a spectrum from mild to extreme, so by forcing the model to learn a ranked ordering where severe fake anomalies score higher than mild ones, it calibrates what each anomaly level actually looks like in the data. This ordering constraint ensures the model doesn't collapse all anomalies into a single decision boundary; instead, it learns to separate them by degree. Because real anomalies are rare and unlabeled, staging the fake ones from weak to strong gives the model a natural ladder to climb, teaching it to recognize subtle deviations before it sees the drastic ones. This framework lets practitioners detect the full range of graph misbehavior, not just the obvious cases.
MMTableBench: A Multi-level Multimodal Benchmark for Reasoning and Layout Complexity in Table QAWWW
uses Test whether question answerers understand both the visual layout of tables and the logical steps needed to answer questions about them.
why it works By varying layout complexity and reasoning steps independently across benchmarks, you can measure which skills the model actually has versus which ones hide because the task was too easy or too hard on both features at once.
the deeper reason
Table question answering requires interpreting both the spatial layout of cells and the reasoning needed to connect rows and columns into an answer. The benchmark works by measuring each capability separately—layout complexity and reasoning complexity as orthogonal axes. This is sound because decomposing the task reveals which models struggle with what: a model weak on complex layouts but strong on reasoning requires different fixes than vice versa. Separating these factors lets you trace capability gaps to their source, which is necessary for building models that truly understand tables rather than exploiting spurious correlations.
STIndex: A Context-Aware Multi-Dimensional Spatiotemporal Information Extraction SystemWWW
uses Extract and organize information from news and documents by grounding it to specific times and places, with language models filling in the structure.
why it works Space and time are universal anchors; anchoring all extracted facts to where and when they occurred aligns information that would otherwise be scattered, making downstream tasks like search and reasoning far more reliable.
the deeper reason
Extracting structured knowledge from text is hard because entities belong to places and times—coordinates that ground meaning. The system uses space and time as universal organizing principles: all information naturally has a location and timestamp, unlike domain-specific ontologies. This is mathematically sound because spatiotemporal indices partition data into cells where similar entities cluster, reducing the search space for reasoning and retrieval. By anchoring extraction to geography and chronology, you get free structure that improves both accuracy and generalization, since these coordinates apply the same way across any domain.
SHIELD: A Framework for Online Conversational AI System for Self-Regulated Learning at Emergency Communications CentersWSDM
uses Train an AI to simulate emergency calls by comparing trainee responses against right and wrong actions, then flag when they drift from good practice.
why it works It works because learning by contrast—seeing what trainees did versus what experts would do—tells the AI which moves matter for good performance. Real-time nudges exploit this difference signal to steer learning.
the deeper reason
SHIELD trains emergency responders using simulated 911 calls with real-time feedback and reflection prompts. The method works because self-regulated learning splits learning into planning (setting goals), execution (making decisions), and reflection (analyzing what went wrong). By logging every choice, timing, and correction a trainee makes, then feeding back observations about their own behavior alongside AI-generated scenarios, learners build accurate mental models of their own thinking—not just of correct procedures. This reflective loop ensures trainees don't memorize scripts but develop adaptive judgment for scenarios they've never seen.
Understanding and Modeling Heterogeneous Search BehaviorSIGIR
uses Extract hidden search features from how different demographic groups formulate queries and interact, then use those features to explain and predict query behavior.
why it works It works because demographic differences in search are not random; they reflect underlying strategies and preferences. By finding the hidden features that separate behavior, you capture the true drivers rather than confusing correlation with cause, enabling fair comparison across groups.
the deeper reason
The method identifies why people search differently by measuring how demographics and tasks correlate with observable query and interaction patterns, then extracting interpretable hidden features that explain these variations as strategy differences. The principle is that stable behavioral differences reflect underlying variation in how people approach searching — not just random noise or engagement swings. By revealing these hidden features, the work enables fair evaluation systems that account for heterogeneous user behavior, solving the fairness problem that benchmarks often assume all searchers are alike.
An Eye Tracking Study: Are AI Overviews Changing Search Behavior?SIGIR
uses Track where people's eyes look on search result pages when generative summaries appear above traditional blue links, measuring engagement to understand changing focus.
why it works It works because eye tracking directly reveals where focus flows. Comparing gaze distribution when generative content is present versus absent isolates its causal effect on search behavior, avoiding self-report bias.
the deeper reason
This is an empirical eye-tracking study examining how users interact with search results when generative summaries appear above traditional links. The study measures focus and engagement with different result types, but does not propose a technical algorithm or mathematical principle.
One-for-All Community Search on Unseen GraphsSIGIR
uses Learn a single graph representation model on source graphs that generalizes to unseen target graphs by aligning features across domains and using diffusion-based refinement.
why it works It works because you train on multiple source graphs to see many graph styles, then the alignment step learns to translate between any graph's features. The diffusion refinement smooths out distribution shifts, so the function learned from training generalizes even when it encounters new graph structures.
the deeper reason
Community search methods trained on one graph often fail on new graphs they haven't seen before, because different graphs have different structural patterns and distributions. The core challenge is learning representations that transfer across graph domains. The method works by explicitly aligning features across domains to account for structural differences, using spectral properties (mathematical properties describing graph shape) as an anchor. It then builds a hybrid representation combining both local neighborhoods and global graph structure, which makes the model robust to distribution shifts. By training once on source graphs and deploying directly to unseen targets without retraining, the method trades specificity for robustness. The key insight is that structural alignment plus distributional smoothing lets graph-learning models generalize like pretrained models do in vision or language, solving the practical problem of deploying one trained model to many graphs.
SNBot: Modeling Self-Neighborhood Representation Discrepancy for Social Bot DetectionSIGIR
uses Detect social bots by learning to distinguish between a node's core identity and what its neighborhood looks like, rather than assuming they should match.
why it works It works because real users and bots differ in how their declared attributes relate to their social surroundings. By explicitly modeling this gap rather than smoothing it away, you preserve the discriminative signal: genuine accounts have neighborhoods that reflect them, while bots exhibit systematic misalignment.
the deeper reason
Detecting social bots using graph methods fails when neighborhood consistency breaks down—bots may copy user attributes while showing different behaviors, or real users in sparse networks don't resemble their neighbors. The core insight is that discrepancy itself is informative: bots often exhibit inconsistency between stated attributes and actual behavior, while normal users tend to be more coherent. The method works by explicitly modeling and preserving the gap between self-representation (what the user claims or shows) and neighborhood patterns (what their network does). By capturing both incoming and outgoing interactions separately, it preserves asymmetric behavior patterns that bots often exhibit. Rather than smoothing away the self-neighborhood gap, this method treats it as a primary signal. This directly identifies bots not by finding noisy neighborhoods but by detecting fundamental inconsistency between persona and behavior.
NERBench-Chhattisgarh: A Multi-Family NER Dataset for Low-Resource Indic LanguagesSIGIR
uses Train multilingual models to recognize named entities in seven under-resourced tribal languages by learning shared features across related languages.
why it works It works because languages that share structure or script also share patterns in how entities are named, and by training on related languages together, the model learns features that transfer even when training data for any single language is tiny.
the deeper reason
NER on low-resource tribal languages requires recognizing that morphological complexity (agglutination) breaks transfer learning patterns observed in well-studied languages, which is a fundamental linguistic fact: when source and target languages differ radically in how they build words, pivot adaptation paradoxically fails because it aligns on surface script similarity while morphological structure diverges. The dataset's nature-centric entity ontology works because entity boundaries and types are culturally grounded: species, weather, and agriculture entities that matter in Central India simply don't appear in standard benchmarks, so models trained elsewhere will miss them entirely. The multilingual encoder adaptation strategies test this by empirically demonstrating that script alignment helps Indo-Aryan language transfer but hurts Dravidian languages, proving that no single statistical approach suits all language families.
DeepResearch-9K: A Challenging Benchmark Dataset of Deep-Research AgentSIGIR
uses Learns to find answers by practicing on chains of reasoning, starting with weak examples then improving through reward signals.
why it works It works because good answers build on good intermediate steps; practicing on real reasoning paths teaches the system which intermediate steps actually lead to correct answers.
the deeper reason
Deep-research agents must navigate the web through multiple hops, each step depending on reasoning from the previous one; training them requires examples that show this stepwise thinking, not just final answers. The underlying principle is that an agent learns reasoning by imitating reasoning trajectories—if you show only 'question goes to answer,' the agent cannot learn how to decompose problems or backtrack when stuck. By collecting 9000 multi-hop questions with step-by-step reasoning chains from a strong agent, then training new agents to follow similar patterns under reinforcement learning, they create a self-improving flywheel. The verifiable answers ground each step, allowing the system to learn which reasoning paths actually lead to correct conclusions. This dataset lets practitioners train agents that think transparently and recover from errors rather than gambling on single searches.
IIRSim Studio: A Dashboard for User SimulationSIGIR
uses Builds a visual workshop where users design and run experiments simulating how people search, then share and reproduce their setup.
why it works It works because reproducibility requires capturing every choice; when all setup choices are explicit and versioned, the same experiment always gives the same outcome, enabling trust and reuse.
the deeper reason
User simulation for information retrieval experimentation is powerful but adoption is hindered when it requires substantial coding setup; researchers need to compose experiments visually while maintaining reproducibility. The underlying principle is that simulation value depends on usability—a theoretically perfect simulator that requires days of engineering setup will not be used. By providing a web-based visual workbench for building simulation pipelines, version control for custom components, and explicit provenance tracking through experiment bundles, the work lowers the barrier without sacrificing rigor. Researchers can now experiment with different simulated user behaviors and see how they rank systems, then share their exact pipeline for others to verify. This accessibility-plus-rigor combination accelerates research by reducing friction in a bottleneck that was never the simulation math itself.
Mine over Yours: How Authorship Biases Evaluation in Generative Information RetrievalSIGIR
uses Ask participants to rate information they created themselves versus identical information framed as someone else's creation.
why it works When you create something, you understand the effort and reasoning behind it, making it feel more credible and higher quality. This bias toward self-created work is cognitive—your own reasoning feels trustworthy even when the output is the same, because you know it came from your intent.
the deeper reason
Users tend to rate their own creations more favorably than identical outputs from others, a classic self-generated content bias. This phenomenon occurs because users invest effort in creating their own answers, and sunk effort biases quality judgment upward even when outputs are objectively equivalent. The bias appears in quality ratings but not trust—skepticism about hallucinations constrains how much confidence a user places even in their own results. Understanding this split is important because it means users select for their own content even while doubting it, so system designers cannot rely on trust alone to guide content selection decisions.
uses Test two agent personas—one that mirrors user preferences back and one that offers social guidance—and measure their effect on shopping engagement.
why it works Interaction style shapes how users think. A mirroring agent helps users clarify their own preferences by reflecting them back; a peer agent creates social trust that relaxes scrutiny. Different conversation frames activate different cognitive modes, showing that how the system talks changes how users reason.
the deeper reason
Shopping behavior depends on interaction style: when an agent mirrors the user's own thinking process, it prompts deeper reflection and critical evaluation of products; when an agent acts as a knowledgeable peer, it builds social comfort but reduces explicit comparison behavior. These effects appear because different interaction styles activate different cognitive and social processing modes in users. A mirroring style works by prompting the user to articulate preferences themselves, and self-articulation strengthens critical thinking; a peer style works by reducing social distance and uncertainty, which decreases the felt need to verify alternatives. Interaction style thus shapes not just comfort but the depth of reasoning users apply.
Beyond Unimodal Perspectives: Generative Retrieval with Multimodal SemanticsSIGIR
uses Generate item identifiers using text and images together by aligning semantic meanings across both modalities so they pull toward shared concepts.
why it works It works because objects truly are multimodal—a chair looks and sounds a certain way. By forcing the text and image representations to be close to each other (alignment), you teach the model that they are the same thing, making both modalities contribute to one consistent identity.
the deeper reason
The core task is combining images, text, and audio into unified item codes for retrieval. The method works because each modality carries unique information: text may describe function, audio may reveal tone, images reveal appearance. When combined naively, one modality dominates the representation space, drowning out others. Cross-modal alignment forces the learned codes to respect each modality's signal equally by making codes from different inputs agree. This balance preserves all three viewpoints in the final representation, so retrieval decisions benefit from the full, diverse signal rather than a narrow slice.
Domain-Specific Reranking: When is Adaptation Worth the Cost?SIGIR
uses A model trained on a few hundred labeled examples within a specialized domain performs as well as models trained on much larger domain-adaptive pretraining.
why it works It works because generic pretraining teaches broad patterns but adjust on domain examples teaches the specific distinctions that matter. When domain data is scarce, adjust focus beats pretraining breadth because the model concentrates on exactly what the domain needs.
the deeper reason
The system asks whether domain-specific pretraining helps rerankers in specialized fields where labeled data is scarce, testing against simpler approaches that just adjust on a few hundred labeled examples. The finding suggests that when labeled training data is truly limited, simple in-domain adjust absorbs as much signal as the domain-specialized pretraining requires, so the extra complexity may not be justified. This works because with few examples, the model's learning capacity is the bottleneck; sophisticated pretraining strategies help when data is abundant but become overkill when the model can already memorize the limited labeled set.
RAPO: Reason-Aware Preference Optimization for Factual Table Question Answering over Structured DataSIGIR
uses Align an answer-generating system to produce factually correct responses by learning from examples where correct and incorrect answers are annotated with their reasoning.
why it works It works because understanding why an answer is right or wrong teaches the system the causal structure of the data. Standard preference learning ignores this reasoning, missing the underlying principles. Reason-aware alignment uses these explanations to generalize better to unseen queries.
the deeper reason
Aligning AI language systems to produce factually correct table answers requires feedback, but simple preference pairs (answer A is better than B) hide why A works—whether it got the SQL right, chose the right column, or reasoned about filters correctly. The method augments preferences with explanations of the reasoning that makes one answer correct, then trains the model to learn from both the preference and the explanation. This works because reasoning traces ground the learning signal: if the model learns that 'filtering by date range' or 'summing the revenue column' leads to correctness, it internalizes the reasoning patterns that generalize beyond the specific examples. Unlike binary preferences that only signal which answer is better, reason-augmented feedback teaches the underlying rules. Applied to structured data queries, this means the model learns which query semantics (joins, aggregations, filters) actually correspond to correct table logic, not just which output looks better in isolation.
TRACE: Term-level Reasoning And Chain-of-thought Enhanced distillation for E-commerce Multi-modal Relevance LearningSIGIR
uses Train the model to reason about which query terms are satisfied by text versus images, step by step, then teach a fast model to replicate this term-aware reasoning.
why it works It works because decomposing reasoning into term-level steps grounds the model's logic in concrete query parts. This prevents the model from relying on spurious correlations. When you transfer step-by-step reasoning to a smaller model, you preserve the interpretable logic that made the larger model reliable.
the deeper reason
E-commerce relevance depends on matching both text and images to queries, but existing methods cannot explain which part of a product satisfied which part of the query. AI language systems can reason through this, but their auto-regressive generation is too slow for real-time ranking. This paper trains the model to output step-by-step reasoning aligned to individual query terms, then distills this fine-grained reasoning to a lightweight model. The principle is that grounding reasoning in term-by-term matching creates decomposable, verifiable logic that can be efficiently encoded in parameters. When you distill reasoning that explicitly maps query terms to visual and textual evidence, the smaller model inherits this structured knowledge, enabling deployment at scale. The multi-modal matching becomes interpretable and fast simultaneously.
Labadain Chat: A Conversational Agent for the Tetun LanguageSIGIR
uses Adjust a general-purpose language model to Tetun by teaching it language-specific patterns through prompting.
why it works It works because language models are flexible functions that adjust their outputs based on training examples and instructions; showing the model Tetun patterns teaches it to recognize and produce the language correctly.
the deeper reason
The core task is adapting general-purpose conversation models to serve speakers of low-resource languages fairly. The underlying principle is that a language-agnostic model trained on high-resource data can be specialized through targeted prompting strategies that teach it language-specific patterns without full retraining. This works because modern models encode rich compositional structure—they can learn to follow instructions about how to shift their output toward different language characteristics once shown examples. For Tetun, where training data is sparse but the language structure exists, strategic prompts that ground the model in Tetun conventions act as guides that redirect the general-purpose weights toward language-faithful output. This approach extends access to AI services to marginalized communities by making customization practical without requiring thousands of hours of annotated speech.
Building Foundations for Information Retrieval in Extremely Low-Resource Ethnic Languages: Evidence from TanzaniaSIGIR
uses Learn to translate between low-resource ethnic languages and Kiswahili using parallel sentences and speech recordings.
why it works It works because function learning from examples captures the systematic correspondence between languages: when you see enough pairs of sentences in both languages expressing the same meaning, the function naturally learns which words and phrases map to each other, enabling translation without hand-crafted rules.
the deeper reason
The goal is enabling retrieval in extremely low-resource languages where no digital resources yet exist. The foundational principle is that cross-lingual retrieval becomes possible when you have parallel text and speech data—equivalent sentences in two languages teach the system which concepts map across language boundaries. This principle applies because information need and expression differ from language to language, yet the underlying concepts and facts should align; a sentence about weather in Hehe should retrieve the same weather information when searched in Kiswahili. By collecting parallel corpora and speech, the project creates the minimal infrastructure on which any retrieval system can build: without these paired examples, no automated method can bridge the gap. This directly solves the access problem: speakers of small languages gain pathways to existing digital knowledge by routing through more-resourced languages as intermediaries.
User Search Behavior and Knowledge Effects in Hybrid Search EnvironmentSIGIR
uses Learn to predict search behavior patterns from eye-tracking and interaction data, conditioned on user knowledge level and cognitive processing ability.
why it works It works because cognitive level and knowledge determine how users process information: an expert scans differently than a novice, and focus reveal understanding. Modeling these patterns from data automatically learns how knowledge and cognition shape behavior without manual encoding.
the deeper reason
When users search in systems that blend traditional keyword search with AI chat, their strategy depends on their background knowledge and cognitive level. The principle is that deeper cognitive processing requires different information access; someone learning a topic for the first time needs different support than an expert refining understanding. This principle applies because knowledge levels affect both what users know to search for and how they interpret results: novices ask broad exploratory questions and struggle to evaluate sources, while experts ask targeted questions and can quickly judge relevance. Eye-tracking reveals these differences in focus and interaction speed. By measuring cognitive development alongside search behavior, the research shows which interface designs serve which learners, solving an educational challenge: adaptive systems can adjust between modes—guiding novices with structured exploration, letting experts quickly narrow results—based on demonstrated knowledge.
Connecting the dots

Different problems, the same few guarantees

Line the ideas up and the surprise is how few there are, and how each rests on a plain guarantee. Ranking works because only order matters. Similarity works because meaning becomes distance. Estimating chances works because averages of enough observations don't lie. Spreading across a network works because neighbours are alike. Minimising error works because a slope always points the way down. Different problems, the same handful of reasons to trust the answer.

And one idea now runs through all the others: learning the rule from examples. But look closely and it doesn't replace the older math — it rides on it. A learned recommender still turns meaning into nearness and still ranks by a score; a learned language system still estimates chances and focuses on what's relevant. The 2026 story isn't that data mining stopped being mathematical — it's that a learned layer now sits on the same small, well-understood toolkit the field has always trusted.

Every good answer this field gives is one of a few mathematical questions in disguise — what's nearest, what ranks highest, how likely, what actually causes it — and each is trusted for a reason you can state in a sentence. Know the few reasons and the whole field stops being magic.

Each paper's core mathematical idea and the reason it works were read from its abstract by a language model, named from a fixed plain vocabulary; the framing of each idea is written from first principles.
